Under rule 0-10, an investment company is deemed a small entity if it, together with other investment companies in the same group of related investment companies, has net assets of $50 million or less as of the end of its most recent fiscal year.[16] A group of related investment companies is defined, with respect to management companies, as two or more management companies (including series thereof) that (i) hold themselves out to investors as related companies for purposes of investment and investor services; and (ii) either (1) have a common investment adviser or have investment advisers that are affiliated persons of each other; or (2) have a common administrator.[17] Under rule 0-7, an investment adviser is deemed a small entity if it: (i) has RAUM [18] of less than $25 million (the “RAUM Threshold”); [19] (ii) did not have total assets [20] of $5 million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (the “Total Assets Threshold”); and (iii) does not control, is not controlled by, and is not under common control with (a “control relationship”) another investment adviser that has assets under management of $25 million or more, or ( printed page 69957) any person (other than a natural person) that had total assets of $5 million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (the “Control Relationship Threshold”).
In January 2026, the Commission proposed amendments to the investment company and investment adviser “small entity” definitions. Specifically, the Commission proposed to:
Amend rule 0-10 for funds to: (i) increase the net asset threshold for funds from $50 million to $10 billion; and (ii) refer, for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related funds, to a “family of investment companies” as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN rather than to a “group of related investment companies” as used in the current rule;
Amend rule 0-7 for investment advisers to increase the RAUM Threshold below which an investment adviser is considered to be a “small entity” from $25 million to $1 billion and to conform the assets under management threshold in the Control Relationship Threshold with the revisions made to the RAUM Threshold;
Amend Form ADV to revise the instructions and Item 12 of Part 1A of Form ADV, including through making conforming changes to Form ADV, and amend rule 203-3 providing a continuing hardship exemption from electronic filing requirements; and
Amend rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission to make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds in these rules by order every 10 years in accordance with an inflation adjustment mechanism.
The Commission also requested comment on whether to amend the Total Assets Threshold, as well as the total assets threshold contained in the Control Relationship Threshold, in rule 0-7.
The Commission received approximately 20 comments on the proposed amendments. Commenters generally supported the proposal's goal to modernize the “small entity” definitions.[21] These commenters noted that the current rules are out of date and stated that the proposed amendments would help calibrate the Commission's analysis of the regulatory and compliance costs for small entities under the RFA.[22] Some commenters suggested modifications to the proposal, such as a higher fund net asset threshold, alternative non-RAUM Thresholds, different mechanisms for future threshold adjustments, elimination of the adviser Total Assets Threshold, or different treatment of certain entities.[23] Some commenters expressed concern that the proposal would diminish investor protections and suggested lower asset thresholds.[24] After consideration of the comments received, and as discussed in more detail below, the Commission is adopting the amendments largely as proposed but with some modifications in response to comments.
B. Overview of the Final Amendments
We are amending the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” under the Investment Company Act and the Advisers Act for purposes of the RFA, largely as proposed, but with modifications:
Raising the Fund Net Asset Threshold. As proposed, the Commission is raising the net asset threshold for funds from $50 million to $10 billion.[25]
Amending the Fund Group Definition. As proposed, the Commission is, for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related funds, replacing the term “group of related investment companies” with “family of investment companies” as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN.
Raising the Adviser RAUM Threshold. As proposed, the Commission is raising the RAUM Threshold from $25 million to $1 billion, and making conforming amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold to reflect the increased RAUM Threshold.[26] In a change from the proposal, the Commission is amending the Control Relationship Threshold to help advisers understand how to calculate the threshold.
Eliminating the Adviser Total Assets Threshold. In a change from the proposal, the Commission is eliminating the $5 million Total Assets Threshold, and making conforming amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold to reflect that the Commission is eliminating the Total Assets Threshold.
Periodic Inflation Adjustments. As proposed, the Commission is amending rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission to make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds by order every 10 years in accordance with the inflation adjustment mechanism set forth in section II.C below (the “Inflation Adjustment Mechanism”).
Conforming Amendments to Form ADV and the Hardship Exemption Rule. As proposed, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV, the uniform application for investment adviser registration and report form by exempt reporting advisers, and rule 203-3(b), which sets forth conditions for certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from the requirement to make Advisers Act filings electronically with the Investment Adviser Registration Depository (the “IARD”).[27] The amendments are designed to reflect the Commission's amendments to the RAUM Threshold, the Control Relationship Threshold, and their corresponding periodic Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. In a change from the proposal, the Commission is also making additional conforming amendments to Form ADV and rule 203-3(b) to reflect the determination at adoption to eliminate the Total Assets Threshold.
Smaller firms play an important role in the asset management industry.[28] We are mindful that smaller firms may face disproportionate compliance burdens compared to larger firms.[29] For example, compliance costs—such as staff time, recordkeeping, cybersecurity costs, and reliance on outside expertise or market data—often do not scale with firm size,[30] and have increased, while client fees have decreased.[31] We also are mindful that failure to consider the impact of regulations on small entities could risk reducing innovation, competitiveness, and new market ( printed page 69958) participants.[32] The Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small entities, including through performing regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA.
The final amendments are designed to help ensure the Commission's RFA analyses capture a more meaningful population of “small entities” so the Commission can continue to address the special concerns of small businesses. Updating the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” is appropriate to reflect the substantial growth in, and distribution of, regulatory assets under management and net assets over the decades since these thresholds were set.[33] The updates to the definitions reflect more reliable and consistent metrics for whether an adviser or fund is small, compared to those in the current rules.
Some commenters stated that the proposed amendments would classify too many funds or advisers as small (effectively leading the Commission to prioritize benefits of large funds and advisers instead of truly small funds and advisers),[34] or otherwise could result in regulatory arbitrage between investment advisers and broker-dealers [35] and diminish investor protections.[36] As explained below, the final amendments will not classify too many funds or advisers as small. The final amendments also will not diminish investor protections. Designating an entity as a small entity does not reduce investor protection. Investor protection is a concern regardless of the size of an entity. The purpose of the small entity definition is, in part, to ensure that the Commission considers whether its rules are appropriately calibrated so that smaller entities are not subject to regulations that may be disproportionately burdensome relative to the benefits or improvements in investor protection. The final amendments will enhance the Commission's rulemaking process by helping ensure the RFA analyses reflect current economic realities by incorporating the evolution of adviser and fund growth since the rules were first adopted, as other commenters stated.[37]
One commenter stated that the proposal did not appear to evaluate the investor-protection consequences of the proposed amendments and asserted the proposal focused primarily on industry size, rather than regulatory risk or compliance capacity. It outlined certain areas that the Commission should quantify and analyze in this regard, in particular to focus any regulatory relief on genuinely small entities and in a risk-based manner.[38] Because the final amendments primarily affect the process by which the Commission considers potential impacts on small entities, including benefits and costs of future rulemaking on small entities, the final amendments will not have any immediate impact on investor protection. Rather, the final amendments will require the Commission to consider and address the potential impacts of future rulemaking on small entities, including effects on investor protection.
Separately, the methodology for the proposed thresholds reflects that advisory fees are generally scaled with an adviser's assets under management, where greater advisory fees can support an increased compliance capacity. The updated thresholds also will allow the Commission to more appropriately address in future rulemakings, in a risk-based manner, concerns that are unique to those entities that should be deemed small entities in view of the growth in assets since the rules were adopted and the appropriateness of any regulatory accommodations that may be provided to small entities.
While conducting RFA analyses in future rulemakings, the Commission can take into account any potential for regulatory arbitrage between broker-dealers and investment advisers and adjust its future rules accordingly. The Commission carefully weighs the economic impact of its rules on all regulated entities, including small businesses, and tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of the particular entities regulated. In this way, the Commission works to meet its mandate under the Federal securities laws while at the same time considering any potentially disproportionate costs and regulatory burdens for small entities. The Commission intends to continue this careful, measured regulation that addresses small business concerns within the protections of the Federal securities laws.
A. Amendments to Rule 0-10 Under the Investment Company Act
1. Raising the Net Asset Threshold
The Commission is amending the net asset threshold for small funds, as proposed. The final rule will amend paragraph (a) of rule 0-10 to increase the net asset threshold from $50 million to $10 billion and, as discussed in more detail in section II.C below, establish a mechanism to inflation-adjust this figure every ten years. The increase accounts for the overall growth in the fund industry since the $50 million threshold was originally set in 1982.[39] At that time, 62.4% of funds were deemed “small entities,” but by 2024, the share of funds deemed “small entities” had fallen to 0.6%.[40] Raising the net asset threshold in rule 0-10 to reflect growth in the investment company industry over the past decades will improve the utility of RFA analyses by more closely reflecting the population of funds that does not have the same competitive advantages as larger fund families (for instance, due to economies of scale when these larger families perform certain compliance and other operational functions in-house).[41] It also will more closely reflect the population of funds that does not have the same negotiating power as larger ( printed page 69959) fund families when retaining service providers to perform compliance and operational functions.
In determining how to calibrate the amended threshold, the Commission considered the distribution of assets across individual funds and fund families, with the goal of ensuring that the proportion of funds that may face greater challenges in complying with Commission regulations due to their size be included in the small entity definition. Specifically, the Commission analyzed data reported on Form N-CEN to sort families of investment companies into percentiles according to their cumulative average total net assets. The Commission further analyzed this data to determine the percentage of individual funds and the percentage of average total net assets represented by each percentile.[42] At proposal, the Commission estimated that, as of December 2024, fund families at or below the 80th percentile threshold of $10.04 billion in net assets accounted for 22.91% of individual funds and only 2.13% of fund assets.[43] The analysis that formed the basis for the proposed threshold reflects that the assets of the investment company industry are heavily concentrated at the largest fund families, and these largest fund families not only manage a large majority of assets in the industry, but also account for a majority of the individual funds.[44]
Most commenters supported generally raising the net asset threshold from the current level to account for growth in the industry.[45] Several commenters supported raising the net asset threshold to $10 billion in particular, stating that this threshold appropriately reflects current market size and structure.[46] One of the commenters specifically expressed its support for the distribution-based methodology used to reach the proposed $10 billion threshold for funds.[47] This commenter, while supporting the proposal, further encouraged the Commission to adjust the threshold to $12 billion to account for growth in the industry since the date of the data underlying the proposal. Some other commenters expressed concerns that $10 billion is too high, one of whom requested that the Commission quantify and analyze the investor-protection consequences of the higher threshold and another expressed concerns about the effects of entities with billions of dollars in assets being deemed to be “small” ( i.e., very large firms could receive regulatory accommodations intended for smaller firms with limited regulatory capacity, which the commenter indicated could cause smaller firms to lose the advantages the RFA provides them and have negative investor protection consequences).[48] One commenter suggested adjusting the thresholds adopted in the 1998 amendments for inflation, resulting in a $100 million threshold, or alternatively using the SBA's small entity standard based on $40 million in gross receipts.[49] Another commenter, asserting that the proposed threshold is too high, suggested defining “small entities” as those at or below the 20th percentile of aggregate fund family net assets using a distribution methodology based on Form N-CEN data.[50]
After considering these comments, we are, as proposed, raising the net asset threshold to $10 billion for funds. We agree with commenters' statements that the increased threshold would better reflect the growth in the fund industry and aid the Commission's analysis of regulatory and compliance costs on small funds.[51] Based on analysis of the distribution of data discussed above, we are adopting a “small entity” definition that incorporates a $10 billion net asset threshold, which continues to correspond to the 80th percentile threshold in that distribution-based analysis.[52] While the amended threshold will deem some relatively large individual funds “small” for purposes of the RFA, such an outcome is consistent with the economies of scale rationale for aggregating funds within a family. A single large fund with no other related funds will bear similar regulatory costs to several smaller, related funds that collectively represent a similar level of net assets. Therefore, aggregating assets across fund families reflects the Commission's understanding that funds within a complex typically use the same administrative, management, and compliance systems to oversee all the funds within the complex, so fees imposed on the fund by the adviser or administrator typically reflect economies of scale that the adviser or administrator achieves from managing other funds.
While the Commission seeks to ensure that funds and fund families that may face greater challenges with regulatory compliance due to their size be deemed small entities, we are also mindful that setting the threshold too high has the potential to be counterproductive and to undermine the purpose of the Commission's RFA analyses. A higher threshold would result in a larger pool of small entities and therefore would increase the number of small entities needed to be affected by a rule for the rule to “have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities,” which could lead to fewer RFA analyses being performed.[53] Setting the threshold too high might also inadvertently lead to the Commission overlooking issues that concern the smallest entities when the Commission attempts to tailor its rules, and instead focusing primarily on issues of more general concern to the industry. Such an outcome might have the potential to perpetuate larger funds' advantages in the market, to the detriment of the smaller funds that the RFA was designed to protect.[54] Accordingly, the Commission's amended threshold is meant to identify a level below which a meaningful proportion of funds would be deemed small entities, but above which the size of, and concentration of assets in, fund families increases to such an extent that treating individual funds within those families as small entities would not be consistent with the goals of the RFA. We are therefore not adopting a smaller threshold than the proposed $10 billion threshold. We are also therefore not adopting a threshold of $12 billion as one commenter suggested. We do not believe this change from the proposed ( printed page 69960) approach, based on one-year market movements, would be appropriate, as the proposed threshold was designed to be stable and flexible enough to guide Commission analysis for the next 10 years and not to reflect short-term market fluctuations.
We are not adjusting the current threshold for inflation, as some commenters suggested, but rather are retaining the proposed distribution-based methodology as the basis for the final rules' threshold adjustment. A net asset threshold of $100 million (the result of inflation-adjusting the current rule's threshold) would cover less than 3% of funds and less than .03% of fund assets and would constrain future Commission analysis of small entity issues to this limited group.[55] Further, we are not adopting a threshold based on a gross receipts analysis. As discussed in the Proposing Release, gross receipts are not well suited to the fund industry, primarily because the Commission does not have or collect data for gross receipts of registered investment companies.[56] As the Proposing Release also discussed, funds primarily generate revenue through capital appreciation and other investment returns rather than receipts from the sale of goods or services, and a fund's investment returns may be attributable primarily to its particular investment strategy, meaning that two funds of identical size but pursuing different investment strategies may produce vastly different returns.[57] Commenters did not address or dispute these rationales for using an approach other than a gross receipts analysis.
We are also not adopting an approach that defines small entities as fund families with net assets at or below the 20th percentile as determined annually. The $10 billion net asset threshold and corresponding percentile we are adopting were derived from a distribution analysis particular to that data and set of facts and, therefore, is not necessarily indicative of the proportion of funds that should be deemed small entities in the future. A fixed percentile may become stale over time as the size and distribution of fund family net assets changes. Additionally, as discussed above, we continue to believe that a lower net asset threshold would not appropriately define “small entities” for future Commission analysis.[58]
Some commenters recommended aligning the adviser and fund thresholds so that if either a fund or an adviser qualifies as small, both would be treated as small.[59] These commenters expressed concerns that a mismatch between the fund and adviser thresholds could produce anomalous outcomes where, for example, an adviser managing a few billion dollars is not considered “small,” while the funds it manages are. We continue to believe that independent asset thresholds for advisers and funds are appropriate. Advisers and funds are separate industries with different regulatory requirements and resources available to comply with these requirements. Therefore, the status of a fund as small and not dominant in its field is not indicative of its adviser being similarly situated, or vice versa.
2. Group Definition Amendments
As proposed, we are amending rule 0-10 to replace the term “group of related investment companies” with “family of investment companies,” as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN.[60] Currently, while the “small entity” designation applies to individual funds, whether any individual fund is deemed small depends upon the aggregate net assets of all funds within its respective “group of related investment companies.” The change from using the term “group of related investment companies” to using “family of investment companies” in the small entity definition will enable the Commission to rely on information that is already reported on Form N-CEN to identify small entities for purposes of RFA analyses and to more efficiently consider whether future adjustments to the net asset threshold are warranted. For comparison, the table below provides the existing definition of “group of related investment companies” from rule 0-10 alongside the existing definition of “family of investment companies” from Form N-CEN:
Commenters expressed support for the proposed changes.[61] They agreed that the Commission should leverage data that is already collected in Form N-CEN, so as not to impose the additional burden of a new reporting requirement related to the “group of related investment companies” definition.[62] Some commenters, while expressing support for the proposed changes, also offered views on how the “family of investment companies” definition in Form N-CEN might be improved.[63]
After considering commenters' input, we are adopting a final definition that uses “family of investment companies,” as proposed. As described in the Proposing Release, the definition of “family of investment companies” serves a substantially similar purpose to the definition of “group of related investment companies” in seeking to group together funds that hold themselves out to investors as related (the “holding out prong”) and that share an investment adviser or key service provider (an administrator for a “group of related investment companies” or underwriter for a “family of investment companies”).[64] We acknowledge that specific differences from the “group of related investment companies” concept may produce different outcomes at the margins, such as the extent to which an insurance company's separate account is aggregated (with the insurance company's general account, as well as with other separate accounts) to determine whether individual separate accounts are small entities.[65] Notwithstanding the differences between the two terms, we continue to anticipate, as discussed in the Proposing Release, that funds that are part of the same “family of investment companies” are likely to experience similar economies of scale as those funds that are part of the same “group of related investment companies.” Examples of potential cost savings due to economies of scale might include complex-wide policies and procedures and recordkeeping systems, a shared chief compliance officer or board members, and one legal and compliance function that services the whole complex.
We are not amending the current definition of “family of investment companies” in Form N-CEN as some commenters have suggested. One commenter suggested amending the Form N-CEN definition so that it does not aggregate funds based on a shared principal underwriter, stating that funds that share an underwriter do not necessarily share compliance infrastructure.[66] This commenter, however, did not address the second prong of the Form N-CEN definition that requires registered investment companies to hold themselves out as related companies for purposes of investment and investor services in order to be grouped in the same family of investment companies, which in our view is likely indicative that two funds share compliance and operational infrastructure. Another commenter suggested that the Form N-CEN definition should aggregate separate accounts if they have the same insurance company sponsor or depositor, similar to the current “group of related investment companies” definition that aggregates assets of the general account and all other separate ( printed page 69962) accounts of the insurance company.[67] While this commenter stated that this approach would be appropriate because the financial guarantees of variable contracts issued by the same insurance company are backed by the financial strength and claims-paying ability of the same general account, regardless of whether those contracts are supported by different separate accounts, the commenter did acknowledge that the suggested change would likely not significantly change how separate accounts are grouped for small entity definitional purposes.
As other commenters have noted, leveraging data from an existing definition does not impose an additional burden on registrants of having to amend their filings. If we were to amend Form N-CEN as these two commenters suggest, registrants would have to review and possibly amend their filings, reducing or eliminating the benefit of using existing data. Our final approach reflects a view that the burden on other registrants of amending Form N-CEN would not provide commensurate benefits in any incremental improvements to the Commission's analysis of small entities. Further, the “family of investment companies” definition from Form N-CEN and associated data collection have long been used in assisting the Commission's analysis of multiple funds across the same family of investment companies.[68]
B. Amendments To Rule 0-7 Under the Advisers Act
As proposed, the final amendments will raise the RAUM Threshold from $25 million to $1 billion and add the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.[69] Rule 0-7 currently provides that an adviser is a small entity if it has assets under management of less than $25 million “or such higher amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act.” [70] As proposed, the final amendments remove the phrase “or such higher amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act (15 U.S.C. 80b-3a(a)(1)(A)).” [71] The final amendments are designed to update the RAUM Threshold to reflect the growth of advisers' assets under management over time.[72]
a. Consideration of Alternative Non-RAUM Thresholds
As proposed, the final amendments use an RAUM-based metric for threshold purposes. In the Proposing Release, we discussed feedback the Commission received suggesting alternatives to an asset-based approach to identifying small advisers and requested comment on alternatives to the RAUM Threshold.[73] Some commenters suggested the Commission should replace the RAUM Threshold with a non-RAUM threshold, such as a threshold based on revenue,[74] number of employees,[75] officers, owners, clients, non-accredited investors, or a combination thereof.[76] These commenters expressed concern that RAUM may not reflect the breadth of compliance resources that advisers may or may not have available.[77] According to these commenters, certain other non-RAUM-based thresholds would better evidence compliance burdens and risks of small advisers.[78] Other commenters opposed replacing the RAUM Threshold with a non-RAUM-based threshold.[79]
After considering comments, we are not persuaded to replace the RAUM Threshold with a non-RAUM-based threshold.[80] The Commission has long used RAUM to appropriately differentiate between small and other advisers to identify a universe of entities that are not dominant in the field, a principal element of the small entity status under the RFA.[81] As some commenters stated, RAUM is a meaningful proxy for business scale and compliance capacity,[82] and RAUM metrics directly correlate to the financial resources available for compliance.[83]
In contrast, a non-RAUM-based threshold would not be as reliable a metric to determine whether an adviser is small for RFA purposes as an RAUM-based threshold. An employee-based standard raises implementation challenges in appropriately addressing the use of service providers and outsourcing by investment advisers, which could distort the extent to which the number of an adviser's own employees reflects its actual resources and size. A commenter agreed, stating that an employee-based metric would penalize operational efficiency and outsourcing.[84] This commenter cautioned that moving to an employee-based metric would incentivize the misclassification of staff as contractors to maintain “small entity” status. Similarly, a threshold based on the number of clients or non-accredited investors also would not necessarily reflect an adviser's ability to devote resources towards compliance.[85] For example, while an adviser could have only one fund as a client, that fund could be large both by RAUM and number of investors resulting in the adviser maintaining the capacity to devote significant resources towards compliance-related matters. Conversely, an adviser may have a large number of clients, but those clients' assets could represent a small amount of RAUM, so that the adviser would not have economies of scale comparable to a larger adviser with significantly more RAUM. Likewise, we are not persuaded ( printed page 69963) that a threshold based on the number of officers or owners would be a meaningful measure of adviser size for RFA purposes, because those metrics do not directly relate to how an adviser would scale resources in connection with compliance. A revenue-based threshold also would not provide as meaningful a measure of adviser size for RFA purposes as an RAUM-based threshold. Advisers have diverse fee structures, and as a result, annual receipts may not correlate with firm scale, operational complexity, or available compliance resources. A commenter agreed, stating that revenue recognition practices may differ among firms depending on their accounting methods, further reducing comparability and administrative simplicity.[86]
The Commission has ready access to RAUM data for the types of advisers that are generally subject to our rules, not just those registered with us.[87] Commenters agreed, with one commenter stating that it supported the RAUM-based threshold, in part, because it was readily available to the Commission.[88] For example, while the Commission collects RAUM information from both SEC-registered advisers and exempt reporting advisers, it does not collect revenue information from either type of adviser, and it does not collect employee counts from exempt reporting advisers.[89]
Using RAUM to distinguish between advisers is an approach that is broadly consistent with size standards generally under the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder, as well as advisers' existing reporting and compliance obligations. Congress has repeatedly differentiated the regulations to which an adviser is subject by using assets under management thresholds as size standards under the Advisers Act. For example, Advisers Act section 203(m) sets forth an assets under management threshold for the private fund adviser exemption from registration, and Advisers Act section 203A(a)(2) sets forth an assets under management threshold for mid-sized advisers. Some commenters agreed.[90] For example, one commenter stated that it appreciated the Commission's explanation for proposing to maintain an RAUM-based threshold, including the view that RAUM aligns with existing regulatory frameworks.[91] Another commenter supported maintaining an RAUM metric, in part, because it is well understood and widely used.[92]
A commenter recommended that, no matter the approach, the Commission should establish a structured methodology that grounds any definition of “small entity” in empirical data.[93] The final amendments to the RAUM Threshold address this comment because they help ensure that rule 0-7 continues to use a structured methodology that grounds the definition of “small entity” in empirical data, namely RAUM, as discussed more fully in section II.B.1.b.
b. The $1 Billion RAUM Threshold
As proposed, we are raising the RAUM Threshold from $25 million to $1 billion. Commenters generally agreed that the current RAUM Threshold is too low.[94] Most commenters supported raising the RAUM Threshold to correct the misalignment between the current threshold and the current economic reality created by decades of industry growth,[95] the fact that capital has become concentrated among a small number of advisers,[96] and the structural changes in the investment management industry since the 1998 amendments, including that in 2010, the Dodd-Frank Act raised the SEC-registration threshold, resulting in fewer smaller advisers registering with the Commission.[97] In contrast, one commenter asserted it is counterintuitive that advisers' significantly increased RAUM supports their designation as small entities.[98] Another commenter stated that the Commission should not base the RAUM Threshold on the fact that there are some very large advisers.[99]
We continue to believe that the current RAUM Threshold is too low. The final RAUM Threshold is designed to capture the types and numbers of investment advisers that the Commission now considers to be “small” in light of industry growth since the 1998 amendments.[100] We disagree that industry asset growth or the presence of very large advisers undermines basing “small entity” status on an RAUM Threshold or the particular RAUM Threshold we are adopting.[101] It is appropriate to consider the size of the investment management industry as a whole, as well as how the size is distributed across advisers, in determining adviser size thresholds under the RFA, because it helps ensure that such size thresholds are relevant to the adviser industry. What is “small” is an inherently relative exercise, and in an industry that ranges to very large advisers managing trillions of dollars in assets, even small advisers may manage sizeable amounts of assets. As discussed below, the distribution of advisory assets skewing heavily towards large advisers only exacerbates this effect.
Most commenters supported raising the adviser RAUM Threshold specifically from $25 million to $1 billion, saying that the proposed threshold would better reflect current market realities.[102] Others expressed concern that the proposed threshold would be too high because it would classify too many advisers as small.[103] One commenter cautioned that the Commission should not raise the adviser RAUM Threshold any higher than the proposed $1 billion threshold because it would obscure the impacts of rulemaking on small entities and deprive the public of a clear articulation of, and opportunity to comment on, those impacts.[104]
Some commenters recommended increasing the RAUM Threshold by a lesser amount than proposed.[105] For example, a commenter recommended that the Commission should increase the current RAUM Threshold for inflation since the 1998 amendments, instead, raising it to about $50 million.[106] Another commenter recommended amending the RAUM Threshold to align with the lowest 20th ( printed page 69964) percentile of advisers.[107] We are not persuaded to increase the RAUM Threshold by a lesser amount than proposed because we are concerned that the commenters' recommended thresholds would not account for the fact that the distribution of RAUM across all advisers is highly uneven. As discussed in the Proposing Release, some advisers report having virtually zero RAUM, while a significant amount of the total RAUM is concentrated at the top 5 percent of advisers.[108] As discussed in the Proposing Release, the proposed $1 billion RAUM Threshold would represent 75 percent of advisers, but only under 3 percent of the total RAUM in the industry.[109] Therefore, we continue to believe that in light of the significant concentration of RAUM with the very largest advisers, the $1 billion RAUM Threshold will strike an appropriate balance between the level of RAUM per small adviser and the proportion of total RAUM in the industry.[110]
Some commenters recommended that the Commission provide certain data to support its proposal.[111] For example, a commenter recommended the Commission provide data concerning investor exposure, which the commenter appeared to define as total investor assets managed by firms that would newly qualify as small entities.[112] Another commenter expressed concern that the proposal did not provide details about why the RAUM Threshold should be $1 billion and not another number.[113] This commenter expressed concern that the Commission described the proposed amendment as seeking to separate those who are “dominant in their field” from those who are “not dominant in” their field, but did not explain the “dominance” test or why that test would be appropriate in this circumstance.
Other commenters, however, expressed appreciation that the Commission chose the $1 billion figure based on data, which demonstrated industry concentration.[114] Another commenter stated that it appreciated the Commission's thoughtful and well-reasoned analysis supporting the proposed $1 billion RAUM Threshold.[115] This commenter discussed how the Proposing Release carefully considered both the significant concentration of assets among the largest advisers and the RFA's requirement that a small entity be one that is not “dominant in its field.” The commenter stated that although the proposal would classify a substantial proportion of advisers as small entities, the Commission explained why this result would be appropriate given the comparatively modest amount of assets managed by these firms relative to the largest advisers.
The Commission proposed the $1 billion RAUM Threshold in light of the RFA's default definitions of the terms “small business” and “small organization,” which define such entities as those that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their field.[116] The RFA provides that an agency may establish its own definitions of “small business” and “small organization” under certain circumstances.[117] Rule 0-7's Control Relationship Threshold is designed to address the element of the RFA's default definitions that require the “small business” or “small organization” to be independently owned and operated,[118] whereas the Commission proposed the $1 billion RAUM Threshold to address the requirement that a “small business” or “small organization” not be dominant in its field.[119]
As discussed in the Proposing Release, the Commission used Form ADV reporting data from SEC-registered advisers and exempt reporting advisers to analyze the distribution of investment advisers and RAUM, including data concerning the percentile of advisers, individual RAUM of advisers at the percentile, the total number of all advisers at or below the percentile, and the total RAUM of all advisers at or below the percentile in millions and as a percent.[120] The Commission estimated that the proposed $1 billion RAUM Threshold would still represent under 3 percent of total RAUM in the industry.[121] The Commission published these summary statistics in the Proposing Release, showing the distribution of assets across firms, and the proportion of entities that would qualify under the proposed and other potential thresholds.[122] As discussed in the Proposing Release, these data revealed that the distribution of RAUM across all advisers is highly uneven, in part due to some advisers reporting zero or virtually zero RAUM, and more significantly because of the concentration of RAUM with the very largest advisers in the industry. The Commission compared data concerning the proposed RAUM Threshold to historical definitions, noting that the proposed RAUM Threshold would not result in the same proportion of advisers that were “small entities” as a result of the 1998 amendments.[123]
After considering comments, and in light of the RFA's default definitions and our data analysis, we continue to believe that a $1 billion RAUM Threshold is appropriate, and we do not believe that the final rules would inappropriately afford larger firms RFA accommodations that are intended for small entities.[124] A size standard threshold that is set too high could inadvertently cause Commission RFA analysis to mistakenly focus on issues of more general concern to the industry, instead of on issues that particularly impact smaller entities, as required by the RFA. Conversely, we are concerned that setting the RAUM Threshold too low would not be consistent with the RFA's default definition of “small business” and “small organization,” because it would exclude advisers that are not dominant in their field. We believe such advisers may have fewer compliance resources, and therefore, would benefit from being considered a “small business” or “small organization” under the RFA. Although using $1 billion as the RAUM Threshold would classify a large proportion of investment advisers as small, this is a reasonable and appropriate result for purposes of our analyses under the RFA, in part due to the relative amount of ( printed page 69965) assets managed by these advisers compared to the largest advisers, i.e., those dominant in their field. We continue to believe that a $1 billion RAUM Threshold strikes an appropriate balance between the level of RAUM per small adviser and the proportion of total RAUM in the industry captured by the new threshold.[125]
A commenter recommended that “exempt reporting advisers” should have a higher adviser RAUM Threshold than SEC-registered advisers.[126] An “exempt reporting adviser” is an investment adviser that qualifies for the exemption from registration under section 203(l) of the Advisers Act because it is an adviser solely to one or more venture capital funds, or under rule 203(m)-1 of the Advisers Act because it is an adviser solely to private funds and has assets under management in the United States of less than $150 million.[127] According to this commenter, Congress has chosen to subject exempt reporting advisers to different and generally less burdensome regulatory obligations and it would be inconsistent with the logic underlying the RFA and the Advisers Act to not assess the burden on exempt reporting advisers independently in recognition of Congress's intent to subject these businesses to different regulatory regimes. We are not persuaded to raise the RAUM Threshold higher for exempt reporting advisers than for SEC-registered advisers, because, in our experience, we do not believe exempt reporting advisers and SEC-registered advisers would be subject to different economies of scale that should impact their status as a small adviser. For example, in our experience, both types of advisers could have similar business models or operational structures that could allow them to achieve similar economies of scale to implement certain rules. If a future rulemaking, however, would have a different impact on exempt reporting advisers than on SEC-registered advisers, the Commission could address that in the future rulemaking.
As discussed above, some commenters recommended aligning the adviser and fund thresholds so that if either a fund complex or its adviser qualifies as small, both would be treated as small for purposes of the RFA.[128] We are not persuaded to implement this recommendation, for the reasons discussed above.
The current rule provides that an adviser is a small entity if it has assets under management of less than $25 million “or such higher amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act.” Advisers Act section 203A(a)(1)(A) prohibits advisers from registering with the SEC if they have assets under management below a certain amount. The Commission originally adopted the phrase in 1998 so the RAUM Threshold could increase in tandem with any increase in the minimum threshold for SEC registration.[129] That has not happened in practice, however, despite the SEC registration threshold increasing in 2010.[130] Accordingly, we proposed to remove “or such higher amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act (15 U.S.C. 80b-3a(a)(1)(A)),” because the revised RAUM Threshold would exceed and thus not align with the minimum threshold for adviser registration. The Commission did not receive any comments on this proposed change and is removing the phrase, as proposed.
2. The Total Assets Threshold
The final amendments eliminate the Total Assets Threshold, which currently excludes from the definition of small entity any adviser that has total assets of $5 million or more.[131] The Commission requested comment on whether to adjust or eliminate the Total Assets Threshold and proposed to amend the Total Assets Threshold to include an Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.[132]
The Total Assets Threshold was designed to enable the Commission to differentiate between small advisers and non-small advisers that may not have significant RAUM but do have significant assets related to a non-advisory line or component of their business.[133] The Total Assets Threshold also worked in concert with the Control Relationship Threshold in capturing common types of advisory industry affiliations.[134] The Commission had stated that an adviser in a control relationship with a large broker-dealer or other large financial services firm typically benefits from the financial and technical resources of the large firm, and that the large firm may handle much of the administrative and compliance needs of its affiliated adviser using resources not reflected in the adviser's client assets or business assets.[135]
Some commenters recommended eliminating the Total Assets Threshold, stating that total assets are not a reliable indicator of whether an adviser should be considered a small entity.[136] A commenter stated that total assets reflected on an adviser's balance sheet do not necessarily correlate with operational complexity, staffing levels, compliance capacity, or the scope of its advisory business.[137] This commenter stated that advisers may hold assets unrelated to their core advisory operations, including assets tied to non-advisory activities, temporary capital arrangements, or organizational structure, that do not meaningfully reflect firm size for RFA purposes. Another commenter stated that a balance sheet test can exclude advisers that are operationally small, while failing to meaningfully differentiate among advisers' ability to bear incremental compliance costs associated with Commission rulemakings.[138] According to this commenter, where an adviser has de minimis RAUM but substantial non-advisory assets, the adviser's investment advisory business is, by definition, not a meaningful component of the firm as a whole. The commenter indicated that in that circumstance, total assets may reflect the scale of the firm, taken as a whole, but does not reflect the resources that the firm is willing or able to allocate to an immaterial advisory business line. This commenter stated that when new adviser-specific requirements increase fixed compliance costs, an enterprise with substantial non-advisory assets but minimal RAUM may rationally choose to exit the advisory business rather than ( printed page 69966) devote incremental resources to comply with the rules affecting an immaterial portion of its overall operations.
After considering comments, we are eliminating the Total Assets Threshold. It is not necessary to maintain the Total Assets Threshold, because the RAUM Threshold and Control Relationship Threshold, as amended, are more reliable indicators of whether an adviser is a small entity for purposes of the RFA. Balance sheet assets, such as leases and equipment, do not reflect the scope of an advisory business as well as regulatory assets under management.[139] Furthermore, we understand an adviser that has de minimis RAUM, but significant assets related to a non-advisory business may not be willing or able to allocate resources from the non-advisory line to an immaterial advisory business if the non-advisory line does not share comparable compliance requirements. For example, while advisers and broker-dealers may have some comparable compliance requirements under the Advisers Act and the Exchange Act, respectively, other compliance requirements are not easily scalable for both. For example, both advisers and broker-dealers must deliver 17 CFR 279.1, Part 3 and 17 CFR 249.641, respectively (“Form CRS”) to retail investors under the Advisers Act and the Exchange Act, respectively,[140] but only advisers must file Form ADV Part 1A, as applicable.[141] Therefore, a large broker-dealer under common control with an adviser with de minimis RAUM may be able to scale certain resources to the adviser concerning Form CRS, but not Form ADV Part 1A, because that requirement only concerns the adviser.
The RFA defines a “small business” and “small organization” as entities that are “not dominant in their field.” [142] The final rules will continue to be consistent with the Commission's efforts to take into account the structure of business concerns and organizations in the securities industry when defining the terms “small business” and “small organization” and to preclude entities with significant economic or financial resources from obtaining potential regulatory benefits under the RFA.[143] The Control Relationship Threshold will continue to prevent affiliates of large advisers from obtaining potential regulatory benefits under the RFA. Currently and under the final rules, the Control Relationship Threshold precludes advisers from being considered small if they have de minimis RAUM, but control, are controlled by, or are under common control with another adviser that has assets under management equal to or greater than the RAUM Threshold. In such a case, the adviser with de minimis RAUM would appropriately continue to be precluded from obtaining potential regulatory benefits under the RFA.
Although the Commission originally aligned the Total Assets Threshold with the total assets test used in the “small entity” definition in 17 CFR 240.0-10 (“Exchange Act rule 0-10”), it is not necessary to continue to align them through a total assets metric, as a commenter discussed.[144] Currently, Exchange Act rule 0-10(a) provides, among other things, that when used with reference to an “issuer” or a “person,” other than an investment company, the term “small business” or “small organization” means an “issuer” or “person” that, on the last day of its most recent fiscal year, had total assets of $5 million or less.[145] The Commission stated that it aligned the values of the “small entity” definitions under the Advisers Act and the Exchange Act in view of financial industry affiliations between advisers and other large financial services firms to which the Exchange Act definition would apply.[146] However, as discussed above, the RAUM Threshold is a more reliable indicator of whether an adviser is a small entity for purposes of the RFA. As indicated by a commenter, RAUM is a more meaningful proxy for business scale and compliance capacity for advisers, rather than the amount of assets carried on the adviser's balance sheet.[147] The “small entity” definitions under the Advisers Act and the Exchange Act will continue to be aligned in other ways, including by both having thresholds that concern control relationships.[148]
The Commission receives limited information regarding advisers' total assets that would allow it to analyze with specificity the impact of potential changes to the Total Assets Threshold over the distribution of investment advisers. The Commission only receives information in Item 1.O. of Part 1A of Form ADV regarding investment advisers with $1 billion or more in total assets as well as information in Item 12 from registered investment advisers with less than $25 million in RAUM regarding whether they have less than $5 million in total assets. Commenters did not support adopting additional reporting requirements to preserve this element of the definition of “small entity.” [149] Given that the RAUM Threshold and Control Relationship Threshold are more meaningful thresholds to determine whether an adviser is small for purposes of the RFA than the Total Assets Threshold, we are not persuaded that imposing new reporting burdens to calibrate the Total Assets Threshold would be justified.
3. The Control Relationship Threshold
The Commission is amending the Control Relationship Threshold, with modifications from the proposal. Currently, the Control Relationship Threshold disqualifies an adviser from being considered small if it is in a control relationship with an affiliated adviser exceeding an assets under management test that mirrors the current RAUM Threshold of $25 million.[150] To continue to maintain a consistent threshold between the Control Relationship Threshold and the RAUM Threshold, the Commission is amending the value of the Control Relationship Threshold to conform it to the revised $1 billion RAUM Threshold, including its corresponding Inflation Adjustment Mechanism, as proposed.[151] Also, as proposed, the Commission is removing “(or such higher amount as the Commission may deem appropriate)” to further conform the Control Relationship Threshold with the revised RAUM Threshold, for which the Commission removed a similar phrase.[152] In a change from the proposal, the Commission is removing from the Control Relationship Threshold the elements that concern the Total Assets Threshold, namely that an ( printed page 69967) adviser is disqualified from being considered a small entity if it has a control relationship with any person (other than a natural person) that had total assets of $5 million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (as well as the proposed inflation adjustment to this amount).[153] As discussed above, an RAUM threshold is a more reliable indicator of whether an adviser is a small entity than a total assets threshold.[154] In another change from the proposal, the Commission is further amending the Control Relationship Threshold, after considering comments, to help advisers understand how to calculate the assets under management referenced in the Control Relationship Threshold, as discussed more fully below.[155] As a result, under the final amendments, an adviser would meet the Control Relationship Threshold if it does not control, is not controlled by, and is not under common control with another investment adviser that has assets under management equal to or greater than the RAUM Threshold.
The Control Relationship Threshold is designed to preclude entities with significant economic or financial resources from obtaining potential regulatory benefits under the RFA.[156] We continue to believe that Congress did not intend affiliates of large businesses to receive benefits under the RFA.[157] Only those businesses and organizations that are “independently owned” may qualify as small entities pursuant to the definitions contained in the RFA.[158] The final amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold are designed to help ensure the Control Relationship Threshold continues to preclude entities with significant economic or financial resources from their large business affiliates from obtaining potential regulatory benefits under the RFA.
Commenters supported the Commission's proposal to make conforming amendments to the Control Relationship Threshold to reflect the revised $1 billion RAUM Threshold, with its corresponding Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.[159] Commenters also offered recommendations concerning the Control Relationship Threshold. A commenter requested that the Commission confirm that RAUM as reported on Form ADV is the operative metric for adviser small entity status.[160] Under the current rule, the RAUM Threshold sets forth how to calculate assets under management: as defined under Advisers Act section 203A(a)(3) and reported on an adviser's annual updating amendment to Form ADV.[161] The current Control Relationship Threshold, however, only discusses assets under management, without detailing the calculation method.[162]
After considering the comments, the Commission is confirming that advisers must calculate assets under management for the Control Relationship Threshold using the same method as the RAUM Threshold: as defined under Advisers Act section 203A(a)(3) and reported on the adviser's annual updating amendment to Form ADV. In this regard, in a change from the proposal, the Commission is amending the Control Relationship Threshold so that instead of specifying the amount of assets under management of an affiliated investment adviser to surpass the threshold, as it currently does, it instead references rule 0-7 paragraph (a)(1), which sets forth the RAUM Threshold, including its corresponding Inflation Adjustment Mechanism and the calculation method.[163] This amendment does not change how the Control Relationship Threshold operates as compared to the current rule. Instead, it is designed to ensure that advisers understand how to calculate the assets under management in the Control Relationship Threshold.
A commenter recommended the Commission amend the Control Relationship Threshold to provide a special rule for insurance companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated retail advisers.[164] This commenter stated that institutional advisers and retail advisers involve substantially different infrastructures, systems, and regulatory requirements, they do not share management or advisory personnel, they have distinct costs and burdens, and there are few opportunities for economies of scale between them. The commenter expressed concern that a retail adviser may be disproportionately and unfairly impacted by changes in Commission regulation if its assets under management are cumulated with an institutional adviser merely due to common control.
We are not persuaded to provide a special rule for insurance companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated retail advisers. Currently, the requirements in rule 0-7 do not distinguish between retail advisers and institutional advisers. We are not persuaded that advisers should be treated differently under rule 0-7 solely based on the fact that they are affiliated with an insurance company. We disagree with this commenter's assertion that an adviser's retail and institutional advisory businesses involve substantially different regulatory requirements. Retail and institutional advisory businesses involve substantially similar regulatory requirements, because both are subject to the Advisers Act, and the rules thereunder, among other things which do not generally differentiate between the type of client. Even if affiliated advisers choose different infrastructures, systems, management, or advisory personnel, there remain opportunities for economies of scale concerning compliance with and operation under the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder, even if some particular provisions do not apply to each adviser. Therefore, we disagree with the commenter's assertion that a retail adviser would be disproportionately or unfairly impacted by changes in Commission regulation if its assets under management are cumulated with an institutional adviser due to common control.
4. Conforming Amendments to Form ADV and the Adviser Hardship Exemption Rule
The Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV, General Instruction 17, and Item 12 of Part 1A, as well as Advisers Act rule 203-3(b), with modifications from the proposal. Form ADV is the uniform application for investment adviser registration and report form by exempt reporting advisers. General Instruction 17 summarizes the conditions for certain small advisers to apply for an ( printed page 69968) exemption from filing Form ADV electronically with the IARD. Item 12 of Part 1A requires an eligible SEC-registered adviser to report how it qualifies as a “small business” or “small organization” under rule 0-7. It is designed to provide information to the public and the Commission about advisers, including information that enables the Commission to consider the effect of its regulations on small entities, as required by the RFA.[165] Rule 203-3(b) sets forth conditions for certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from the requirement to make Advisers Act filings electronically with the IARD, among other things.
As proposed, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV, including General Instruction 17 and Item 12, as well as rule 203-3(b) to reflect the final amendments to the RAUM Threshold, the Control Relationship Threshold, and their corresponding inflation adjustments. Currently, General Instruction 17 states, in part, that an adviser is a small business, and may be eligible for a continuing hardship exemption, if it is required to answer Item 12 of Part 1A “(because you have assets under management of less than $25 million)” and it is able to respond “no” to each question in Item 12. As proposed, the Commission is removing the parenthetical “(because you have assets under management of less than $25 million).” This parenthetical is implicit, given that the sentence also directs advisers to Item 12, which provides the relevant instructions. Removing this phrase will avoid requiring the Commission to update it periodically, as the Commission adjusts the RAUM Threshold for inflation. Also, as proposed, the Commission is revising General Instruction 17 and rule 203-3(b) so they explicitly apply to an adviser that is either a “small business” or “small organization,” as Item 12 does, rather than just a “small business.”
In a change from the proposal, the Commission is making additional conforming amendments to Form ADV, Item 12 of Part 1A to remove references to the Total Assets Threshold, to reflect that the Commission is eliminating the Total Assets Threshold from rule 0-7. In connection with this change, the Commission also is amending rule 203-3(b)(5) to remove the phrase “that you were required to answer” because it is no longer relevant in light of the amendments to Item 12. In another change from the proposal, the Commission is revising the language of Form ADV Item 12, so that it refers to rule 0-7, rather than re-stating the threshold, as proposed. This amendment does not change the substance of Item 12 as compared to the proposal. The purpose of this amendment is to help ensure Item 12 remains operative, without additional rulemaking, in light of future Commission orders that may adjust rule 0-7's threshold for inflation.
One commenter supported the proposed amendments to Form ADV, discussing that the proposed amendments would help ensure internal consistency across Commission rules.[166] This commenter, along with another commenter, recommended not imposing any additional reporting requirements.[167] The Commission did not propose additional reporting requirements, and is not adopting additional reporting requirements at this time. A commenter requested the Commission quantify and analyze regulatory relief consequences, which the commenter described as Commission reporting, compliance, or procedural accommodations that would become newly available once firms qualify as small entities.[168] We are confirming that rule 203-3(b) provides such an accommodation and its continuing hardship accommodation will become newly available once firms qualify as small entities.[169]
C. Periodic Future Adjustments
The final amendments to rules 0-10 and 0-7 will, as proposed, provide an Inflation Adjustment Mechanism for periodic future adjustments of the asset-based thresholds used in these rules' small entity definitions.[170] Specifically, the amendments provide that the Commission will issue an order every ten years adjusting: (i) the net asset threshold in the investment company small entity definition; and (ii) in the investment adviser small entity definition, the RAUM Threshold (which will also now have the effect of adjusting the Control Relationship Threshold). As proposed, the final amendments to rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 will require that the adjustment of the asset-based thresholds be calculated by reference to the Personal Consumption Expenditures Chain-Type Price Index (the “PCE Index”).[171] The final amendments providing the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will require rounding the investment company small entity net asset threshold to the nearest multiple of $1,000,000,000 and rounding the investment adviser small entity RAUM Threshold (and thus the Control Relationship Threshold) to the nearest multiple of $100,000,000.[172]
In order to adjust the asset-based thresholds for the “small entity” definitions as discussed above, the Commission considered an analysis of the distribution of fund and adviser assets and the growth in these assets over time. As described in the Proposing Release, however, these amended thresholds may become less useful over time due to growth in markets and any subsequent changes in the fund and adviser industries. The proposed Inflation Adjustment Mechanism was designed to ensure that the thresholds are adjusted every ten years, because the adjustment would be required by rule and effected through a Commission order.
Some commenters supported the proposed inflation adjustments.[173] Other commenters supported the goal of periodic adjustments, but expressed concern about the details of the proposal.[174] For example, some commenters recommended the Commission use a shorter cadence for adjustments, such as five or seven years, to ensure that the thresholds remain reasonable.[175] Some commenters recommended using an adjustment mechanism they consider more relevant than inflation, such as a broad-based index of asset prices,[176] or the proposal's own asset-based distribution ( printed page 69969) analysis for RAUM and net asset percentiles.[177]
After considering comments, we are adopting the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism substantially as proposed.[178] Adjustments that the Commission makes mechanically by order could help maintain the thresholds at levels that reflect the buying power of money over time, without the need for Commission action through rulemaking.[179] We expect, as discussed in the Proposing Release and by commenters, that the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will prevent the thresholds in the small entity definitions from becoming less meaningful over time on account of anticipated changes in dollar value.[180] Specifically, because a fund's or adviser's size is related to its ability to bear compliance costs, adjusting the asset-based thresholds is designed to account for potential increases in those compliance costs.
While certain comments recommended a shorter adjustment cadence, the final amendments' Inflation Adjustment Mechanism reflects the same ten-year cadence as proposed. Given the distributions of different-sized entities for funds and investment advisers, inflationary changes over shorter periods would generally not result in a meaningfully different set of funds and investment advisers being considered small entities under their respective definitions.[181]
Likewise, after considering comments recommending an adjustment mechanism based on a metric other than inflation, we are adopting this aspect of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism as proposed. We acknowledge that inflation may not perfectly represent growth in the fund and adviser industries. Nevertheless, as discussed above, our view continues to be that inflation adjustment is the most appropriate mechanism for periodically and mechanically adjusting the asset thresholds and implementing the adjustments by order. Inflation, unlike the asset-based distribution analysis mechanisms described by commenters, is a known factor for which a precise value can reliably be derived from a defined index. Periodically adjusting the thresholds to a set percentile from a distribution analysis would similarly be inappropriate. The percentile that resulted from the distribution analysis performed in the Proposing Release is particular to that data and set of facts and, therefore, is not necessarily indicative of the proportion of funds or advisers that should be deemed small entities in the future. In addition, performing the same or similar analysis to determine a future percentile based on then-current data would involve a level of analysis that would require a future rulemaking rather than an adjustment by Commission order. Similarly, we do not consider using a broad-based index of asset prices as the basis for adjustment as suggested by commenters to be appropriate in light of the breadth of fund and adviser strategies. Any one particular index of asset prices would not be appropriate for certain strategies, and if multiple indexes were used, this could result in different levels of adjustment depending on the index, as well as operational complexity.
It is possible, but less predictable, that the asset-based thresholds may become less useful over time even taking the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism we are adopting into account (for example, with the advent of market events, changes in the makeup or distribution of size of the fund or adviser markets, or other industry changes). In this case, the Commission could consider performing appropriate analyses to propose amendments to the thresholds again in the future independent of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. Similarly, in the future, the Commission also could consider proposing a periodic adjustment approach using analysis other than one based on the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.
D. Effective Date and Compliance Date
The effective dates and compliance dates are as follows:
Final amendments to rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 are effective February 4, 2027, which is 90 days from the date of publication in theFederal Register .
Final amendments to rule 203-3 and Form ADV are effective, and have a compliance date of, February 4, 2027, which is 90 days from the date of publication in theFederal Register .
One commenter recommended an implementation period of 180 days, so advisers can reassess their “small entity” status, update internal Form ADV filing procedures, train compliance and personnel on the revised Form ADV Item 12 logic and hardship exemption eligibility, and coordinate updates with third-party compliance vendors or filing service providers where applicable.[182] We are not persuaded to provide an implementation period of 180 days. While additional SEC-registered advisers will have to update their small entity status in Item 12 of Form ADV and will be newly eligible for the hardship exemption under rule 203-3(b), the information required to comply with the final amendments is readily available to advisers and the additional cost of the final amendments would be minimal. Also, as a practical matter, most advisers will have additional time to update their Form ADV because Form ADV does not require advisers to file an other-than-annual amendment to update Item 12; most advisers will update Item 12 as part of their regularly scheduled annual amendments.[183] The compliance period for rule 203-3 and Form ADV is designed to provide the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (“FINRA”) sufficient time to update the IARD to reflect revised Item 12.[184]
In the event that FINRA is unable to update the IARD by the end of the compliance period, until the IARD is updated, advisers should leave Item 12 blank, and provide responses to revised Item 12 in the miscellaneous section of Schedule D of Form ADV.
We are adopting an effective date for rule 0-7, rule 203-3, and Form ADV that matches the compliance date for rule 203-3 and Form ADV, because these rules and form are connected to each other. We are adopting the same effective date for rule 0-10 for consistency.
The Commission is mindful of the economic effects, including the costs and benefits, of its rules. The Commission has a long-held focus on small entities when engaged in rulemaking. A purpose of the RFA is to promote the effectiveness and efficiency of regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory approaches, with the goal of minimizing ( printed page 69970) the significant economic impact on small entities consistent with the stated objectives of applicable statutes.[185] The Commission is required to determine if a rulemaking is likely to have a “significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities” under the RFA.[186] In applicable rulemakings, the Commission's definitions of “small entities” determine the scope of the regulatory flexibility analyses conducted at the proposal and final stages. The updated definitions are expected to better tailor the Commission's analyses of the specific regulatory challenges faced by small entities by expanding the scope of the analyses that the Commission conducts under the RFA. These analyses, in turn, are expected to better inform the Commission of the regulatory impacts faced by small entities so that it may consider adapting its rulemaking accordingly.[187] To the extent such adaptations to future rulemakings will occur, the use of the amended definitions of “small entities” in RFA analyses could result in different benefits and costs of such rulemakings.[188] For example, if the Commission, informed by the more tailored RFA analyses, determined to scope fewer small entities into future rulemakings or tailor obligations imposed by such rulemakings differently for small entities, there could be lower compliance costs imposed on such entities.
In addition to these indirect effects, the final rule will have direct economic effects arising in situations where the updated small entity definitions affect the application of existing Commission rules and regulations. Currently, the Commission's definition of “small entity” under the RFA is incorporated into the Commission's other rules and regulations only in connection with an adviser's responses to Form ADV (and this release is implementing corresponding amendments to the form) and to rule 203-3(b). We thus consider the effects of the updated definition as it relates to the use of that definition in Form ADV, as well as the effects of the other associated changes to the form and to rule 203-3(b).[189]
First, we are amending Form ADV to revise General Instruction 17, which currently permits registered or registering investment advisers to receive a continuing hardship exemption from Form ADV electronic filing requirements, pursuant to rule 203-3(b), if such investment adviser is a small business and can demonstrate that filing Form ADV electronically would impose an undue hardship.[190] As proposed, we are revising General Instruction 17 to define an investment adviser as a “small business” or “small organization” if it is required to answer Item 12 (which itself relies on the definition in rule 0-7) and if it is able to respond “no” to each question in Item 12. Since the amendments to Item 12, in conformity with rule 0-7, reflect the removal of the Total Assets Threshold and that the RAUM Threshold is increasing from $25 million to $1 billion, General Instruction 17 will similarly reflect these changes for the availability of the continuing hardship exemption.
As a result, 10,180 [191] additional registered investment advisers may be eligible for the exemption under the revised definition, as reflected in the amended General Instruction 17, before any future adjustment for inflation. However, we expect that the increased availability of the continuing hardship exemption to registered investment advisers meeting the updated definition will have minimal economic impact. Due to the ubiquity of inexpensive access to computers and the internet—both to advisers themselves and to the service providers they may employ—any newly eligible advisers are unlikely to be able to demonstrate that filing Form ADV electronically would impose an undue hardship.[192] We therefore anticipate that few, if any, additional advisers will be able to rely on the exemption.
Second, as proposed, we are amending Item 12 of Part 1A of Form ADV to align the RAUM threshold for completing the questions in that item with the final amendments to the definitions of “small business” and “small organization” under rule 0-7.[193] In a departure from the proposal, we are revising Item 12 and rule 203-3(b)(5) to reflect that the final amendments eliminate the Total Assets Threshold from rule 0-7.
As a result of the final amendments, approximately 10,180 194 additional registered investment advisers will be required to complete Item 12 of Part 1A (before any future adjustment for inflation). These advisers may incur costs associated with training their compliance personnel, updating internal procedures, and coordinating updates with third-party service
providers,[195] and will incur costs associated with preparing the disclosure. Because the information needed to complete the corresponding questions will be readily available to advisers, we estimate the cost increase for each affected adviser will be minimal, averaging approximately $91 per adviser per year,[196] or $928,925 per year for the industry as a whole.[197]
