Comment: The applicant submitted a public comment regarding the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) and confirmed that only the TIDALTM Fusion Cage received both Breakthrough Device designation and marketing authorization from FDA and reiterated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the newness requirement for device pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's input. We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage within 3 years of the date of FDA 510(k) clearance. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we have determined that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
In the proposed rule, we also invited public comment on whether the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
We did not receive public comments regarding whether the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4). Based on our review of the application, we agree with the applicant and have determined that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we noted regarding the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1) that the applicant stated that no existing (current or previous) device pass-through payment categories appropriately describe the TIDALTM Fusion Cage. Per the applicant, the existing pass-through code C1713 (Anchor/screw for opposing bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone (implantable)) does not appropriately describe the TIDALTM Fusion Cage because C1713 is typically used to represent fixation components, such as an intramedullary nail or other fixation screws, but does not represent the TIDALTM Fusion Cage.
Based on the description the applicant provided, we stated in the proposed rule that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is a porous cage used as part of a limb salvage arthrodesis construct to bridge bone loss or a critical bone defect in the ankle and restore length due to bone void, absent bone, or surgical resection and therefore, could be described by C1713 (Anchor/screw for opposing bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone (implantable)). Specifically, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1713 may appropriately describe the TIDALTM Fusion Cage because C1713 is defined as implantable pins and/or screws inserted or drilled into bone, principally with the intent to facilitate stabilization or oppose bone-to-bone contact and may include orthopedic plates with accompanying washers or nuts as well as synthetic bone substitutes that may be used to fill bony voids or gaps.[27] In this context, we stated our belief that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage may be appropriately described by C1713. We also stated that, after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we were unable to determine that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the device category eligibility criteria, and therefore, we proposed to deny transitional pass-through payment status for CY 2027.
We invited public comment on whether the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1). We also invited public comments on our proposal to deny transitional pass-through payment status for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage for CY 2027.
Comment: A commenter expressed its support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input.
Comment: The applicant and a few commenters submitted public comments urging CMS to approve device pass-through payments for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage. A few commenters stated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage provides an alternative treatment to certain patients who are at risk of limb loss and without other good ( printed page 70439) treatment options. The commenters added that denying the TIDALTM Fusion Cage device pass-through payment would limit patients' access to this treatment option. One of these commenters also stated that when a patient loses their leg, besides the physical and mental anguish, the cost for the prosthetic is ever increasing.
With respect to whether the TIDALTM Fusion Cage may be appropriately described by C1713, the applicant stated that there are no existing categories or categories previously in effect that appropriately describe the TIDALTM Fusion Cage. Specifically, the applicant stated that C1713 describes fixation hardware such as anchors, screws, pins, plates, washers, and nuts used to facilitate stabilization or oppose bone-to-bone contact as well as certain conventional synthetic bone substitutes used to fill voids or gaps. The applicant compared this description to the TIDALTM Fusion Cage, which it stated is an FDA-cleared ankle fusion cage that is a permanent, porous, load-bearing structural spacer used with a tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) intramedullary rod to reconstruct a critical-size ankle/hindfoot bone defect, restore limb length, and enable salvage fusion in patients at risk of limb loss. The applicant also stated that CMS's preliminary conclusion relies on an overly broad interpretation of C1713 that stretches the device category beyond its natural scope of fixation hardware and void-filling substitutes. The applicant stated that CMS's interpretation of C1713 includes any implant associated with stabilization, fusion, or a bone defect and would result in the device category code inappropriately including a broad range of musculoskeletal reconstructive implants. The applicant stated that this would be inconsistent with the device category eligibility criterion, which asks whether an existing pass-through category appropriately describes the nominated device. According to the applicant, the appropriate question is not whether C1713 can be stretched to cover a device that touches bone or participates in fusion, but rather, whether C1713 appropriately describes the TIDALTM Fusion Cage. The applicant reiterated that C1713 does not describe the TIDALTM Fusion Cage because the device is a structural, porous, titanium ankle fusion cage with a central window for an intramedullary nail, used to replace absent bone and restore limb length in limb-salvage TTC fusion and not an anchor, screw, pin, plate, washer, nut, or conventional synthetic bone substitute.
The applicant stated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is not an anchor, screw, pin, or plate. Per the applicant, C1713 describes an anchor/screw for opposing bone-to-bone or soft tissue-to-bone with the defining function of fixation by anchoring, screwing, pinning, drilling, or opposing tissue or bone surfaces. The applicant stated that, by contrast, the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is not drilled into bone like a screw or pin, does not attach tendon or soft tissue to bone, and is not a plate, washer, nut, or fixation assembly. The applicant reiterated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is a porous titanium cage with a circular window to contain an intramedullary nail and is used to restore length due to bone void, absent bone, or surgical resection during TTC fusion procedures in patients at risk of limb loss. The applicant stated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage's function is categorically different from opposing two tissues or two bone surfaces. The applicant stated that the nominated device is an interpositional, load-bearing reconstructive implant placed where bone is missing, and the intramedullary nail provides the primary internal fixation pathway through the construct while the cage replaces the segmental defect and provides a porous osseointegrative scaffold around the rod.
Furthermore, the applicant stated that CMS should not treat the TIDALTM Fusion Cage as a conventional synthetic bone substitute used to fill bony voids or gaps under C1713. The applicant stated that CMS uses synthetic bone substitutes to collapse every device used in or around a bone defect into C1713. The applicant further stated that conventional bone void fillers are typically indicated for bony voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, and many are resorbable materials that are replaced by bone over time.
The applicant noted that FDA's product code for this device is directly relevant to CMS's analysis of C1713 and confirms that a conventional synthetic bone graft or bone-void filler is a different type of device. The applicant stated that FDA classified the TIDALTM Fusion Cage under product code SAI, Ankle Fusion Cage, under regulation 21 CFR 888.3020. The applicant further stated that FDA's product-code for an ankle fusion cage describes a permanent metal structure that acts as a structural spacer where the defect is intrinsic to stability and limb length. The applicant compared this ankle fusion cage product-code to FDA's separate product classification MQV for Filler, Bone Void, Calcium Compound, regulated under 21 CFR 888.3045, which is defined as a resorbable implant intended to fill bony voids or gaps caused by trauma or surgery that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure. The applicant stated that treating the TIDALTM Fusion Cage as a synthetic bone substitute would disregard the separate regulatory identities FDA assigned to these materially different device types. The applicant further explained that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is used precisely where the defect is intrinsic to stability, limb length, and salvage reconstruction and that FDA's product classification likewise describes the device as a metal open-space structure that acts as a structural spacer as part of a TTC fusion construct. Additionally, the applicant stated that, although the TIDALTM Fusion Cage may be packed with autograft or allogenic bone graft, this does not make the cage itself a bone substitute. The applicant noted that labeling for the nominated FDA-cleared device indicates that it is intended for use with autograft and/or allogenic bone graft, confirming, per the applicant, that the cage is the structural implant and the graft is the biologic fusion material.
In addition, the applicant contended that CMS should give substantial weight to FDA's classification because FDA's product-code framework directly addresses devices' technological and clinical identity. The applicant reiterated that the SAI product code for ankle fusion cage describes the device type as a metal cylinder, spherical, or rectangular-box physical state with open space throughout that is used as a structural spacer and an accessory to a TTC intramedullary rod. The applicant explained that it believes this regulatory identity is materially distinct from screws, anchors, pins, plates, washers, nuts, and conventional synthetic bone substitutes. The applicant requested that CMS not deny transitional pass-through payment status for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage on the basis that it is described by C1713. The applicant stated that a more accurate category would be a new ankle joint fusion device category, such as joint fusion device, ankle, including all system components (implantable).
Other commenters also stated that the nominated device is different from the types of anchors, screws, plates, or bone void fillers classified in existing device categories because it is a structural ankle fusion cage that sits in place of missing bone and permits the leg to carry weight while it heals in. A commenter further described the TIDALTM Fusion Cage as a porous titanium spacer and stated that the nominated device restores leg length. ( printed page 70440)
Response: We appreciate the applicant and commenters' input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we agree there is no existing category or category previously in effect that appropriately describes the TIDALTM Fusion Cage because no pass-through category describes a device that is a structural component used to replace absent bone and restore limb length in an ankle fusion, and not an anchor, screw, pin, plate, washer, nut, or conventional synthetic bone substitute. Based on this information, we have determined that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
We also invited public comment on whether the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the cost criterion at § 419.66(d)(3).
Comment: With respect to cost significance criteria, the applicant reiterated that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets all three of the cost significance criteria.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our findings from the first, second, and third cost significant tests, we agree that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the cost significance criteria specified at § 419.66(d).
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the device pass-through application, we have determined that the TIDALTM Fusion Cage meets the requirements for device pass-through status described at § 419.66. We are approving the TIDALTM Fusion Cage for device pass-through payment status effective January 1, 2027, under the alternative pathway for devices that have an FDA Breakthrough Device designation and FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation.
(3) Traditional Device Pass-Through Applications
(a) EndoForceTM Connector for Endovascular Venous Anastomosis
Phraxis Inc. submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the EndoForceTM Connector for Endovascular Venous Anastomosis (the EndoForceTM System) for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the EndoForceTM System provides an endovascular method for attachment of a non-autogenous arteriovenous graft (AVG) to a vein in the upper arm in patients with end stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring hemodialysis. Per the applicant, the EndoForceTM System is provided as a sterile, single-use EndoForceTM Connector Delivery System with a pre-mounted EndoForceTM Connector that is attached endovascularly at the venous anastomosis, in conjunction with a standard 6mm expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) vascular access graft, to establish an end-to-end endovascular anastomotic conduit designed to help absorb the shear forces of blood flow at the AVG-vein junction and to provide a physical barrier to the ingress of neointimal hyperplasia.
Table 54 provides an overview of the transitional pass-through payment status application for the EndoForceTM System and CMS's preliminary assessment. For additional details provided by the applicant, please refer to the online application posting available at https://mearis.cms.gov/​public/​publications/​device-ptp/​DEP260228AHPFT.
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we invited public comments on whether the EndoForceTM System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4), and the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
Comment: The applicant submitted a public comment reiterating that the EndoForceTM System meets the newness, eligibility, and device category eligibility criteria for device pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's input. We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the EndoForceTM System within 3 years of the date of FDA premarket approval. We also agree with the applicant that the EndoForceTM System is an integral part of the service furnished, used for one patient only, comes in contact with human tissue, and is surgically implanted or inserted or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion. Additionally, we agree with the applicant that the EndoForceTM System is not equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets, or a material or supply furnished incident to a service. We believe that there is no existing category or category previously in effect that appropriately describes the EndoForceTM System. Therefore, after consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we have determined that the EndoForceTM System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4), and the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1).
Regarding the substantial clinical improvement criterion at § 419.66(c)(2), after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that we had the following concerns regarding whether the EndoForceTM System meets the substantial clinical improvement criterion.
In support of claims one through four and eight, the applicant submitted three studies evaluating the EndoForceTM System: Burgess et al. (2024), Kramer et al. (2026), and Astor et al. (2026), and three background studies: Halbert et al. (2020), Harms et al. (2016), and Woodside et al. (2021), which did not assess the nominated device.[28] In ( printed page 70442) support of claims five through seven, the applicant submitted three background articles (Pisoni et al., 2021; Berland et al., 2019; Hull et al., 2018) which did not assess the nominated device.[29 30 31]
We noted that the Burgess et al. (2024) study is a single-arm, non-randomized study that analyzed the use of the EndoForceTM System in 158 patients aged 18 and older diagnosed with ESRD scheduled to have an AVG for hemodialysis placed in their upper arm in 10 U.S. institutions between 2018 and 2021 after a 6-month follow-up period.[32] We stated we had several concerns with this study.
Firstly, we stated we were concerned that the study does not provide a comparison to a control group, such as patients treated with standard graft-to-vein sutured anastomosis. Without a comparison to currently available treatments, particularly in the clinical setting where it is most likely to be used, we stated we were unable to assess whether the EndoForceTM System demonstrates substantial clinical improvement over currently available treatments. To demonstrate substantial clinical improvement, we stated we consider supporting evidence, preferably published peer-reviewed clinical trials, that show improved clinical outcomes, such as reduction in mortality, complications, subsequent interventions, future hospitalizations, recovery time, pain, or a more rapid beneficial resolution of the disease process compared to other currently available treatments.
Secondly, we were concerned that the smaller patient population and study design of Burgess et al. (2024), and the lack of stratification by key clinical factors known to affect AVG outcomes, may limit both the reliability of the cumulative patency findings and the generalizability of results to the Medicare population. We stated that stratification factors, such as coronary artery disease, hypertension status, and ipsilateral access placement, which have all been shown to be associated with thrombosis, need for intervention, and cumulative patency would be helpful to assess the outcomes.
In addition, we stated it was unclear to what extent any improvement in cumulative patency is due to use of the EndoForceTM Connector versus the less invasive endovascular procedure used for implantation. We stated we would welcome additional information on differentiating how the EndoForceTM System's connection to AVG versus the less invasive nature of the endovascular procedure leads to improvements in cumulative patency.
Furthermore, we noted that, in Burgess et al. (2024), the authors compared results to three background studies, Halbert et al. (2020) (submitted in support of claim 4), Harms et al. (2016) (submitted in support of claim 8), and Woodside et al. (2021) (submitted in support of claim 8), none of which directly address the EndoForceTM System.[33 34 35] We questioned the appropriateness of comparing cumulative patency, intervention rates, and AVG abandonment in Burgess et al. (2024) to outcomes reported in the three background studies, as observed differences may be influenced by variations in study design, study location, patient population and characteristics, and study period. Specifically, we stated that Burgess et al. (2024) reports a 6-month cumulative patency of 92 percent in its patient population and compares it to the 80 percent rate reported in Halbert et al. (2020). However, we noted that Halbert et al. (2020) is a meta-analysis of 32 studies conducted across 14 countries between 2007 and 2019, representing 3,381 AVGs placed in patients with chronic kidney disease or ESRD undergoing or preparing for hemodialysis using ePTFE grafts. In contrast, we stated that Burgess et al. (2024) analyzed ESRD patients between 2018 and 2021. Thus, we questioned whether the results in Halbert et al. (2020), which included studies dating back more than a decade, reflect current operative techniques and perioperative care in the U.S. and therefore whether they are an appropriate comparator to Burgess et al. (2024). Similarly, we stated that Harms et al. (2016) is a retrospective study of 599 patients treated between January 2006 and December 2011, and Woodside et al. (2021) is an observational cohort study of 73,027 patients using data from July 2012 to December 2014. We noted that these studies reflect earlier clinical practices and patient populations that differ from those in Burgess et al. (2024), which evaluated patients between 2018 and 2021. We stated that Burgess et al. (2024) compared its reported intervention rate of 1.22 per patient-year to higher rates reported in Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. (2021), 1.58 and 1.87 respectively; however, these comparisons may not be appropriate given the significant differences in study design, time periods and patient populations. We also stated that these earlier studies do not adequately account for changes in clinical practice over time and any observed differences in outcomes are likely confounded by these factors rather than attributable to the technology itself. As such, we stated that these studies may not provide a valid basis for comparison to Burgess et al. (2024).
Moreover, we noted patient populations varied across studies, and it is unclear how these differences may have affected intervention rates per patient-year. We stated, for example, Burgess et al. (2024) included patients with two or fewer previous vascular accesses in the treatment arm, while Woodside et al. (2021) included patients undergoing a first-time AVG placement between dialysis initiation and 1 year. We noted that patients who have had previous hemodialysis access points experience damage to the blood vessels regardless of whether the access point is a central venous catheter, AVG, or ( printed page 70443) AVF.[36 37] Further, we stated having prior vascular access points in the ipsilateral arm has been shown to decrease cumulative patency in Harms et al. (2016). We stated that we would welcome additional studies that control for patients with comparable vascular access placement histories, to more accurately quantify the contributions of the EndoForceTM System to improvements in interventions per patient-year.
Finally, we stated that we were concerned that differences in vascular location for patients in the Burgess et al. (2024) compared to patients in the background studies may influence outcomes and adversely impact comparability of results. Specifically, while Burgess et al. (2024) evaluated patients with upper arm AVGs consistent with the EndoForceTM System's FDA approved indication, we stated that this varied across the comparator studies: Halbert et al. (2020) excluded studies that exclusively assessed lower extremity AVGs, Harms et al. (2016) included patients who had AVGs in the chest and thigh in addition to the upper extremity, and Woodside et al. (2021) did not specify the anatomical location of AVGs. We noted that it was unclear whether some of the studies included patient populations with upper extremity, lower extremity, and chest AVGs. As discussed in greater detail later in this section for the second claim, we stated that it was unclear whether upper extremity and upper arm are used interchangeably. We questioned whether vascular access location influences clinical outcomes, and as such, the results in these background studies may be confounded by inclusion of patients with additional graft locations that could adversely impact the comparability of the results to Burgess et al. (2024).
With regard to the second claim that the EndoForceTM System improves patency and reduces AVG abandonment, the applicant submitted a study by Astor et al. (2026) that compared the primary patency (defined as the time interval from initial implantation until first intervention) and cumulative patency (defined as the time interval between implantation of the graft to abandonment) results from Burgess et al. (2024) to pooled results from a meta-analysis of 34 studies of AVGs implanted using traditional surgical techniques.[38] We expressed concern that Astor et al. (2026) may not demonstrate that the EndoForceTM System substantially improves the diagnosis or treatment of an illness when compared to the benefits of other available treatments. We stated that Astor et al. (2026) reported a high degree of variability among the comparator studies included in the meta-analysis (primary patency I2 = 99.44; cumulative patency I2 = 99.36), many of which showed similar or higher primary patency (60.21 percent; 95 percent confidence interval (CI): 50.84, 69.59) and cumulative patency (92.08 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.98, 97.18) compared to results from Burgess et al. (2024). We noted that 19 of the 31 studies that provided data on cumulative patency in Astor et al. (2026) did not specifically report 6-month patency outcomes in tables or text; the studies only provided data in survival curves from which the authors of Astor et al. (2026) derived 6-month patency measurements. We stated that the estimated 6-month cumulative patency including all 31 studies was 83.23 percent (95 percent CI: 80.18, 86.28), whereas the 6-month cumulative patency estimated from the 12 studies reporting numerical values was 86 percent (95 percent CI: 81.78, 90.22). We noted that Astor et al. (2026) did not state whether the difference between the 6-month cumulative patency rates of 92 percent in Burgess et al. (2024) and 86 percent was statistically significant. However, we noted the lower 95 percent CI bound reported in Burgess et al. (2024) was 86.98 percent, lower than the upper 95 percent CI bound of 90.22 percent for the 12 studies in Astor et al. (2026) providing numerical data. We also noted that Astor et al. (2026) states that the primary patency for the EndoForceTM System is similar to pooled results from comparator studies (60.21 percent vs 60.35 percent; p = 0.75). Additionally, we noted that the 20 percent AVG abandonment rate used as a baseline by Astor et al. (2026) which they report was reduced to 8 percent, comes from a single meta-analysis (Halbert) based on 32 studies from 14 countries conducted between 2007 and 2019. We questioned whether this is an appropriate comparator to the 158 patients treated between 2018 and 2021 in 10 U.S. institutions reported in Burgess et al. (2024).
We also noted that the criteria for comparator studies included in the meta-analysis in Astor et al. (2026) excluded those studies which only assessed lower extremity or chest AVGs. However, we questioned whether some of the studies included patient populations with upper extremity AVGs as well as lower extremity and chest AVGs. We stated that, as previously discussed, vascular access location may influence outcomes, therefore, the results in these background studies may be confounded by inclusion of patients with additional graft locations that could adversely impact the comparability of the results to Burgess et al. (2024). Additionally, because of the EndoForceTM System's FDA approved indication for use in the upper arm, we questioned whether the comparison is appropriate. Further, we noted it is unclear in the application whether the upper arm means the entire upper extremity, including the forearm (distal to the elbow) or only a portion of the arm (proximal to the elbow). We stated that we would be interested in additional information clarifying the meaning of upper arm to help us evaluate the evidence provided in support of substantial clinical improvement and determine if it is applicable.
With regard to the third claim that the EndoForceTM System sustains patency and requires fewer interventions to maintain patency, the applicant submitted one extended follow-up study (Kramer et al. (2026)) of 37 patients from Burgess et al. (2024), that evaluates the number of interventions performed to achieve cumulative patency for an additional 6 months beyond the most recent intervention.[39] We stated, similar to our concerns regarding Burgess et al. (2024), we were concerned that Kramer et al. (2026) does not provide a control group for comparison. We noted that the authors in Kramer et al. (2026) stated that, since both the EndoForceTM System's pivotal trial (Burgess et al, 2024) as well as this extended follow-up study do not directly compare outcomes ( printed page 70444) to sutured AVGs, a meta-analytic approach to compare endovascular anastomosis of an AVG with a traditional sutured anastomosis may be warranted. We stated that we would welcome additional information directly comparing endovascular anastomosis of an AVG with a traditional sutured anastomosis.
We noted that, like Burgess et al. (2024), the authors of Kramer et al. (2026) compared results to two background studies, Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. (2021), neither of which directly address the EndoForceTM System. As mentioned previously, we questioned whether the comparison of rates of interventions per patient-year in Kramer et al. (2026) to Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. (2021) are appropriate and reflect true improvements or are attributable to differences in study design, patient population, and study period. We noted that Kramer et al. (2026) reported a rate of 1.32 interventions per patient-year in its patient population using the nominated technology and compared it to rates of 1.58 and 1.87 reported in Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. (2021). We stated, however, as previously noted in our discussion of the first claim that the EndoForceTM System improves patency, reduces intervention burden, and reduces AVG abandonment at 6 months, due to the differences in study periods between Kramer et al. (2026) and Harms et al. (2016) and Woodside et al. (2021), we questioned whether the results in the comparator studies, some of which are over a decade old, reflect current operative techniques and latest perioperative care in the U.S. We also stated that, as previously noted in our discussion of the first claim, the extent of variance in vascular access locations of the patient populations assessed in these three studies was unclear. As such, we stated our concern that the results in these background studies may be confounded by inclusion of patients with additional graft locations which could adversely impact the comparability of the results to Kramer et al. (2026).
We also expressed concern about whether the patient population in Kramer et al. (2026), which included 29 active patients at the end of the study period from the 37 patients initially assessed, is powered sufficiently to assess statistical significance, especially compared to Burgess et al. (2024), which included 134 active patients at the end of the study period from the 158 patients initially assessed. We noted that when a study is not adequately powered for the statistical analysis, the statistics may appear artificially inflated and do not reflect confounding effects. We also expressed concern that the cohort in Kramer et al. (2026) was selected and analyzed post-hoc, rather than identified as a variable of interest at the initiation of Burgess et al. (2024) and questioned whether quality of the study was diminished due to selection bias.
Additionally, we questioned whether Kramer et al. (2026) conclusively demonstrates that the EndoForceTM System provides a substantial clinical improvement compared to other available treatments. We noted that Kramer et al. (2026) estimated a cumulative patency of 78.4 percent at 180 days into the extended follow-up period (12 months from AVG implant at the start of Burgess et al. (2024)). We stated that, in comparison, Halbert et al. (2020) reported a 12-month cumulative patency of 70 percent (95 percent CI: 64, 75). We also noted the high degree of variability (I2 = 91) among the comparator studies in Halbert et al. (2020), many of which showed similar or higher cumulative patency compared to Kramer et al. (2026). Therefore, we stated we were unable to conclusively attribute the difference in outcomes to the nominated device.
Lastly, we questioned the appropriateness of comparing measures of cumulative patency that are not equally defined. Kramer et al. (2026) compared cumulative patency between participants with and without graft interventions within the 6-month study period discussed in Burgess et al. (2024) and stated that the cumulative patency at 6 months was nearly identical (91.79 percent versus 91.80 percent, respectively). We stated that, in Kramer et al. (2026), for patients without an intervention, time to loss of patency was measured from the date of implant, while for patients with interventions, time to loss of patency was measured from the date of first intervention. We questioned the appropriateness of comparing cumulative patency between AVGs used at first hemodialysis without intervention and those that required intervention prior to first hemodialysis use. We stated, as Harms et al. (2016) notes, intervention prior to first hemodialysis use is associated with a shortened cumulative patency. As such, we questioned if making such comparisons could be potentially misleading.
In support of claims five through seven, that the EndoForceTM System improves cumulative (secondary) patency compared to mature AV fistulas (AVFs), and devices used for AVF creation, including WaveLinQTM, and EllipsysTM, the applicant submitted three background articles (Pisoni et al. (2021); Berland et al. (2019); Hull et al. (2018)) which did not assess the nominated device. The applicant stated that improvement in AVG patency is comparable to the 6-month cumulative patency associated with mature AVFs (71 to 93 percent) (Liu, P. et al. (2023)). However, we noted that the EndoForceTM System is indicated for attachment of an AVG to a vein, not for the creation of an AVF. We also noted that an AVF involves a direct anastomosis between an artery and a vein, whereas an AVG uses a graft as a conduit between the artery and the vein. Therefore, we questioned whether it is clinically appropriate to compare the EndoForceTM System, a device used for AVG attachment, to mature AVFs and devices used for AVF creation, including WaveLinQTM and EllipsysTM. Given these fundamental differences in mechanism and clinical use, we questioned whether these claims demonstrate a substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies.
We invited public comment on whether the EndoForceTM System meets the device category criterion at § 419.66(c)(2) and the cost criterion at § 419.66(d)(3).
Comment: A commenter expressed its support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the EndoForceTM System due to their belief that it does not meet all criteria for approval.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input.
Comment: The applicant and several commenters recommended that CMS approve of device pass-through payment for the EndoForceTM System. These commenters stated that the EndoForceTM System exhibits a genuinely different technological approach to an important and persistent problem in dialysis vascular access compared to traditional hand-sewn venous anastomosis, and therefore, offers a promising opportunity to improve the durability and preservation of permanent dialysis access via an AVG. Commenters stated that, without approval, hospitals may face a financial disincentive or be unable to offer the EndoForceTM System even when the surgeon believes it is the best option for a patient for whom an AVG is the appropriate permanent-access strategy. Commenters expressed concern that this would thereby limit physicians' ability to gain experience with a new technology, restrict patient access, and impede generation of the broader real-world clinical evidence CMS seeks and is necessary to determine the technology's long-term value. The ( printed page 70445) commenters also stated that, given that important dialysis vascular access and management innovations are slow-developing and infrequent, device pass-through payment status would create disciplined adoption that can allow appropriate Medicare beneficiaries to receive an innovative technology while physicians, investigators, and other interested parties continue to develop evidence regarding its clinical performance and value. In addition, a few commenters stated that approving transitional pass-through payment for the EndoForceTM System would not end the evidence discussion and does not require CMS to conclude that this technology has already established all its potential long-term clinical or economic benefits.
A few commenters stated that, for patients requiring an AVG, preserving a usable graft with fewer interventions per patient-year and avoiding a catheter is not marginal improvement, but rather, is the difference between stable dialysis and another cycle of access failure. These commenters also stated that the EndoForceTM System will reduce disruptions in dialysis care and caregiver burden, while also decreasing frequency of invasive procedures that expose patients to procedural risks; pain, anxiety, and recovery; and additional demands on limited vascular anatomy.
A few commenters stated that the EndoForceTM System is particularly important for Medicare beneficiaries who are unsuitable candidates for a usable AVF and for whom an AVG may be the most appropriate, as it is the most likely to become promptly usable and shortens catheter exposure. Moreover, a commenter stated that providers embrace new technologies, such as the EndoForceTM System, which has the potential to reduce catheter dependence and improve AVG patency, and that beneficiaries deserve the choice of innovations that could improve their access care.
A few commenters agreed with some of CMS's concerns in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41837 through 41839), specifically regarding the absence of a concurrent control group, differences among comparator populations and treatment periods, variation in vascular-access history and graft location, and uncertainty regarding the source of the observed clinical benefit, further agreeing that they warrant appropriate caution. However, the commenters stated that the concerns alone do not warrant a negative determination of substantial clinical improvement. The commenters stated that CMS should evaluate the evidence in the clinical context of patients who actually received an AVG and the persistent clinical problem that the EndoForceTM System intends to address. The commenters stated that, in evaluating the evidence for substantial clinical improvement, the available statistical comparisons have recognized limitations, and therefore, CMS should consider the totality of the circumstances, including the nature of the patient population, the historical difficulty of maintaining dialysis vascular access, the burden imposed by repeated access procedures, and the potential significance of reducing those interventions.
Additionally, the commenters suggested that CMS also consider the potential downstream consequences of denying transitional pass-through payment status, including the need for repeated interventions, vascular access-related hospital and outpatient encounters, vascular access failure, catheter exposure, and the cumulative burden these events impose on Medicare beneficiaries and the Medicare program. These commenters also stated that CMS's substantial clinical improvement standard recognizes long-term catheter use and decreased rate of subsequent diagnostic or therapeutic interventions as a clinically important outcome and, from a dialysis patient's perspective, they may be the most important outcomes CMS can consider.
A commenter emphasized the clinical challenges of dialysis vascular access, such as their path-dependent nature and how a functioning graft's loss may consume additional vascular territory, require another access procedure, and return a patient to catheter dependence, and that this patient population has limited options available. The commenter stated that transitional pass-through payment status for the EndoForceTM System would enable its availability for appropriately selected patients while its additional cost is not yet included into payment rates. Additionally, the commenter stated that device pass-through payment status would not imply that the EndoForceTM System should replace conventional AVG in every patient, but it would permit physicians to consider the technology in the select patients for whom its clinical advantages justify use.
Response: We thank the applicant and commenters for their comments. We have taken these comments into consideration in our final determination for pass-through payment status for the EndoForceTM System.
Comment: In response to our concerns regarding Burgess et al.'s (2024) lack of a control group and differences from the available comparator populations, the applicant commented that, while a study comparing the EndoForceTM System to a control group would be a useful addition to the available evidence, no such study exists at this time. The applicant explained that because of this, its evidence strategy was to rely on comparison to other studies through systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The applicant stated that it provided sufficient information to support an apt and revealing comparison, enabling a reasonable judgement about a complicated issue. Citing a publication on randomized control trials (RCTs), the applicant added that the most rigorous form of a study with a control group is a RCT, and that while RCTs are generally regarded as a methodological gold standard, they can be subject to several forms of bias that are not necessarily defeated by randomization.[40]
The applicant further stated that when meta-analyses are well-specified and review high-quality studies, methodologists place them at the top of the evidence hierarchy and consider them to be likely superior to even randomized clinical trials when well conducted.[41 42] As a result, the applicant stated that CMS should not readily dismiss the evidence available from the comparative studies provided in its application. The applicant noted that Burgess et al. (2024) included patients fitted with sutured AVGs by Halbert et al. (2020) and that Halbert et al. (2020) only included studies in which patients had newly created AVGs, as opposed to graft revisions.
The applicant further stated that the patient population in Halbert et al. (2020) aligns with Burgess et al. (2024) and that the Burgess et al. (2024) study design deliberately enables comparison to previously published studies to provide a meaningful historical comparison. The applicant also stated that it specifically intended for Astor et al. (2026) to provide a direct comparison to Burgess et al. (2024). The applicant reiterated comparisons of 6-month cumulative patency between Burgess et al. (2024) and Halbert et al. (2020), and ( printed page 70446) Burgess et al. (2024) and Astor et al. (2026), which CMS discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41837 and 41838, respectively).
Additionally, a commenter stated that while differences among comparator populations are important, those differences reflect the clinical reality of AVG recipients, who are a highly heterogeneous population. The commenter added that factors, including prior catheters and accesses, remaining vasculature condition, ipsilateral access history, anatomical location, and comorbidities, can affect both the decision to place a graft and its subsequent performance. The commenter stated that contemporary literature demonstrates the difficulty of consistently accounting for these variables. The commenter cited a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 63 studies and 357,333 patients (Yang et al.),[43] which found substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity along with inconsistent reporting of variables such as prior AVF or AVG use, first-access status, and prior catheter use. The commenter noted that Yang et al. (2026) could not include several of these clinically important variables into its meta-regression because they are inconsistently reported. The commenter stated that the same variables CMS identified as necessary for comparability ( e.g., prior access history, anatomical location, ipsilateral vascular history, and relevant comorbidities) are both clinically consequential and inconsistently reported in contemporary vascular-access literature. The commenter stated that the absence of a study comparing the EndoForceTM System to a concurrent control group remains a meaningful limitation and reduces strong causal inference, but this limitation should not be interpreted to mean that existing conventional-AVG experience has little comparative value or that the submitted evidence is clinically uninformative. Instead, the commenter stated that the lack of a perfect contemporary comparator should affect the weight and certainty assigned to the available evidence.
In response to our concerns about the small patient population in Burgess et al. (2024), the applicant stated that the reliability of the study's findings was not compromised by the patient population's size and that the study team selected the sample size to support FDA premarket approval and intended to provide adequate statistical power to demonstrate that AVG placement with the EndoForceTM System met a pre-specified performance goal of 75 percent cumulative patency at 6 months (p<0.001).
Regarding our concerns about lack of stratification in Burgess et al. (2024), the applicant stated that the study's generalizability to the Medicare population is unlikely to be a practical problem as the preponderance of patients requiring vascular access are eligible for Medicare and, while the study did not report patients' insurance status, the provided demographic information comports with the Medicare population. The applicant also stated that the possible stratifications in which CMS expressed interest are among the factors clinicians wrestle with daily in developing patients' treatment plans. The applicant added that the 2019 Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guideline do not specify in detail how physicians should handle such factors but defer to clinicians' judgement to take these factors, among others, into account when dealing with the complex specifics of cases before them.[44] The applicant stated that although Burgess et al. (2024) includes information about the extent of a number of diseases and other factors, stratified analysis within the study would have been of questionable value given the sample size. Lastly, the applicant stated its interest in investigating some of these clinical aspects in future research, recognizing that additional reliable studies could help improve clinical practice, but questioned CMS's concern that the available information at present is inadequate to find the EndoForceTM Connector represents substantial clinical improvement relative to other available technologies.
In response to our concern about whether the EndoForceTM Connector is the cause of any cumulative patency improvement or if it can be contributed to the less invasive endovascular procedure used for implantation, the applicant stated that it does not see how these two aspects can be meaningfully separated for investigation because it is the EndoForceTM Connector itself that enables the endovascular approach and no purely endovascular AVG placement procedure, with or without an additional device, is available. A commenter stated that while this is a legitimate causal question, the distinction should not obscure how the EndoForceTM Connector functions in clinical use. The commenter stated that the endovascular implantation method is not a separate, unrelated co-intervention, but the means by which the EndoForceTM Connector performs its FDA-approved function of creating the venous graft attachment. The commenter further stated that the available evidence may not establish whether any observed benefit predominantly results from reduced surgical trauma, altered geometry or hemodynamics, the EndoForceTM Connector's physical characteristics, or some combination of those effects, but the remaining mechanistic uncertainty does not require CMS to treat the EndoForceTM Connector and the procedure as clinically unrelated. The commenter stated that the clinically relevant comparison is between the EndoForceTM System as used according to its FDA indication and the conventional sutured venous anastomosis it replaces.
In response to our concern about the appropriateness of comparing Burgess et al. (2024) to the three provided background studies (Halbert et al., 2020; Harms et al., 2016; and Woodside et al., 2021) due to differences in study design, study location, and patient population, the applicant stated that Burgess et al. (2024) and Halbert et al. (2020) have very similar population characteristics, outcomes, and other factors, noting that detailed information about the patient populations and other aspects of the studies included in Halbert et al. (2020) are provided in a set of Supplemental Tables available on the journal's website. Further, the applicant stated that Halbert et al. (2020) showed no statistically significant difference across average outcomes in U.S. studies versus those conducted overseas; type of AVG used; observational studies versus randomized controlled trials; and sex, race, or presence of diabetes. The applicant also stated that Halbert et al. (2020) reviewed studies using a bias risk assessment procedure and found no statistically significant difference in bias between the studies.
Moreover, the applicant provided additional information about the population characteristics of studies included in the Astor et al. (2026) meta-analysis and compared them to Burgess et al. (2024), noting that patients included in Burgess et al. (2024) were older (mean age: 58.24 years vs. 62.6 years); had higher rates of diabetes ( printed page 70447) (51.99 percent vs. 62.0 percent, p = 0.013), higher rates of cardiovascular disease (16.05 percent vs. 49.4 percent, p<0.001), higher tobacco use (10.63 percent vs. 14.6 percent, p = 0.12); and lower rates of hypertension (75.96 percent vs. 56.3 percent, p<0.001). In addition, the applicant stated that Burgess et al. (2024), Halbert et al. (2020), and Astor et al. (2026) had patient populations similar in a number of key characteristics that are generally thought to influence patency and compared them to values reported in the United States Renal Data System (age: 62.6 years, 61.0 years, 58.24 years, and 63.21 years respectively; sex (percent male/female): 39/61, 45/55, 42/58, and 58.6/41.4, respectively; and diabetes prevalence: 62 percent, 48 percent, 52 percent, and 45 percent, respectively). (2024) are more closely associated with worse outcomes for cumulative patency, and insofar as these variables might affect cumulative patency, they would tend to depress rather than elevate the cumulative patency results relative to those in the other studies; however, the EndoForceTM System showed a clinically significant improvement.
In response to our concern that results in Halbert et al. (2020), Harms et al. (2016), and Woodside et al. (2021) may be inappropriate comparators to Burgess et al. (2024) as older studies may not reflect current operative techniques and perioperative care in the U.S., the applicant stated that basic procedures and technology related to AVGs have not materially changed in the last 20 years. The applicant added that further analysis of studies in Halbert et al. (2020) illustrate slightly higher (69.5 percent vs. 68.8 percent), but not statistically significant, 12-month cumulative patency results in the older cohort of studies (published pre-2014) compared to the more recent cohort (published between 2014 and 2019). The applicant also noted that, in Burgess et al. (2024) and Halbert et al. (2020), included studies' time periods overlap (2018 to 2021 compared to 2007 to 2019, respectively). The applicant stated that this suggests that no meaningful improvement in AVG vascular access outcomes occurred and that the studies in question are all comparable regardless of publication date. The applicant stated that the EndoForceTM System represents a meaningful technological advance in AVG, because it directly targets the longstanding failure point through a sutureless endovascular venous anastomosis. Another commenter stated that although the concern warrants consideration, the significance of a study's age should depend on whether the treatment being compared has materially changed. The commenter stated that although imaging, graft materials, perioperative management, surveillance, and techniques used to treat failing access have advanced, the basic surgical method for creating venous anastomosis in a conventional AVG has remained largely the same for decades. The commenter added that the EndoForceTM System's design avoids the conventional sutured graft-to-vein junction by creating an end-to-end endovascular venous anastomosis, reduces local vessel trauma and adverse flow conditions, and may lessen the drivers of neointimal hyperplasia. The commenter concluded that older studies comparing ePTFE grafts with conventional surgical anastomosis are still relevant if that comparator and its underlying failure mechanism remain a cause of graft failure, even if the study predates Burgess et al. (2024). Lastly, the commenter stated that older evidence may warrant less weight than a contemporary controlled comparison, but this does not negate the older evidence's value when the conventional treatment remains materially similar and the failure mechanism under study remains clinically relevant.
In response to our concern that differences in vascular access location for the patients in the Burgess et al. (2024), Halbert et al. (2020), Harms et al. (2016), and Woodside et al. (2021) studies may be confounding factors that influence patency and adversely impact comparability of results, the applicant stated that the most important difference that might matter for the outcomes of interest is the size of the vessels: the major veins and arteries in the upper arm being larger than in those the lower arm. The applicant cited a study stating this difference is more pertinent for AVFs, which generally appear to work best when vessels have a larger diameter.[45] The applicant stated that for AVGs, vessels as small as two millimeters in diameter generally work well and such vessels are available in the lower arms of most individuals. In addition, the applicant cited another study that investigated AVGs' optimal location (upper arm versus forearm) and concluded that upper arm AVGs have similar graft patency and access-related complications compared with forearm AVGs despite the fact that [upper arm AVGs] are assumed to be constructed based on larger outflow veins.[46] Further, the applicant cited a study that reviewed records of over 52,000 accesses placed between 2021 and 2022 and found that only 9.7 percent of AVGs were placed in forearms and that this percentage had declined over time.[47] Based on these studies, the applicant stated that although the comparator studies may include lower-arm cases while Burgess et al. (2024) does not, any confounding effect on the outcomes of interest may be minimal.
In response to our concern regarding differences in vascular access locations in Burgess et al. (2024), which evaluated upper arm AVGs, compared to the background studies' (Halbert et al., 2020; Harms et al., 2016; and Woodside et al., 2021), which had various access locations, and our concern that comparator studies included in the Astor et al. (2026) excluded studies which only assessed lower extremity or chest AVGs, the applicant stated that lower extremity AVGs have generally been regarded as a last resort for patients who have exhausted their upper extremity access possibilities. The applicant added that, although good estimates of the extent of use in the dialysis population are unavailable, a few studies suggest the number may be less than two percent of patients. Additionally, the applicant cited a study that found recent case studies show cumulative patency rates at 6 months for leg (thigh) grafts and arm (upper extremity) AVGs are generally comparable, ranging between 75 and 85 percent. The applicant further stated that this study found that leg AVGs may exhibit slightly superior or equal cumulative patency compared to arm grafts due to femoral vessels' larger diameter.[48] Based on this information, ( printed page 70448) the applicant stated that, if the comparator studies did include patients with lower extremity AVGs, the net effect would likely be a higher cumulative patency, which in turn would understate the EndoForceTM System's comparative advantage.
Finally, with regard to our concern about the potential inclusion of chest AVGs in the comparative data, the applicant stated that chest AVGs appear to only be used in an exceedingly small number of cases. The applicant also cited one medical center's case-series, which reported chest AVGs in only 0.56 percent of 1,192 patients between 2007 and 2012.[49] The applicant stated that the possibility of cases with AVGs in the legs or chest does not appear to be a major concern, and specific to chest AVGs, the possibility of the comparator studies' results being affected is remote enough to be negligible.
A commenter stated that, taken together, the Burgess et al. (2024), Kramer et al. (2026), and Astor et al. (2026) studies support substantial clinical improvement for the EndoForceTM System. The commenter also stated that, while the studies are not randomized, concurrent comparisons, and have identified limitations, they provide prospective, multicenter evidence in the specific upper-arm AVG population for which the EndoForceTM System is indicated. The commenter added that these limitations affect the precision of attributing outcomes solely to the EndoForceTM System, but they do not negate the clinical significance of the observed results or justify CMS disregarding the comparative evidence altogether.
In response to the totality of our concerns regarding Burgess et al. (2024), a commenter stated that experienced, specialized dialysis-access physicians prospectively designed Burgess et al. (2024) to support FDA review and understood the difference between a statistically attractive endpoint and an access that remains useful to a real patient, and therefore, the consistency of the patency findings across the pivotal study, systematic reviews, and the Astor et al. (2026) meta-analysis should be given meaningful weight.
In response to our concerns about Astor et al.'s (2026) comparison of primary patency results, a commenter agreed that the evidence does not suggest that the EndoForceTM System improves every AVG performance measure but stated that primary patency and cumulative patency measure different clinical outcomes. Per the commenter, primary patency measures how long an access remains functional before the first intervention, and cumulative or secondary patency concerns whether the access can ultimately be preserved rather than abandoned. The commenter stated that, therefore, an AVG that requires an intervention but remains available for dialysis is not clinically equivalent to an AVG that is lost. The commenter added that it believes the available evidence suggests that the EndoForceTM System may be more beneficial for preserving AVG access than for preventing all subsequent interventions. Additionally, the commenter stated that this distinction is particularly important for patients whose permanent-access options are already limited, because AVG preservation is a clinically meaningful outcome and can prevent loss of a functioning AVG, use of additional vascular territory, interruptions in reliable dialysis access, and a patient returning to catheter dependence. The commenter concluded that substantial clinical improvement should be based on whether the EndoForceTM System improves the ability to maintain durable permanent access and avoid graft abandonment, not by measures of primary patency.
In response to our note that Astor et al. (2026) derived 6-month patency measurements from studies that did not specifically report 6-month patency outcomes, the applicant stated that 6-month patency outcomes in Burgess et al. (2024) were higher than both cohorts of studies. The applicant further stated that Astor et al. (2026) provided comparison information indicating little difference between studies that relied on survival curves versus other studies. The applicant also stated that relying on information in survival curves where such information is not reported in text or tables is methodologically appropriate. The applicant further stated that Astor et al. (2026) used commercial software specifically designed to extract numerical data from plots and that these studies, among many others, have found excellent accuracy and no differential bias in estimates abstracted using such tools. The applicant concluded that there is, therefore, no reason to suspect that this effect is considerable or would manifestly affect results' reliability to the extent that they should be excluded from the analysis. Lastly, the applicant noted that a peer-reviewed journal accepted the study which included this methodology after publication of the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule.
In response to our concern about whether Halbert et al. (2020)'s 20 percent AVG abandonment rate is an appropriate comparator to Astor et al. (2026)'s 8 percent AVG abandonment rate due to varied study locations and time periods, the applicant stated that the Astor et al. (2026) meta-analysis summarized 30 of the 32 studies published in the last 10 years and that studies conducted in the U.S. and outside the U.S. reflect no significant difference based on supplemental tables for Halbert et al. (2020).
In response to our interest in additional information clarifying the meaning of upper arm, the applicant stated that the term upper arm in the EndoForceTM System's FDA approval refers to the portion of the arm above the elbow.
In response to our concern that Kramer et al. (2026) lacked sufficient power to assess statistical significance, the applicant stated that the study authors do not claim the results are statistically significant. The applicant stated that Kramer et al.'s observed number of interventions per patient-year (1.32), while somewhat higher than the rate of 1.22 reported for the larger sample in Burgess et al. (2024), does compare favorably with the rates of 1.58 and 1.87 shown in Halbert et al. (2020) and Woodside et al. (2021), respectively. The applicant further stated that Kramer et al. (2026) is an extension of Burgess et al. (2024), capturing up to an additional 6 months of data for a subset of Burgess et al. (2024) patients who were high risk due to their experience of early interventions, were not lost to follow-up, and consented to additional evaluation. Additionally, the applicant noted that Kramer et al. (2026) is an intentional sub-group analysis with some additional observations on patients treated with the EndoForceTM System, and therefore, the sample size was ipso facto limited by the number of Burgess et al. (2024) patients that received at least 1 intervention in 6 months, were available for further study, and consented to extended follow up; however, the characteristics of the patient groups in both studies are very similar.
In response to our concerns regarding Kramer et al.'s (2026) insufficiently-sized patient population, inconclusive results, and differences from the available comparator populations, a commenter stated that although the study was not a randomized efficacy ( printed page 70449) trial and had a small sample, it should be viewed as an assessment of durability and procedural burden in a particularly challenging subgroup from the pivotal cohort, including patients who required early maintenance. The commenter also stated that Kramer et al.'s (2026) lower intervention rates are clinically meaningful because each potential avoided intervention reduces procedural risk, preserves veins, protects future options, and reduces the likelihood that a patient will experience access failure and return to catheter dependence.
In response to our concern about whether the strength of evidence of Kramer et al. (2026) may have been impacted by selection bias, as the patient cohort was selected and analyzed post-hoc, rather than identified as a variable of interest at the Burgess et al. (2024) initiation, the applicant explained that it selected and analyzed the Kramer et al. (2026) cohort post-hoc because, during the Burgess et al. (2024) study with input from FDA, it realized that durability results may be skewed if the patients in Burgess et al. (2024) received more maintenance services than normal. The applicant stated that it sponsored Kramer et al. (2026) to examine whether patients with an AVG and the EndoForceTM System received more maintenance procedures than normally expected and that the study determined the patients received fewer interventions than comparator studies.
In response to our concern about the appropriateness of comparing measures of cumulative patency in Burgess et al. (2024) and Kramer et al. (2026) that are not equally defined, the applicant stated the measure of cumulative patency for both studies was identical with respect to whether those who received an intervention before first cannulation were included, and how patency was measured did not differ between the studies, though obviously the measurement periods were different. The applicant stated the design of Kramer et al. (2026) was intended to capture 6 months of patient experience after either a first intervention (if the patient experienced 1 within the first 6 months) or after an implant (in the case of those who received no maintenance interventions during the 6 months). The applicant further stated a patient who received a first intervention on day 179 after implant would then be followed for an additional 6 months for a total of 1 year less a day (in the absence of some other censoring event), and investigation of a patient with no interventions by day 180 would be censored on that day. Per the applicant, how patency was measured did not differ between the Burgess et al. (2024) and Kramer et al. (2026) studies, though obviously the measurement periods were different.
In response to our concern that it is clinically inappropriate to compare the EndoForceTM System to devices used for AVF creation to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies, the applicant stated AVFs and AVGs are indisputably different, but it objects to CMS's dismissal of the comparison. The applicant stated its claim that the improvement in AVG patency means that an AVG with the EndoForceTM System would exhibit patency comparable to mature AVFs is important because greater patency has been recognized as one advantage of AVFs over AVGs, and therefore, impacts clinical decision making relating to choice of vascular access for a particular patient at a particular time. The applicant additionally stated that comparison of AVGs with the EndoForceTM System to AVFs is entirely pertinent as reviewing a technology as it compares to other relevant clinical choices should be an important point of examining substantial clinical improvement. The applicant further stated that patients and their physicians are frequently able to choose between AVFs and AVGs where both would be anatomically and otherwise suitable, and speed to maturity for dialysis (on which AVGs dominate), cumulative patency (on which AVFs have dominated), extent of maintenance procedures required, and risk of infection are among the factors taken into consideration. Lastly, the applicant stated that achieving comparable cumulative patency to that reported for AVFs, including the two percutaneous AVF devices (WavelinQTM and EllipsysTM), would thus improve AVGs' clinical attractiveness in comparison to an existing, widely used therapeutic option for the dialysis population and that this improvement could be particularly important for patients that may be marginal as candidates for an AVF ( e.g., those with smaller vessels, such as many females).
In contrast to the applicant, a commenter stated that because the EndoForceTM System creates an AVG in such patients, the relevant comparator for assessing substantial clinical improvement is the conventional surgically-created graft-to-vein anastomosis, not mature AVFs and devices used to create AVFs as these technologies involve fundamentally different mechanisms and clinical uses. The commenter also agreed with CMS that AVFs and AVGs differ in mechanism and use and noted that AVF creation may be unsuccessful or inappropriate for some patients, making an AVG the more appropriate permanent-access option.[50] The commenter further stated that for patients who are appropriate candidates for permanent AVG access, maintaining this access can help avoid prolonged catheter dependence, its greater infection risk, and other associated clinical risks.
Further, the commenter stated that CMS's prior application of the substantial clinical improvement standard supports granting the EndoForceTM System transitional pass-through payment status despite meaningful evidentiary limitations because overall the evidence supports the technology producing a clinically important benefit. The commenter cited three precedents it believes support evaluating the limitations in the provided evidence as factors affecting weight and certainty, rather than as categorical barriers to approval. The commenter cited CMS's approval of the Hemospray® Endoscopic Hemostat in the CY 2021 OPPS/ASC final rule (85 FR 85997 through 86003), in which CMS considered concerns including single-arm studies, selection bias, and differences in study populations but approved transitional pass-through payment status; the AUGMENT Bone Graft in the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule (84 FR 61292 through 61294) after initially questioning the evidence's adequacy, the appropriate comparator, and the duration of follow-up; and the Tablo System in the CY 2022 ESRD PPS final rule (86 FR 61889 through 61906), in which CMS stated that randomized controlled trials are not required to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. We agree with the applicant and commenters that the EndoForceTM System and the endovascular procedure should be assessed together for the purposes of evaluating substantial clinical improvement. However, we continue to have several of the concerns listed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. In particular, we are concerned about the lack of comparative evidence based on matched patient data. We note that imbalance in baseline patient characteristics could confound the association between EndoForceTM and patency. We acknowledge the comments from the applicant and a ( printed page 70450) commenter regarding vascular access location and the time periods, or ages, of different studies, but remain concerned about the extent to which the findings of the Burgess et al. (2024), Astor et al. (2026), and Kramer et al. (2026) studies might have been biased by measured and unmeasured confounders. We expressed concern in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that Burgess et al. (2024) lacked stratification by key clinical factors known to affect AVG outcomes, and therefore, there are insufficient data to rule out the possibility that factors other than EndoForceTM may also have impacted cumulative and primary unassisted patency. We acknowledge the comparison provided by the applicant, in its comments, of the average age and body mass index (kg/m2) of the patients in the Burgess et al.(2024) and Astor et al. (2026) studies, and the percentages of those who were male, white, diabetic, with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or current tobacco use. However, we note that other risk factors, such as prior catheter use, low albumin, an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) level, low fetuin-A, low diastolic blood pressure, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, peripheral artery disease, and low initial intra-access blood flow (< 650 mL/min), have also been associated with decreased patency.[51 52 53 54 55] Although the applicant noted that the sample size would have limited the value of stratified analyses within the Burgess et al. study (2024), this limitation does not resolve our concerns about differences across studies in patients' baseline characteristics, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and study designs. These differences could increase the uncertainty [56] around the estimates for the endpoints.[57 58]
While we agree with the commenter who stated that cumulative patency is a clinically relevant endpoint for evaluating the EndoForceTM System, we continue to have concerns about the high degree of variability, or heterogeneity, among the comparison studies in the two meta-analyses, Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020). Although commenters discussed several potential sources of heterogeneity, we did not receive sufficient information or analyses to determine the extent to which those factors account for the high degree of variability among the included studies. We note that the values of the I[2] statistic in Astor et al. (2026) (I[2] =99.36 percent for cumulative patency at 6 months; I[2] =99.44 percent for primary unassisted patency at 6 months) and Halbert et al. (2020) (I[2] =91 percent for cumulative patency at 12 months) indicated considerable heterogeneity among included studies. We remain uncertain whether the pooled estimates of 83.23 percent and 60.35 percent in the Astor et al. study (2026) accurately represented the 6-month cumulative and primary unassisted patency, respectively, of AVGs with a sutured venous anastomosis. Similarly, we remain concerned about the reliability and validity of the patency rates reported by Halbert et al. (2020) and whether these serve as an appropriate standard for comparison. While we acknowledge that heterogeneity can be difficult to avoid when comparing the results of different studies, we remain concerned that substantial variability may affect the extent to which generalizable conclusions can be formed about EndoForceTM 's impact on patency relative to existing technologies.[59] As a result, we remain concerned that the comparisons between EndoForceTM and existing treatments for those endpoints may not be reliable indicators of EndoForceTM 's substantive clinical improvements.
In addition, we note that the primary endpoint of Burgess et al. (2024), cumulative patency at 6 months, was compared to the pre-specified 6-month performance goal of 75 percent. Per Burgess et al. (2024), this performance goal was based on five published studies.[60] However, we note that these studies reported cumulative and primary unassisted patency at different time points, ranging from 6 to 22.5 months. We also note that while three of the studies reported patency at 12 months, only one [61] reported patency at 6 months. As a result, we are unable to determine whether the 75 percent performance goal was a valid indicator of the 6-month performance of existing technologies, or the extent to which comparing EndoForceTM 's effects on cumulative patency against the 75 percent performance goal could reliably indicate whether EndoForceTM performs better than existing technologies in maintaining patency.
In addition, we remain concerned about the use of a digitization tool by Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) to abstract data on 6-month patency measurements from Kaplan-Meier survival curves from studies that did not specifically report 6-month patency outcomes. We note that the 6-month patency rates from more than half of the studies in Astor et al.'s (2026) meta-analysis were abstracted using DigitizeIt software, a digitization tool.[62] We note that studies validating abstracted data have found DigitizeIt ( printed page 70451) and similar software in general to be highly accurate.[63] However, we also note that the reliability and validity of the abstracted data have been found to be independent of the specific software program, but are dependent on the properties of the figure being digitized.[64] In particular, the reliability of the abstracted data depends on the quality of the initial input and the level of information provided by the publication.[65] Published figures, like low-quality or rasterized images, rather than the abstraction, were a major source of errors.[66] Halbert et al (2020) reported that some survival curves could not be digitized because of the poor quality of the original publication graphics.[67] A recent study found that digitization tools like DigitizeIt could be limited by operator precision and image resolution.[68] Even tools developed using automated image-based approaches remain constrained by figure quality and rasterization artifacts. Errors introduced during digitization can propagate and affect downstream analyses, such as treatment effect estimation and meta-analysis. Another recent study found that pixelation and color blending could degrade coordinate accuracy, introducing noise during digitization.[69] The study also found visual representations of censoring to be another common source of errors. Specifically, when censoring ticks are missing or poorly resolved, algorithms may misplace event timings, leading to biased survival estimates. Dense clustering of early censoring marks can obscure later events or make digitization unreliable. Because a 6-month patency point sits exactly in this early, censoring-dense region, we are concerned that these limitations may have important implications for the Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) meta-analyses. We remain concerned about the quality of these abstracted data and the potential impact on the pooled 6-month patency among currently available AVGs, and uncertain whether the results reported by Astor et al. (2026) and Halbert et al. (2020) indicate that EndoForceTM produced better clinical outcomes than the AVGs with a standard sutured venous anastomosis. Regarding Astor et al. (2026), it also remains unclear whether the difference between the 6-month cumulative patency rates of 92 percent in Burgess et al. (2024) and 86 percent in the 12 studies reporting numerical values was statistically significant.
We continue to have concerns about the appropriateness of comparing EndoForceTM 's effects on patency with those of AVFs.
