First, we identified instances in which respondents that were not participating in the 340B Program during the relevant study time period (as verified using the 340B Office of Pharmacy Affairs Information System (340B OPAIS)) reported acquisition cost data in the 340B fields of the survey. These observations likely reflected reporting errors, given that these hospitals could not have accessed 340B discounts. Therefore, we proposed to exclude 340B acquisition cost data submitted by non-340B hospitals from analyses of 340B acquisition cost to maintain consistency with the survey design and statutory framework. This refinement removed 850 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey.
Second, we identified instances in which respondents reported purchasing drugs through the 340B Program for 58 ( printed page 70509) NDCs that did not have a 340B ceiling price during the survey time period. These observations may reflect reporting errors, such as reporting acquisition data for the incorrect NDC within a drug that was intended, given that no 340B agreement, or associated discount, was available for these NDCs. In some cases, where these NDCs had 340B ceiling prices during other quarters outside the survey time period, these observations may be the result of respondent confusion over the survey reporting period or the time period when these NDCs had a 340B ceiling price in place. Alternatively, hospitals may have acquired non-340B NDCs through the 340B Prime Vendor Platform (PVP) without receiving a 340B discount price; [114] while hospitals may have considered these purchases to be 340B acquisitions for the purposes of their survey reporting, evaluating these responses as part of 340B margin calculations would provide an inaccurate picture of the acquisition costs for NDCs with 340B discounts. We also did not elect to evaluate these responses as part of non-340B margin calculations as it was impossible to separate instances of reporting errors from non-340B purchases made through the 340B PVP. Therefore, we proposed to exclude 340B survey responses for these NDCs without 340B ceiling prices from analyses of both 340B and non-340B acquisition cost to maintain consistency with the survey design and statutory framework. This refinement removed 839 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey.
Third, we identified a small number of responses from hospital subunits that submitted identical data to their parent unit. Hospital subunits were identified as entities where the third digit of its CMS Certification Number (CCN) is T (representing inpatient rehabilitation units) or S (representing psychiatric units). Parent units were identified as entities where all six digits of its CCN are numeric.[115] To identify a parent unit for each subunit, the T or S in the third digit was replaced with the numeric digit associated with the provider type of that subunit (either 0, 2, 3, or 4). If this replacement yielded more than one possible parent unit, the subunit was further matched with a parent unit based on CCN name and ZIP code. Identical parent-subunit data were identified as survey responses with the exact same number of total units and total net acquisition costs reported for the exact same NDCs. These observations likely reflect duplicative data reported by one submitter who was responsible for multiple entities. Accordingly, we proposed to exclude these duplicative responses from subunits in favor of only retaining the equivalent responses from the parent unit. We identified 27 subunits with duplicative data to their parent unit, and this refinement removed 4,799 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey.
Fourth, we identified instances in which reported acquisition costs for drugs purchased under the 340B Program exceeded the maximum applicable 340B ceiling price during the survey time period. By statute, covered entities cannot be required to pay more than the 340B ceiling price for drugs acquired under the 340B Program. Such observations are not representative of actual acquisition costs and are likely attributable to reporting or data entry errors (for example, miscalculations or incorrect decimal placement). Accordingly, we proposed to exclude 340B drug purchases with average acquisition costs above the maximum ceiling price from our analysis. This refinement removed 4,667 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey.
Fifth, we observed that certain respondents reported units for specific drugs, including clotting factors and certain respiratory therapies, in international units (IU) or milligrams (MG) rather than the required NDC-based units. IU is the HCPCS billing unit for the clotting factors and MG is the HCPCS billing unit for the respiratory therapies; [116] however, because the survey requires reporting at the NDC level, the use of IU- or MG-based units would result in substantial distortions in calculated per-unit acquisition costs, typically producing extremely high reported unit volumes and correspondingly low per-unit costs. These observations are not comparable to properly reported NDC-level data. To avoid possible selection bias that may result from specifically excluding responses with units reported in IU or MG, we therefore proposed to exclude all survey responses for affected NDCs with units reported in IU or MG from the analysis. This refinement removed 4,398 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey. We note, if CMS included this data, the acquisition cost margins would have been significantly lower than Medicare payment rates.
The exclusion of these anomalous observations, in conjunction with the application of the outlier trimming methodology and other data standardization approaches described previously, improved the reliability and validity of the resulting estimates of acquisition costs. In particular, it ensured that the resulting estimates reflect plausible and internally consistent acquisition costs while minimizing the influence of erroneous or noncomparable data. Moreover, applying these five data refinement exclusions did not have a substantial impact on the overall number of survey records included in analyses of acquisition cost. Collectively, these five refinements removed 14,313 records out of the 160,430 records received through the survey. In other words, after applying these five exclusions, there remained 146,117 survey records in the dataset, 91.1 percent of the total 160,430 original records we received from respondents. We note that there are some overlaps in each individual exclusion of survey records, where the same survey record was excluded for meeting more than one exclusion criterion.
For each of the five scenarios discussed previously, we proposed to exclude survey responses for values that are not plausible given statutory requirements or that exhibit clear inconsistencies in reporting. Specifically, we proposed to exclude survey responses that were identified as meeting at least one of the five scenarios listed previously based on our manual review of the data, ASP pricing files, Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) 340B ceiling pricing files, and relevant policy and billing guidance. We believed that this approach represented the most appropriate and methodologically sound means of estimating the typical margin in the survey data between hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs and ASP. We solicited comment on our approach to identifying and excluding anomalous data, as well as on the overall methodology used to ( printed page 70510) evaluate the survey data for purposes of our proposal.
c. OPPS Drug Acquisition Cost Survey Results
(1) Survey Response Rate and Respondent Characteristics
We first determined the response rate and hospital characteristics of survey respondents to understand which entities had submitted a survey response, then compared them to the characteristics of nonrespondents and the survey-eligible population to assess their representativeness relative to the overall population. We also applied a methodology to refine the population of survey-eligible hospitals to more precisely reflect those entities with meaningful outpatient acquisition volume for drugs included in the survey.
Approximately 43.6 percent of the 4,494 entities eligible for OPPS payment (hereinafter referred to as “survey-eligible hospitals”) submitted a survey response and approximately 29.8 percent of eligible hospitals reported that they had acquisition costs during the survey time period. We received a number of responses, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters, from eligible hospitals indicating that they would not be providing their acquisition data and explaining their reasons for not doing so. Before refining the population, approximately 34.9 percent of non-340B hospitals and approximately 23.1 percent of 340B hospitals responded to the survey and reported that they had acquisition costs for survey-eligible drugs during the surveyed time period (Table 64).
However, claims analysis of the eligible hospital population determined that a subset of entities that were included in the survey had zero outpatient claims for survey-relevant HCPCS codes during the survey study period. Many of these entities did not submit a survey response, likely because they did not acquire any survey-relevant drugs during the time period. Other entities were hospital subunits that did not submit a survey response or submitted a response reporting zero acquisition costs, but their parent unit submitted a survey response reporting acquisition data.
Consequently, we applied population refinements to consolidate subunits with their parent units and to remove entities from the survey that neither reported acquisition costs nor had outpatient billing volume for HCPCS codes corresponding to NDCs included in the survey during the specified time period. These refinements resulted in a slightly smaller population that may more appropriately reflect the universe of eligible hospitals with meaningful and relevant outpatient drug acquisition volume. This population was almost exclusively composed of short-term acute care hospitals: 2,977 out of 3,147 total CCNs (94.6 percent) in the refined population are short-term acute care hospitals as compared to 3,018 out of 4,494 total CCNs (67.2 percent) in the original population. This change occurred for two reasons. First, by consolidating subunits with their parent unit, all subunits (that is, psychiatric units and inpatient rehabilitation units), which had accounted for 742 (16.5 percent) in the original population no longer appear in the population as distinct hospitals. Second, this refinement also markedly reduced the number of psychiatric hospitals, long-term care hospitals, and rehabilitation hospitals in the refined population because the majority of these hospitals neither reported acquisition costs nor billed any relevant outpatient claims.
Of this refined study population, approximately 41.4 percent of hospitals responded to the survey and reported that they had acquisition costs during the surveyed study period. Additionally, approximately 53.3 percent of non-340B hospitals and approximately 28.6 percent of 340B hospitals in the refined population responded to the survey and reported that they had acquisition costs during the surveyed study period (Table 65). For discussion of analyses that we undertook to confirm that this response rate is sufficiently large to yield a statistically valid sample, we refer readers to the calculation of confidence intervals in section (3) Population Weight Adjustment and Statistical Validity.
Using the refined population, we then compared observable hospital characteristics of survey respondents that reported acquisition costs to the characteristics of the survey-eligible population (Table 66). Compared to the overall survey-eligible population, hospitals that responded to the survey and reported acquisition cost data were slightly more likely to have lower claims billing volume, be smaller, be located in a rural area, and not be major teaching hospitals.
Given these slight differences in hospital characteristics between respondents and the overall population, we performed inverse probability weighting (IPW) to confirm that respondents' data yielded statistically representative estimates of hospital outpatient drug acquisition costs. We refer readers to the discussion of IPW-adjusted margins in section (3) Population Weight Adjustment and Statistical Validity.
We received public comments on our survey response rate and respondent characteristics. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Two commenters raised concerns about the creation of the refined hospital population, especially in relation to analysis of the survey response rate. A commenter pointed out that the refinements resulted in a larger increase in the response rate for non-340B hospitals (from 34.9 percent to 53.3 percent) than for 340B hospitals (from 23.1 percent to 28.6 percent).
Response: The population of 4,494 CCNs that CMS initially identified for ODACS eligibility was intended to be maximally inclusive in order to identify all entities paid under the OPPS that could have purchased survey-relevant outpatient drugs during the ODACS study period. However, further claims analysis revealed that a subset of the 4,494 eligible CCNs did not submit any OPPS claims for survey-relevant HCPCS codes during the study period. Many of these entities, which were predominantly subunits or non-acute care hospitals, also did not submit an ODACS response or submitted a response reporting zero drug acquisitions. These observations are not unexpected given that many subunits likely acquire their outpatient drugs in conjunction with their parent unit and some non-acute care entities do not acquire or administer the specific outpatient drugs included in the survey at all.
To create a population with evidence of survey-relevant OPPS drug utilization—either via their ODACS response or claims data—CMS applied two refinements. CMS refers readers to Section 3.1.2 of the ODACS Technical Report for details on these refinements and their impact on the hospital population. Consequently, the refined population of 3,147 CCNs more precisely reflects the universe of hospitals with meaningful and relevant outpatient acquisition volume for drugs included in the survey and, in turn, better focuses on the universe of hospitals that would be impacted by the proposed policy change.
The survey response rate changes as a result of these refinements because the denominator of response rate changes. The response rate is calculated as the number of CCNs that submitted an ODACS response divided by all survey-eligible CCNs. In the initial population, the denominator of 4,494 CCNs yields a response rate of 29.8 percent ; in the refined population, the denominator of 3,147 CCNs yields a response rate of 41.4 percent. CMS believes that the refined population response rate of 41.4 percent better represents the share of hospitals that reported acquiring surveyed NDCs out of all hospitals that could have reasonably been expected to report OPPS acquisitions of the surveyed NDCs. These refinements had a larger impact on the non-340B response rate only because the vast majority of subunits and non-acute care entities in the initial population are non-340B entities.
Comment: Many commenters contended that the response rate, especially from 340B hospitals, does not meet section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act's statutory threshold of a “large sample of hospitals” and is therefore too low to justify the proposed policy change. One commenter cited the 2005 acquisition cost survey conducted by GAO, which aimed to receive responses from 1,000 hospitals after sampling 1,400 hospitals out of an initially eligible 3,450 hospitals, to justify a 29.8 percent response rate as meeting the requirement for a large sample. Some commenters also linked the response rate to concerns over data representativeness, arguing that because the response rate among 340B hospitals was lower than among non-340B hospitals, it calls into question the representativeness and comparability of the 340B and non-340B respondent populations.
Response: We note that CMS sampled more hospitals than the GAO. Rather than limit the survey to a subset of hospitals, CMS ensured through its methodology that the maximum number of hospitals could participate and fulfill their statutory obligation to respond to the survey. For a discussion of this statutory requirement, see the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule (90 FR 53764-53765). Nowhere in statutory language is “a large sample of hospitals” defined nor is a particular threshold set for achieving “a large sample of hospitals.” Moreover, determining adequate sample size in any survey-based quantitative analysis is a complex challenge that involves evaluating factors unique to that analysis, including the sampling design, population size, and population variability. For instance, the 2005 GAO survey design employed a stratified random sampling methodology that explicitly sampled from the initial hospital population; therefore, applying a threshold of 29.8 percent is not comparable to CMS's ODACS survey design, which did not employ a sampling methodology. Rather, CMS invited all 4,494 hospitals identified as paid under the OPPS to respond to the survey and contribute any acquisition data for surveyed NDCs. A response-rate floor defined for a stratified sample does not have an established meaning for a census survey.
Consistent with generally accepted statistical practice, sample size sufficiency was evaluated through the calculation of confidence intervals (CIs) and IPW adjustment rather than seeking to meet an arbitrary threshold. CMS notes that a smaller sample size does not necessarily make a sample less representative; rather, representativeness is governed by response mechanism instead of sample size. Large samples can be more skewed in certain characteristics, yielding potentially larger biases. This possibility is why CMS performed IPW adjustment and statistical diagnostic tests to understand and account for potential sample size and data representativeness issues. The IPW adjustment and calculation of CIs indicated that the response rate yielded sufficiently precise estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs. As we explained in Section 3.5.2 of the ODACS Technical Report, to evaluate whether the number of survey responses received was sufficient to produce statistically valid estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs, we calculated CIs for both unadjusted and IPW adjusted acquisition cost margins. The CIs provide measures of whether the response rate adequately captures true population results. When response rate is insufficiently low, CIs are wide due to the high degree of uncertainty regarding where the true result lies. Conversely, when response rate is sufficient, CIs narrow as uncertainty lessens. CMS calculated the CIs using a bootstrap methodology. First, the full dataset of survey records (after applying data refinements and excluding geometric mean outliers) was repeatedly sampled with replacement using hospitals as the sample unit; acquisition cost margins were recalculated for each repeated sample. This process was repeated 10,000 times to generate distributions of unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margin estimates. Finally, the 95% CIs were identified for each margin estimate using the 2.5th percentile as the lower bound and the 97.5th percentile as the upper bound.
We reported the impact of IPW adjustment and CI calculation on acquisition cost margins in Section 4.4.2 of the ODACS Technical Report which described that applying IPW adjustment had minimal impact on acquisition cost margins for either non-340B or 340B acquired drugs. For drugs acquired outside the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs were 2.7 percent above the mean ASP before ( printed page 70514) IPW adjustment and 2.8 percent above the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. For drugs acquired through the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs were 33.4 percent below the mean ASP before IPW adjustment and 33.1% below the mean ASP after IPW adjustment (Table 67). The consistency between unadjusted and IPW-adjusted results supports the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses.
The 95 percent CIs for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins did not substantially differ from each other, indicating that the weighting adjustment had minimal impact on the resulting estimates. For non-340B drugs, the CIs spanned 3.8 percent below the mean ASP to 6.9 percent above the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and between 1.6 percent below the mean ASP to 6.5 percent above the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. For 340B-acquired drugs, the CIs were much narrower and spanned 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and from 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin.
The narrow CIs for 340B-acquired drugs support the statistical validity of the survey results on 340B drugs and indicate that the received sample is sufficiently large to produce reliable estimates of hospital outpatient drug acquisition costs for 340B drugs. The CIs for the non-340B drugs span a wider range of potential acquisition cost margins, which is expected given the greater distributional spread in the survey data for non-340B drugs.
Comment: Many commenters noted slight differences in composition between the respondent population and overall population of survey-eligible hospitals along observable hospital characteristics. Some alleged that CMS had not demonstrated data representativeness for groups of their interest such as major teaching hospitals, rural hospitals, and high-volume purchasers. Other commenters also requested more information about representation along particular stratifications ( e.g., payer mix and patient populations) and for particular groups ( e.g., rural referral centers, Disproportionate Share Hospital [DSH] status), expressing concern that there could be differences in population composition along these factors that were not considered. Finally, some commenters raised concerns that the outlier trimming and data exclusions could disproportionately impact certain hospital characteristics, impairing representativeness.
Response: CMS previously published results that evaluated data representativeness along many of the hospital characteristics mentioned by commenters, including, hospital size, geographic rurality and location, 340B participation, academic teaching status, and OPPS drug claims volume. CMS refers readers to Table 6 of the ODACS Technical Report for these results. CMS acknowledges that the population composition differed slightly across some of these characteristics between the respondent population and the overall survey-eligible population. These differences are precisely why CMS applied IPW, a widely used statistical technique that reweights received data to account for under- or overrepresentation of particular hospital characteristics such that the weighted sample replicates the characteristics of the overall population. Applying IPW adjustment had minimal impact on acquisition cost margins for non-340B and 340B-acquired drugs, supporting the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses. CMS refers readers to Section 4.4.2 of the ODACS Technical Report for a full discussion of the IPW adjustment methodology and results.
To address commenters' concerns that the respondent population is not representative along additional hospital characteristics not previously discussed, CMS conducted further analysis of the population by share of Medicare patients, DSH percentage, and hospital type. Unadjusted results show that the respondent population does not meaningfully differ from the overall population of survey-eligible hospitals by either Medicare share or DSH percentage, two indices of payer mix and patient population. When stratifying by hospital type, the respondent population is composed of slightly more IPPS hospitals and slightly fewer RRCs or RRC/SCHs, relative to all survey-eligible hospitals. CMS then integrated these three new variables as covariates in our IPW adjustment, and their inclusion had no impact on existing acquisition cost margins for either 340B-acquired or non-340B drugs.
Comment: Many commenters raised concerns that CMS's IPW adjustment methodology does not adequately address the risks of nonresponse bias and therefore does not ensure representativeness of the resulting acquisition cost margins. Commenters noted that IPW adjustment, which uses observable hospital characteristics to reweight population composition, can be insufficient if either or both of (i) the likelihood of survey response and (ii) drug acquisition costs are influenced by unobservable factors. Commenters offered various examples of potential unobservable factors that could hypothetically be exerting influence, including administrative complexity, drug purchasing arrangements, health system affiliation, and access to bulk purchasing discounts. As such, ( printed page 70515) commenters stated that CMS lacks evidence that the adjustors and covariates are able to close potential gaps in responses or acquisition costs. Additionally, some commenters stated that the narrow confidence intervals produced by the margin analyses indicate consistency among the respondent hospitals but do not demonstrate that the respondents accurately reflect the population as a whole. Finally, one commenter questioned why CMS did not report the distribution of respondents by OPPS drug volume quintile after IPW adjustment.
Response: As CMS describes below, we believe the acquisition cost data received are representative of acquisition costs among the eligible hospital population. We acknowledge that to sufficiently account for all determinants of hospital response and acquisition cost is a complex challenge given that acquisition costs for nonrespondents are, by definition, unobservable. CMS conducted an internal analysis to address concerns about nonresponse bias, with the specific goal of addressing whether nonresponse is correlated with acquisition costs. We used cost-to-charge ratios (CCR) from hospital cost reports and claim line charges from each providers' Fee-For-Service (FFS) drug claims data to create a proxy measure of acquisition cost that could be evaluated for the full population of survey-eligible hospitals. This analysis found that, for the 340B hospital population, respondents and nonrespondents had no statistically significant difference in costs, and the magnitude of the difference was close to zero, suggesting that a hospital's cost burden was not associated with their likelihood of response. CMS believes the consistency of proxy drug acquisition costs among respondents and nonrespondents supports the conclusion that the narrow confidence intervals obtained through the analysis do not simply reflect a homogenous respondent group, but rather are consistent with a sample that is representative of the eligible hospital population in terms of acquisition cost.
CMS conducted other tests to ensure the appropriateness of the IPW model and its covariates. First, we ran diagnostics on the distribution of estimated propensity scores and the resulting weights. In none of our IPW models did the estimated response probabilities fall below 10 percent; this is within the range where weight instability is not a concern and implies that weight trimming or truncation is not necessary. Second, CMS calculated Kish's effective sample size for each model, a diagnostic that summarizes how concentrated influence is across the weighted sample (a value close to the actual sample size indicates that weights are spread evenly across hospitals, while a value near 1 would indicate the estimate is driven by a single observation). In all cases, the effective sample size was close to the actual sample size, indicating that no small set of high-weight hospitals exerted disproportionate influence on the results.
As to why CMS did not report the distribution of respondents by OPPS drug volume quintile after IPW adjustment, OPPS drug volume quintile was highly correlated with the hospital size (bed count) quintile variable; given this, OPPS drug volume quintile was not included as a covariate in the IPW adjustment model to avoid collinearity issues. To address this comment, CMS also tested whether the final IPW weights balance the observed OPPS drug volume quintiles. We found that the reweighted sample effectively replicates the distribution of the OPPS drug volume quintiles in the population, even when this variable was not directly included. See Table 60.
(2) Margins Between Survey-Reported Hospital Acquisition Costs and Volume-Weighted ASP
Using the methodology, refinements, and processes discussed throughout Section (2)(b) Data Analysis and Methodology, we evaluated the received survey data to determine the difference between hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs and ASP-based Medicare payment amounts. We first identified the percent margin between aggregate acquisition costs and volume-weighted ASP for both non-340B and 340B drug acquisitions, then performed an analogous calculation to identify the margin between 340B ceiling prices and ASP as additional context for the 340B acquisition cost margins. Next, we tested alternate methodological specifications to evaluate whether these margins varied depending on the methods used. Finally, we stratified margins by individual therapeutic classes to identify possible variation in acquisition costs relative to ASP along drug type.
The survey provides valuable information regarding hospitals' drug acquisition costs. Following the GAO recommendation to validate Medicare payment rates using hospital acquisition costs, we assessed the survey data for trends where acquisition cost did not align with Medicare payment. The most immediately evident difference was between Medicare payment rates and acquisition cost data for 340B-acquired drugs by 340B-participating hospitals. Based on the survey response data and applying the methodologies discussed previously, we found that for drugs acquired through the 340B Program, hospitals' reported acquisition costs during the specified time period were approximately 33.4 percent below both the mean and the median ASP. For drugs acquired outside of the 340B Program, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs during the specified time period were approximately 2.7 percent above the mean ASP and 2.8 percent above the median ASP.
To help validate these findings, we compared aggregate 340B ceiling prices for drugs included in the survey during the corresponding survey period to ASP amounts.[117] Based on this analysis, during the survey study period 340B ceiling prices were, in aggregate, 28.0 percent below the mean ASP and 29.2 percent below the median ASP, respectively. These findings help validate the survey response data for 340B-acquired drugs, as the ceiling price average discount is generally representative of the maximum acquisition cost and minimum discount, though hospitals can negotiate additional discounts resulting in a sub-ceiling acquisition cost. This is reflected in the survey results where the aggregate 340B acquisition cost margin is approximately 33.4 percent below the mean ASP—several percentage points lower than the aggregate ceiling price margin of 28.0 percent below the mean ASP.
We sought to ensure that the resulting margins precisely reflected the relationship between hospitals' acquisition costs and ASP, and did not manifest substantial changes under different methodological specifications. To do so, we tested the impact of weighting acquisition cost margins by OPPS claims volume and retaining 340B survey responses above the maximum ceiling price (Table 68). Although we did not propose to adopt these alternative methodologies at this time for the reasons outlined in section V.B.8.b of this final rule with comment period, calculating acquisition cost margins with these specifications emphasizes two key points about 340B-acquired drugs. First, regardless of how ( printed page 70516) one analyzes the data, there are considerable differences between hospitals' acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs and ASP-based payment amounts for 340B drugs. Second, these alternate methodologies had minimal impact on the acquisition cost margins for 340B-acquired drugs; regardless of calculation methodology, hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs remained relatively consistent between approximately 29.9 percent and 33.4 percent below the average ASP and between 29.8 percent and 33.4 percent below the median ASP.
Application of different methodological specifications resulted in slightly more variation in the estimated margin between hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs and mean or median ASP-based payments for drugs acquired outside the 340B Program. This greater variability could be attributed to wider distributional spread in the reported acquisition costs for non-340B drugs; this, in turn, could cause the non-340B margins to be more sensitive to application of different weighting methodologies.
To assess whether the magnitude of margins remained the same across different drug categories, we also examined acquisition cost margins by therapeutic class [118] for both 340B-acquired and non-340B-acquired drugs. Hospitals' survey-reported 340B acquisition costs were at least 28.9 percent below the mean ASP—and for most therapeutic classes lower than that—for drugs in all high-spending therapeutic classes (that is, those with more than $100 million in reported acquisition costs) (Table 69). Again, this reinforces the significant, and consistent, differences between hospitals' acquisition cost for 340B-acquired drugs and ASP for these drugs regardless of therapeutic class.
The margins for non-340B drugs displayed greater variation relative to the 340B drugs, which is likely attributable to greater heterogeneity in drug mix, provider type, and purchasing arrangements present outside the 340B Program. For instance, only certain drugs and biologicals can be acquired through the 340B Program and only certain types of hospitals can enroll as 340B participants. These restrictions necessarily limit which drugs and hospitals can be included in the 340B calculations, leading to a somewhat more homogenous population. These restrictions do not play a role in the non-340B calculations. Additionally, and perhaps most significantly, certain types of 340B-participating hospitals have historically been prohibited from purchasing covered outpatient drugs through GPO arrangements,[119] which limits the purchasing arrangements applicable to 340B drugs, while non-340B drugs can be purchased under a variety of GPO or other buying group arrangements.
We received public comments on the margins between survey-reported hospital acquisition costs and volume-weighted ASP. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters suggested that the published 340B acquisition cost margin of ASP minus 33.4 percent may be influenced by respondents with particular characteristics ( e.g., large hospitals that could access bulk purchasing discounts) and requested that CMS release additional details about these margins stratified by hospital characteristics.
Response: CMS recognized the possibility of acquisition costs varying by hospital characteristic and calculated margins along these traits in our initial analysis. Results show remarkably little variation based on all measured hospital characteristics; regardless of stratification, acquisition cost margins for 340B drugs range from 30.4 percent to 39.7 percent below the mean ASP and 30.3 percent to 39.6 percent below the median ASP.
Comment: Several commenters discussed concerns regarding variation in acquisition costs by individual drug and/or therapeutic class, pointing out that a single adjustment to ASP may lead to underpayment for certain drugs and overpayment for others. Commenters referenced Table 53 from the proposed rule, which presents margins by drug class, as illustrating that acquisition costs for 340B drugs vary substantially by drug type. Commenters consequently noted against the implementation of any payment adjustments that are not drug-specific.
Response: As we noted in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we considered calculating payment rates derived from individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B drugs; however, given the dynamic nature of drug pricing, we concluded that it would be more appropriate to apply a single discount factor to ASP. We also explained that we believed that this approach would be more appropriate as ASP is also dynamic in nature. ASP changes over time (quarter to quarter), so tying the payment amount to an average discount of ASP results in a more accurate payment amount, by quarter, than if hospitals had to wait until the next survey cycle. Each drug HCPCS code has its own specific payment rate calculated that is unique to the drug described by the applicable HCPCS code. We indicated that we would apply an average discount, calculated as described under V.B.9.b. and V.B.9.c.(2). of the proposed rule, to the drug-specific ASP amount. This would make our proposed payment rate specific to the average acquisition cost for the drug. We also stated that applying the payment rate in this manner would allow for this average discount to apply to newly calculated ASPs as they are updated on a quarterly basis. We further explained that it would not be practical to calculate a drug-specific payment rate for each NDC, and each HCPCS code, based on the survey data, as the survey-collected data is based on a snapshot in time and would not reflect future changes in average acquisition costs. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.
With respect to commenters' observation that a single adjustment to ASP may lead to underpayment for certain drugs and overpayment for others, we emphasize that the purpose of our policy is to better align payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs in the aggregate, not to ensure that hospitals receive a payment amount greater than the cost of acquisition for every drug purchase. This approach is not unique to the policy for 340B-acquired drugs; because the OPPS is a prospective payment system, payment for an individual item or service may be more or less than a hospital's cost in any specific case. We would additionally note that the alternative payment rate that we are finalizing, ASP minus 28 percent, is greater than the ASP minus 33.4 percent amount demonstrated by the survey and would therefore partially mitigate commenters' concerns.
We also note that payment rates are already set on a drug-by-drug basis using the ASP methodology, and this policy will similarly reflect the differing acquisition costs of specific drugs. The percentage adjustment applied to ASP has never been tailored to individual HCPCS codes and this policy is consistent with that longstanding approach. Further, CMS chose to ( printed page 70520) volume-weight the proposed ASP percentage adjustment to reflect the relative utilization and differing margins of individual drugs.
CMS performed an additional variation of the IPW analysis in an effort to further address concerns about differences in drug utilization mix across providers. We first analyzed drug utilization by therapeutic class in the respondent and non-respondent populations. For those drug classes that displayed differences between the two groups, we included variables measuring each respondent's utilization of the drug classes of interest into the IPW adjustment. The introduction of these drug mix variables showed no impact on the existing aggregate margins, indicating that differing drug mix across providers does not appear to be exerting undue influence on the comparisons of acquisition costs to ASP.
(3) Application of Population Weight Adjustment and Calculation of Confidence Intervals To Assess Statistical Validity
In accordance with section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act, after completing initial analysis of survey respondents' acquisition costs, we evaluated whether survey respondents comprised a large sample that is sufficient to generate statistically significant and representative estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs. To do so, we conducted sensitivity analyses using inverse probability weighting (IPW) and confidence intervals, which we believe support the statutory objective of obtaining acquisition cost estimates from survey responses that are accurate and representative of the outpatient drug acquisition costs incurred by all hospitals paid under the OPPS.
IPW is a widely used statistical technique in survey research [120 121 122 123 124] to ensure that sample data produce estimates that accurately represent the population of interest. We applied IPW to account for the potential underrepresentation or overrepresentation of hospitals with particular characteristics among survey respondents and to evaluate whether acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses sufficiently reflected outpatient drug acquisition costs for all OPPS hospitals.
For purposes of the IPW analysis, we constructed respondent and nonrespondent populations that align with the refined hospital population discussed previously in (1) Survey Response Rate and Respondent Characteristics. We defined the respondent population as hospitals that submitted a survey response reporting the purchase of at least one surveyed NDC during the survey study period. We defined the nonrespondent population as survey-eligible hospitals that did not submit a survey response but billed at least one Fee-For-Service outpatient claim associated with a survey-relevant HCPCS code during the same period. Because acquisition cost margins were calculated separately for drugs purchased through the 340B Program and drugs purchased outside the 340B Program, we further stratified hospitals based on evidence of 340B drug use. Hospitals were identified as 340B participants using HRSA's 340B OPAIS enrollment information and claims submitted with 340B modifiers. Hospitals that neither submitted an ODACS response nor billed relevant outpatient claims during the survey period were excluded from the IPW-adjusted population. Subunits were collapsed with their corresponding parent unit prior to constructing the respondent and nonrespondent populations.
After identifying the respondent and nonrespondent groups, we calculated response propensity scores using logistic regression models based on observed hospital characteristics, including number of beds, teaching hospital status, geographic rurality, and Census division. Propensity scores were estimated separately for hospitals purchasing drugs outside the 340B Program and hospitals purchasing drugs through the 340B Program. A higher propensity score means that the hospital was more likely to submit a survey response; a lower propensity score means that the hospital was less likely to submit a survey response.
We then calculated inverse probability weights equal to the inverse of each hospital's estimated probability of responding to the survey. Hospitals with a higher likelihood of responding received smaller weights, while hospitals with a lower likelihood of responding received larger weights. The weights were used to adjust for differential representation of hospital characteristics between the respondent sample and the broader population of survey-eligible hospitals. Down-weighting hospitals with a high probability of response (which are overrepresented in the received sample) while upweighting CCNs with a low probability of response (which are underrepresented in the received sample) accounted for the differential representation of hospital characteristics in the sample as compared to the full population.
Finally, we calculated the IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins by first applying the calculated weights to hospitals' average acquisition costs and corresponding ASP-based payment amounts, then recalculating aggregate acquisition cost margins by finding the difference between the IPW-adjusted acquisition costs and IPW-adjusted ASP-based payment and then dividing that difference by the IPW-adjusted ASP-based payment. We also applied the same methodology when calculating IPW-adjusted margins between acquisition costs and 340B ceiling prices.
To evaluate whether the number of survey responses was sufficient to produce statistically valid estimates of hospitals' acquisition costs, we calculated confidence intervals for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins. The confidence intervals provide measures of whether the survey response rate adequately captures true population-level results. When response rate is insufficiently low, confidence intervals are very wide due to the high degree of uncertainty regarding where the true result lies. Conversely, when response rate is sufficient, confidence intervals become narrower as uncertainty lessens.
We calculated confidence intervals using a bootstrap methodology. Specifically, we repeatedly sampled with replacement from the original survey dataset and recalculated acquisition cost margins for each repeated sample. We repeated this process 10,000 times to generate distributions of unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margin estimates. We then identified the 95 percent confidence intervals for each acquisition cost margin estimate using the 2.5th percentile as the lower bound and the 97.5th percentile as the upper bound. ( printed page 70521)
(iii) Results of Population Weight Adjustments and Confidence Intervals From ODACS Data
Application of inverse probability weighting improved the alignment between the distribution of respondent hospital characteristics and the broader population of survey-eligible hospitals. We found that IPW-adjusted respondent characteristics more closely resembled the full population across measures such as rural/urban, teaching status, Census division, and 340B participation (Table 71).
(iv) Weighted Adjusted Acquisition Cost Margins
We found that application of IPW had minimal impact on estimated acquisition cost margins for either non-340B drugs or 340B-acquired drugs. For drugs acquired outside the 340B Program, the analysis conducted estimated that acquisition costs were approximately 2.7 percent above the mean ASP prior to IPW adjustment and approximately 2.8 percent above the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. For drugs acquired through the 340B Program, the analysis estimated that acquisition costs were approximately 33.4 percent below the mean ASP prior to IPW adjustment and approximately 33.1 percent below the mean ASP after IPW adjustment. The consistency between unadjusted and IPW-adjusted results supports the robustness and representativeness of the acquisition cost margins derived from survey responses (Table 72).
The 95 percent confidence intervals for both unadjusted and IPW-adjusted acquisition cost margins were not substantially different from each other, indicating the weighting adjustment had minimal impact on the resulting estimates. For non-340B drugs, the confidence intervals ranged from approximately 3.8 percent below the mean ASP to 6.9 percent above the mean ASP for unadjusted margin and between 1.6 percent below the mean ASP to 6.5 percent above the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. For 340B-acquired drugs, the confidence intervals were much narrower and ranged from approximately 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below the mean ASP for the unadjusted margin and from 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below the mean ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin (Table 72).
We believe the relatively narrow confidence intervals for 340B-acquired drugs support the statistical validity of the survey results on 340B drugs and indicate that the received sample is sufficiently large to produce reliable estimates of hospital outpatient drug acquisition costs for 340B drugs. We note that the confidence intervals for the non-340B drugs span a wider range of potential acquisition cost margins. This is expected given the greater distributional spread in the survey data for non-340B drugs, as discussed in this section V.B.2.8. of this final rule with comment period.
For an additional summary of our analysis of the survey results we refer readers to the 2026 Outpatient Prospective Payment System Drug Acquisition Cost Survey Technical Report posted on the Medicare Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) Drug Acquisition Cost Survey website.[125] We solicited comment on our process for how we evaluated ODACS data to determine the magnitude of the margins between hospitals' survey-reported acquisition costs and ASP-based Medicare payment amounts.
We received public comments on the application of population weight adjustment and calculation of confidence intervals to assess statistical validity. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: One comment noted that the quarterly ASP payment rate fluctuates across quarters. While CMS accounted for this fluctuation by publishing results comparing acquisition costs to both the mean and median ASP payment rate across the four quarters of the ODACS study period, this commenter suggests that a volume-weighted mean ASP would be a better comparison for scenarios when purchase volume is not evenly distributed across quarters.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for raising this consideration. CMS did not volume-weight the mean ASP payment rate for two key reasons. First, the ASP payment rates for most drugs did not vary substantially across the quarters in the study period, so volume-weighting was not needed to make the mean ASP an appropriate measure. Additionally, drugs may not be acquired in the same quarter as they are administered, leading to potential misalignment between hospitals' acquisition cost and the applicable ASP payment rate. Still, CMS did perform additional analyses comparing reported acquisitions costs to the minimum, or lowest, payment rate published for each HCPCS during the study period in order to construct lower bound estimates of the margin between ASP and hospitals' acquisition costs. These analyses revealed only a small impact on the aggregate margins.[126] Thus, CMS proceeded with comparisons to the ( printed page 70523) mean ASP as more representative of average payment rate during the study period.
Comment: Some commenters took issue with CMS's selected methodology to weight each drug's ASP by the total number of NDC units reported by all respondents. A commenter stated that because NDCs reported in higher volume have a greater impact on aggregate acquisition cost margins, these margins would be biased if respondents do not reflect the overall survey-eligible population. Another commenter compared the selected methodology with an alternate approach that CMS considered to weight by OPPS claims volume, contending that the latter is more appropriate because it would better reflect the services that would be impacted by the proposed 340B-acquired drug payment change. Commenters noted that the two methodologies yielded slightly different aggregate acquisition cost margin results and contended that CMS had arbitrarily chosen to weight by survey-reported unit volume without sufficient justification.
Response: CMS is unpersuaded by arguments that volume-weighting by survey-reported unit volume is inappropriate. Rather, this approach ensured that the ASPs for NDCs that represented a larger share of total survey-reported purchasing activity were proportionally represented in the estimated acquisition cost margins. Of key importance is the fact that hospitals' acquisition cost survey data captures all outpatient drug purchases, making weighting by survey volume necessary for internal consistency, whereas volume-weighting by OPPS unit volume only reflects Medicare FFS drug utilization. Additionally, there can be time lags between when a hospital purchased a drug and when it is administered, which would lead to misalignments between survey-reported unit volume for drugs purchased during the surveyed time period and OPPS claims volume for drugs billed during the surveyed time period. Accordingly, CMS believes that the selected volume-weighting method should consider all reported utilization volume, not just that for Medicare FFS beneficiaries, and ensure alignment with the surveyed time period to enable fair comparisons between survey-reported acquisitions and equivalent Medicare payment amounts. CMS does not find it problematic that the acquisition cost margins differ slightly between weighting methodologies. Slight divergences are to be expected given that unit volume is not identical between survey responses and billed claims for the two reasons listed above, and CMS believes that the merits of selecting the survey-reported unit volume weighting approach have been sufficiently justified. Finally, CMS refers readers to the discussion of representativeness analyses in section V.B.8.c. of this final rule with comment period to address concerns regarding potential respondent bias related to drug utilization volume.
Comment: Some commenters requested additional information and rationale regarding the selected outlier trimming methodology, noting that this methodological decision has significant impacts on the resulting acquisition cost margins. A commenter requested that CMS publish acquisition cost margins calculated before outliers were removed to better understand the impacts of the outlier trimming approach. Another commenter contended that using the geometric mean outlier trimming approach was inappropriate for these data and would result in only high outliers being removed while retaining low outliers in cases where three standard deviations below the mean is less than $0, thereby driving down the calculated acquisition cost margins. This comment suggested that CMS should have considered winsorizing these outlier observations instead of trimming them.
Response: CMS selected the geometric mean trimming approach to be consistent with our standard methodology for processing extreme outliers to develop policy under the OPPS.[127] This outlier identification was performed separately for 340B and non-340B drug acquisitions of each NDC, producing tailored outlier thresholds based on the unique data distribution for each drug through each purchasing channel. While CMS also considered the Tukey interquartile range (IQR) method as an alternate approach to trim outliers, we chose not to adopt it for reasons outlined in Section 3.4.1 of the ODACS Technical Report. CMS also notes that the majority of outliers, approximately 82 percent, identified and removed through the selected outlier trimming methodology were non-340B purchases. Due to the clustering of reported 340B acquisition costs at or closely below ceiling price, far fewer 340B responses were identified and trimmed as outliers.
When including survey responses that were identified as geometric mean outliers (while still applying all five data exclusions enumerated in Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report), the calculated acquisition cost margin for 340B-acquired drugs was ASP minus 35.9 percent when compared to both the mean and median ASP and for non-340B drugs was ASP minus 0.2 percent (mean ASP) or ASP minus 0.1 percent (median ASP). In other words, the aggregate acquisition cost margin for both 340B and non-340B drugs was slightly lower with outliers retained, contrary to commenter's hypothesis. This indicates that, in aggregate, the geometric mean trimming method did not systematically remove only high outliers; on the contrary, including these outliers would have suggested that hospitals' acquisition costs are even lower than Medicare payment rates. CMS thanks the commenter for their suggestion of winsorizing outliers and may consider this approach in any future survey analyses, as applicable.
Comment: Multiple commenters indicated that there are scenarios in which covered entities' acquisition costs for 340B drugs may exceed the published ceiling price ( e.g., obtaining products during drug shortages or supply chain disruptions when 340B inventory is unavailable; drugs purchased at WAC price before 340B replenishment). Thus, these commenters contend that survey responses above the ceiling price should have been retained in the 340B margin calculations.
Response: CMS appreciates the additional context discussed in these comments. CMS notes that any such acquisitions that were ultimately acquired through non-340B channels should have been reported as non-340B purchases in the survey data. Additionally, drugs initially purchased at WAC price should have had their acquisition costs reported post-340B replenishment, with all adjustments to comply with ceiling pricing already factored in. That said, in the event that these purchases were still reported as 340B acquisitions with costs exceeding the ceiling price, CMS conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the impact of retaining these observations. These results showed only a small impact, less than 2 percent, on the observed margins. Still, given the likelihood that responses above the ceiling price were not reported in accordance with survey guidance, CMS proceeded with excluding these observations.
Comment: One commenter requested more information regarding CMS's exclusion of certain clotting factor and respiratory therapy NDCs because CMS identified a subset of survey records for these NDCs were reported in IU or MG rather than NDC package units. The commenter requested CMS to clarify how these records were identified, how many records were reported in IU or MG units out of all records received for those NDCs, and whether conversion of IU or MG figures into NDC package units was considered as an alternative to exclusion. Finally, the commenter contended that the exclusion of these drugs meant that CMS was unable to determine acquisition cost estimates for the affected NDCs.
Response: CMS identified survey records as reported in IU or MG units by comparing each record's average acquisition cost to the average ASP and maximum ceiling price (reported in IU or MG) and average adjusted ASP (adjusted for NDC package size using an NDC-HCPCS conversion factor) for the NDC. As stated in Section 3.3.5 of the ODACS Technical Report, survey records reported in IU or MG units also displayed extremely high unit counts relative to their acquisition costs, which is to be expected given that hundreds—or even thousands—of IU or MG units are contained in one NDC package.
Between one-quarter and one-third of total survey records for these NDCs were identified as reported in IU or MG units; in many cases, the same hospital reported in IU/MG for multiple affected NDCs. These percentages were high enough that IU- and MG-based records were unable to be comprehensively detected as outliers using either of the two tested outlier methodologies. As such, including these NDCs in acquisition cost calculations (while applying all other data exclusions enumerated in Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report and trimming geometric mean outliers) yielded a substantially lower aggregate 340B acquisition cost of ASP minus 55.3 percent. This is due to the substantial distortions in per-unit costs for IU/MG-reported survey records.
CMS tested the impact of fixing the IU/MG records by converting their units to NDC package units. With this adjustment, the 340B margin remained ASP minus 33.4 percent and the non-340B margin slightly lowered to ASP plus 2.6 percent (instead of ASP plus 2.7 percent). Margins with affected NDCs adjusted were very similar to the margins with affected NDCs removed because converting the IU/MG units to NDC package units greatly reduced their reported unit volume, so their margins had much less impact on the volume-weighted aggregate calculation. As such, CMS was in fact able to produce acquisition cost estimates including these NDCs.
However, CMS ultimately chose to not pursue this approach given our overarching objective to not alter hospital-submitted data. CMS was also unable to conduct outreach to hospitals submitting affected data given limited time and resources, particularly because a large number of entities did not submit their response until the end of the data collection period.
Comment: Some commenters felt that the proposed rule's analyses showing ceiling prices to be 28.0 percent below ASP overall introduced uncertainty regarding the main analyses comparing hospital-reported acquisition costs and ASP, particularly when they compared this percentage with the proposed ASP adjustment of ASP minus 33.4 percent. They requested further explanation for the difference between these two percentages.
Response: CMS believes these comments reflect a misunderstanding of what the ceiling price represents, as it is logical and expected that the results comparing ceiling price to ASP differ from results comparing hospital-reported 340B acquisition cost to ASP. The ceiling price is the maximum amount that covered entities can be required to pay by manufacturers, but hospitals are able to acquire drugs for less than the ceiling amount, and often reported doing so in the survey data. This is why the 340B acquisition cost data shows a larger percentage discount relative to ASP than the ceiling price data.
Comment: Several commenters expressed concerns with what they characterized as differential interpretation and treatment of the 340B and non-340B data received from hospitals via the ODACS. They requested clarity on why CMS is choosing to take action on payment rates impacting 340B covered entities while stating that more data and analysis are necessary before proposing any policy changes to payment rates affecting non-340B hospitals. A ( printed page 70525) commenter noted that since CMS is proposing to vary payment rates based on hospital group, it must determine not only acquisition costs for the 340B hospital group but also how those compare to the relative acquisition costs for the non-340B hospital group.
Response: CMS analyzed the data received for 340B and non-340B drugs using identical methodological approaches. What differed, however, were the results obtained from these analyses.
The acquisition cost margin calculated for 340B drugs of ASP minus 33.4 percent displayed a clear and substantial difference from the existing payment rate of ASP plus 6 percent. This finding was strengthened after calculating IPW-adjusted margins and 95 percent CIs for both the unadjusted and IPW-adjusted point estimates. Across both methodologies, 340B margins ranged from ASP minus 34.7 percent to ASP minus 32.1 percent, a narrow range spanning only 2.6 percentage points. The narrow CIs for 340B-acquired drugs support the statistical validity of the survey results on 340B drugs and underscore the stark difference between hospital-reported acquisition costs and current Medicare payment policy.
On the contrary, the acquisition cost margin calculated for non-340B drugs of ASP plus 2.7 percent was only slightly below the existing ASP plus 6 percent payment rate. CMS notes that this is consistent with GAO's findings in 2004 and 2005, which found average purchase prices for drugs in their survey to equal roughly ASP plus 3 percent. The data are not conclusive enough for CMS to take policy action at this time regarding non-340B-acquired drugs. The data must be analyzed further by CMS, including the addition of GPO discounts, and CMS seeks more information to understand whether hospital acquisition costs for drugs purchased outside the 340B Program differ notably from the existing ASP plus 6 percent payment rate.
340B covered entities may, and often do, acquire drugs outside of the 340B Program, and these acquisitions would continue to be paid at the ASP plus 6 percent rate in recognition of the fact that 340B covered entities cannot access the 340B discount price for those purchases.
Comment: Some commenters noted that the proposed rule did not discuss the impact of “penny pricing” scenarios, in which manufacturers are required to sell 340B drugs to covered entities at a price of $0.01, on the aggregate survey results. Comments expressed concern that including these observations would exert a substantial downward influence on the observed margins.
Response: Very few survey responses (approximately 0.5 percent of received records) were submitted to ODACS that reported acquisitions of apparently penny-priced drugs. This is somewhat of a departure from the 340B drug acquisition cost survey conducted in 2020, which received more responses indicating penny-priced acquisition, therefore necessitating dedicated methodological specifications to analyze these observations. CMS did not explicitly exclude these responses from ODACS in the interest of retaining the largest amount of available data. However, sensitivity analyses that excluded penny-priced drugs showed minimal impact on the final 340B margin. Therefore, in the interest of retaining a maximally large dataset, CMS proceeded with results derived with these observations included.
Comment: A couple commenters raised concerns that respondents may have differentially interpreted how to report financial concessions that could not be reasonably attributed to a specific NDC, leading to some hospitals including a particular rebate or discount into their NDC-level acquisition costs and other hospitals reporting the same type of rebate entirely in the separate Price Concessions field of the ODACS module. Commenters contended that this would produce inconsistencies in acquisition costs across respondents such that they could not be comparable, and that these issues would have a larger impact on non-340B hospitals because most 340B hospitals subject to the proposed policy change have historically been prohibited from using GPOs. Finally, one commenter stated that GAO's previous survey analysis found that hospitals were unable to report accurately or comprehensively on such rebates.
Response: CMS acknowledges the complexity and room for interpretation associated with reporting aggregate ( i.e., non-NDC-specific) price concessions, including those obtained through participation in a GPO. After consulting subject matter experts on GPOs, additional consideration is needed to assess how best to apply the reported numbers; however, all approaches considered would have lowered the final estimated average acquisition cost given that the reported GPO data would have applied an additional discount to hospitals' reported acquisition costs. However, given that the ASP minus 33.4 percent policy change applies only to 340B-acquired drugs and most 340B hospitals subject to the proposed policy change have historically been subject to restrictions regarding GPO participation, concerns over the consistency and comparability of hospital-reported aggregate GPO discount amounts do not meaningfully impact CMS's policy decision on payment for 340B-acquired drugs. These important nuances raised by commenters are one reason why CMS has elected to not advance policy changes to non-340B-acquired drugs at this current time and will continue to assess how to appropriately analyze and include GPO discounts for non-340B drug purchases.
Comment: Commenters brought up a variety of factors, both related to the survey design and external influences, that they state may have impacted the ( printed page 70526) validity of the received data and its applicability to inform Part B drug policymaking. First, commenters mentioned that several drugs included in ODACS were in shortage and/or experienced supply chain challenges during the surveyed time period of July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025; according to these commenters, these disruptions may have influenced acquisition costs, product mix, and purchasing behavior in ways that do not reflect normal market conditions. Second, commenters contended that the one-year survey time period may be insufficient to comprehensively capture hospitals' acquisition costs and does not account for year-to-year variation in acquisitions; in their view, analyzing data from additional years would provide a more robust basis for refining Part B drug payment policy. Third, commenters raised concerns that because the collected data reflect a historical period ( i.e., July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025), their applicability to the current and future Federal drug-pricing landscape is limited given continued evolution in policymaking ( e.g., the forthcoming implementation of negotiated Maximum Fair Prices for selected Part B drugs and ongoing consideration of alternative mechanisms for effectuating 340B ceiling prices) and the impact of these developments on hospitals' financial environment.
Response: CMS notes that all survey analyses inherently represent a point-in-time estimate based on when data were collected. Lengthening the surveyed time period would have increased the administrative burden for hospitals to complete the survey, given increased time necessary to review their purchasing records and aggregate data. Additionally, drugs may experience shortage or supply chain interruptions in any year and the Federal drug policymaking landscape is in continuous evolution, making it impossible to designate a particular time period as “normal” or baseline market conditions against which to form comparisons. CMS notes that the surveyed time period of one year (July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025) aligns with the GAO-selected time period of one year (July 1, 2003 to June 30, 2004).
Comment: Some commenters pointed to CMS's discussion of the five exclusions applied to remove anomalous or duplicative survey records as evidence that the received data were low quality. A commenter specifically cited that 8.9 percent of all received records were excluded due to these criteria, alleging that this represented a large share of total records.
Response: Records that were excluded due to meeting at least one of the five criteria listed in Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report do not necessarily represent inaccurate or low-quality data. In many cases, these records reflect drug- and context-specific misunderstandings of or misalignments with the exact survey design rather than being indicative of larger data quality issues. CMS refers readers to Section 3.3 of the ODACS Technical Report for discussion of each situation and possible explanations underlying these observed anomalies. For the exclusion described in section 3.3.5 specifically, CMS notes that not all responses for affected clotting factor and respiratory therapy NDCs displayed the unit-misalignment issue, but were removed to avoid potential selection bias from specifically excluding those survey records with units reported in IU or MG; therefore, this exclusion removes more than just records featuring the anomaly. Nevertheless, CMS elected to remove records in these five exclusion criteria to promote data alignment with the stated survey design and ensure consistency in analyzing the data.
These five specific exclusions, associated with likely misunderstandings of the exact survey design, resulted in exclusions that only composed a small share of total records. After applying these data restrictions, 146,117 records remained, 91.1 percent of the original records received, with which CMS calculated acquisition cost margins. Moreover, these 146,117 records detail the acquisition cost of drugs that comprise approximately 97 percent of payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. Compared to this preponderance of data retained, these five data restrictions excluded a small share of total records.
Comment: Many commenters requested additional detail on CMS's methodology (including outlier identification and weighting), sensitivity analyses, representativeness of the survey data, and IPW model specifications. Numerous commenters also requested the release of the survey instrument and data collected, with or without anonymization applied.
Response: Hospitals were assured that their acquisition cost data would remain confidential as part of the ODACS data collection and analysis process, and this protection will be honored. Publishing de-identified survey data with anonymized hospital characteristics appended still presents an immense confidentiality risk due to the small number of respondent hospitals identified in multiple specific categories ( e.g., rural hospitals in specific Census regions). For details on methodology and results, CMS refers commenters to the ODACS Technical Report. Further, CMS has provided additional detail on methods and analysis results in comment response throughout this final rule with comment period.
C. CY 2027 OPPS Payment Methodology for 340B Purchased Drugs Based on Survey Results
As described previously, section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act requires the Secretary to conduct periodic surveys to determine the hospital acquisition cost for each SCOD for use in setting the payment rates for SCODs under section 1833(t)(14)(A) of the Act. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act provides that the payment amount for a SCOD for a year is equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug (which at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group) as determined by the Secretary, taking into account the survey data collected under subparagraph (D) of section 1833(t)(14) of the Act. Based on our analysis of the survey data, the most immediately evident and significant difference found between Medicare payment and acquisition cost was for 340B drugs acquired by 340B-participating hospitals, where the selected methodology shows that aggregate acquisition costs were approximately ASP minus 33.4 percent. This indicates average acquisition costs that were 37.2 percent lower than the general OPPS payment rate (ASP plus six percent). These results clearly demonstrate that ASP plus 6 percent is not an appropriate payment proxy for hospitals that acquire drugs through the 340B Program. Consequently, we proposed to adjust the OPPS payment policy for 340B drugs to better align payment with the acquisition costs demonstrated by the survey. Specifically, for CY 2027, we proposed to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
Conversely, for non-340B drugs, after taking into account the survey data, we proposed to maintain the current payment rate, which is generally ASP plus 6 percent, under the authority at section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act. As displayed in Table 67, the heterogeneity in acquisition costs for non-340B drugs is slightly greater than for 340B drugs; this variation has led us to believe this area warrants additional analysis by CMS and input from interested parties. The results of the survey for non-340B drugs generally indicate lower acquisition costs than current OPPS payment; however, the ( printed page 70527) discrepancy is not as clear and significant as with 340B drugs. Therefore, we are continuing to analyze the data from this survey, aligning those reported costs with hospital claims billing patterns, to see if any additional significant trends exist that merit further adjustments to OPPS payment policy in future years. We are also assessing billing patterns among those hospitals that did not respond. Finally, we collected and analyzed information on non-NDC-specific GPO discounts that hospitals receive and are still considering how these discounts could be factored into future analysis and policymaking. We will consider these issues for future rulemaking.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Many commenters supported our proposal to pay for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 33.4 percent based on the survey results. These commenters stated that aligning the 340B payment rate more closely with hospitals' actual acquisition costs, as reflected by the survey data, would improve the accuracy of Medicare payment, reduce incentives to choose more expensive drugs or shift drug administration to higher-cost settings, promote transparency and accountability, direct statutorily-required budget-neutral savings toward non-drug OPPS services and help ensure beneficiaries share in the value of 340B discounts through lower cost sharing. A commenter stated that CMS's findings are consistent with analyses from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) showing that Medicare payments for 340B-acquired drugs have substantially exceeded 340B drug acquisition costs. A commenter endorsed the proposal on the basis that it is a reasonable and overdue correction to the way Medicare pays hospitals for administering drugs. Another commenter stated that this policy reflects that Federal payment rates should rest on evidence of what something actually costs. A commenter stated that the survey made evident that the acquisition cost for SCODs through the 340B Program is far lower than the statutory default rate of ASP plus six percent and that with this clear survey data, CMS is required to set payment based on the average acquisition cost for 340B-acquired drugs. Citing our example of a beneficiary's coinsurance alone exceeding the entire price the hospital paid for the drug, many commenters emphasized the positive effect the proposed policy would have in reducing beneficiary drug copayments due to those copayments being calculated based on the amount Medicare pays the hospital rather than the hospital's acquisition cost for the drug.
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comments: Many of these commenters additionally provided criticisms of the 340B Program generally and proposed various reforms for CMS to consider to address those criticisms.
Response: We note feedback related to 340B Program policies are outside the scope of the proposed rule and are not addressed in this final rule with comment period. However, we thank the commenters for their insights and concerns.
Comment: A few commenters commented on our observation in the proposed rule (91 FR 41880) that we received a number of letters in response to the survey, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters, from eligible hospitals indicating that they would not be providing their acquisition data and explaining their reasons for not doing so. A commenter stated that they supported our proposed payment policy, despite what the commenter believes was a concerted effort to obstruct the survey. Another commenter challenged our observation that we received a number of responses, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters, from eligible hospitals indicating that they would not be providing their acquisition data and explaining their reasons for not doing so. The commenter stated that there is no proof of coordinated non-response among 340B-participating hospitals.
