Using an annual treatment-cost threshold would provide a transparent, objective, and administratively feasible approach that relies on data already available to CMS while protecting access to the therapies most critical to vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries.
Response: We thank commenters for their feedback and analysis of our proposed policy. While we understand drug payment and pricing is a dynamic issue, we believe the most ideal policy is one that is consistent and universal to the extent possible.
Comment: Two commenters suggested that Drugs Covered as Preventive Services (DCAPS), which include HIV PrEP medicines, be excluded because they are covered and reimbursed under a separate statutory framework from traditional Medicare Part B drugs. ( printed page 70539)
Response: We thank the commenters for their suggestion. While the OPPS payment for DCAPS mirrors the amounts set forth in the fee schedule established under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act, DCAPS furnished in HOPDs are paid under section 1833(t) of the Act, not section 1833(a)(1) of the Act. Section 1833(a)(1) of the Act sets forth payment amounts for services described in section 1832(a)(1) of the Act, which excludes medical and other health services (including additional preventive services) furnished by a provider of services (including a hospital). Rather, DCAPS furnished in HOPDs are described in section 1832(a)(2)(B) of the Act—medical and other health services furnished by providers of services. Section 1833(a)(2)(B)(iii) of the Act provides that services described in 1832(a)(2) of the Act (with exceptions not relevant here) are paid an amount determined under section 1833(t) of the Act—that is, the OPPS. In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule (89 FR 94295 to 94304), we finalized an OPPS payment amount for DCAPS, codified at § 419.41(j), that was consistent with the fee schedule established under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act; we did not, however, establish a policy to pay for DCAPS under the section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) fee schedule itself. DCAPS furnished in a HOPD are thus paid under the OPPS, and not under section 1833(a)(1)(W)(ii) of the Act.
However, the OPPS DCAPS payment framework is separate and distinct from the payment methodologies set forth at section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) and (II) of the Act. We did not propose to revise the OPPS payment methodology applicable to DCAPS. As such, DCAPS are not subject to our finalized 340B payment adjustment made pursuant to our authority at 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act at this time. We may consider revisions to the OPPS DCAPS payment methodology in future rulemaking.
Comment: We received a few comments relating to periodic revalidation of the survey. All commenters supported CMS periodically revalidating the survey. A commenter said CMS should periodically repeat or otherwise validate the survey so that the adjustment reflects changes in purchasing patterns, discounts, and the composition of the 340B market rather than allowing a one-time estimate to become a permanent payment convention. Most commenters requested that CMS conduct the survey more frequently than every 4 years, and most commenters requested that CMS conduct the survey on an annual basis. In the commenters' view, conducting an annual survey would be more appropriate because acquisition costs, drug mix and 340B enrollment are not static. One commenter stated that an annual series produces trend data that can inform purchasing patterns and impact on beneficiary access. Another commenter, noting CMS's reporting that it had received a number of responses, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters declining to provide their acquisition data, stated that an annual survey would diminish the leverage of a single year's non-response. Another commenter pointed out that an annual survey cadence would create a more durable evidentiary record for future OPPS rulemaking and would help ensure that payment policy remains responsive to changes in drug pricing, utilization, and provider purchasing behavior. Finally, one commenter acknowledged the administrative burden of an annual survey on hospitals and CMS but noted that the survey infrastructure now exists, and the marginal burden of a repeat administration is materially lower than the burden of conducting the survey the first time. One commenter encouraged CMS to continue refining its data collection and analysis methods in future rulemaking cycles, including by addressing potential non-response when CMS next validates the acquisition cost survey.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' suggestions and will take them into account for future rulemaking. We acknowledge the administrative burden of an annual survey on hospitals but agree, as commenters noted, that the survey infrastructure now exists, and the marginal burden of a repeat administration is materially lower than the burden of conducting the survey the first time.
Comment: A few commenters stated that the survey window was too short.
Response: We disagree with commenters that the survey window was too short. It ran for fourteen weeks (January 1, 2026 through April 7, 2026), was supported by two pre-survey training webinars, a dedicated phone line and email address for technical support, a dedicated web page featuring multiple guidance documents (FAQs, user guides, fact sheets, etc.) and featured a survey instrument designed to minimize, to the extent reasonably possible, the amount of effort necessary for hospitals to collect and report the required information to CMS. Hospitals were put on notice as early as April 2025 with the President's Executive Order that a survey was coming, nearly a year prior to the survey close date, with the majority of the survey requirements being available with the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period published in July 2025.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to apply our payment proposal to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program as proposed, with exceptions as discussed. We are also finalizing our proposal to not apply the payment proposal to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs as proposed.
7. Beneficiary Copayments
An important consequence of our final policy is that it will reduce Medicare beneficiaries' copayments for Medicare Part B drugs. Medicare beneficiaries are liable for a copayment that is typically equal to 20 percent of the OPPS payment rate, which is currently generally ASP plus 6 percent (regardless of the 340B purchase price for the drug). As the survey demonstrates, in some cases, beneficiary coinsurance alone exceeds the amount the hospital paid to acquire the drug under the 340B Program. For example, Lupron Depot (NDC 00074-3663-03) had a mean adjusted ASP of $4,690.08 compared to an average 340B acquisition cost of $667.94, excluding outliers and responses above the 340B ceiling price, yielding an absolute margin of −$4,022.14 and a percent margin of −85.8 percent. As the drug is paid at ASP plus 6 percent, the payment rate for one package of the NDC averaged $4,971.49, of which a beneficiary would pay 20 percent, or $994.30. Therefore, a beneficiary's copay would be over $300 above the average hospital's 340B acquisition cost. During the ODACS study period, 3,544 beneficiaries had an OPPS claim for Lupron Depot, meaning that a sizeable beneficiary population is affected by these high coinsurance amounts. This is also not a small sample size aberration: 137 hospitals reported purchasing this drug through the 340B Program (after excluding outliers and responses above the 340B ceiling price).
Additionally, sections 11101 and 11102 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (Pub. L. 117-169, enacted August 16, 2022) established requirements under which drug manufacturers must pay inflation rebates if they raise their prices for certain drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D faster than the rate of inflation. Specifically, section 11101 of the IRA amended section ( printed page 70540) 1847A (i) of the Act, which establishes a requirement for drug manufacturers to pay rebates into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund for Part B rebatable drugs for each calendar quarter beginning on or after January 1, 2023, if the specified amount, as determined under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act, exceeds the inflation-adjusted payment amount, which is calculated as set forth in section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act. Pursuant to section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act, the IRA also provides for an adjustment to the beneficiary coinsurance amount in cases where the price of a Part B rebatable drug increases faster than the rate of inflation such that the beneficiary coinsurance is calculated based on the lower inflation-adjusted payment amount instead of the applicable payment amount.
Section 11101(b) of the IRA amended section 1833(t)(8) of the Act by adding a new subparagraph (F) to modify OPPS copayments for Part B rebatable drugs. In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we codified the OPPS program payment and cost sharing amounts for Part B rebatable drugs as required by section 1833(t)(8)(F) of the Act by adding a new paragraph (e) to § 419.41, which states in the case of a rebatable drug (as defined in section 1847A(i)(2)(A) of the Act), except if such drug does not have a copayment amount as a result of application of section 1833(t)(8)(E) of the Act, for which payment is not packaged into payment for a covered OPD service (or group of services) furnished on or after April 1, 2023, and the payment for such drug under the outpatient prospective payment system is the same as the amount for a calendar quarter under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act, in lieu of the calculation of the copayment amount and the Medicare program payment amount otherwise applicable under § 419.41(d) (other than application of the limitation described in paragraph § 419.41(c)(4)(i)), the copayment and Medicare program payment amounts determined under §§ 410.152(m) and 489.30(b)(6) of this chapter shall apply. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we codified policies regarding the computation of the inflation-adjusted beneficiary coinsurance, including § 427.201, which specifies that the methodology set forth in § 427.201(b) will be used to calculate the inflation-adjusted beneficiary coinsurance and associated Medicare payment percentage for Part B rebatable drugs as set forth in §§ 410.152(m), 419.41(e), and 489.30(b)(6). The methodology at § 427.201(b) ensures that coinsurance adjustments are not applied in a manner that would increase beneficiary coinsurance. For additional details on this coinsurance policy, we refer readers to the full discussion at 89 FR 98237 and 98238.
Under section 1833(t)(8)(F) of the Act and current OPPS regulations at § 419.41(e), beneficiary coinsurance is adjusted for Part B rebatable drugs paid under the OPPS only where a Part B rebatable drug is paid the same as the amount for a calendar quarter under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act—that is, for single source drugs and biologicals, paid 106 percent of the lesser of ASP or WAC, and for biosimilar biological products, paid the amount determined under section 1847A(b)(8) of the Act. Because, as proposed, separately payable, nonpass-through, 340B-acquired drugs would be paid an amount other than the amount under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act, the coinsurance adjustment provisions of the Medicare Part B Inflation Rebate Program would not apply to separately payable, nonpass-through, 340B-acquired drugs under the proposed payment policy. We believed this was appropriate and consistent with the statutory intent of the Medicare Part B Inflation Rebate Program, as the coinsurance adjustment at section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act is intended to reduce the coinsurance amount to equal that of 20 percent of the inflation-adjusted payment amount described at section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act, and we expected that the applicable coinsurance under the payment proposal for 340B-acquired drugs would likely be lower than 20 percent of such inflation-adjusted payment amount. We sought comment on the interaction between coinsurance adjustments under section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act and the proposed policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
We anticipated that our proposed policy to pay for separately paid drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent would collectively reduce beneficiary copayments by an estimated $1.15 billion for CY 2027.
We received public comments. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Many commenters appreciated the effect of the proposed policy on reducing beneficiary copayments.
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comment: Many commenters challenged our statement that the proposed payment adjustment would reduce copayments for Medicare beneficiaries. In their view we failed to disclose that due to budget neutrality Medicare beneficiaries will pay higher copayments for all non-drug Part B items and services by roughly the same amount. Consequently, in these commenters' view, the out-of-pocket burden on patients is redistributed, not decreased, by the proposed policy. One of these commenters recommended that CMS calculate and report the net impact on beneficiary spending across the complete episode of care, rather than presenting the drug-specific reduction as though it were a direct reduction in total patient expense. A few commenters found fault with the example we cited of a drug, Lupron Depot, for which the beneficiary copayment exceeded the 340B price paid by the hospital. A commenter stated that this one illustration was insufficient data to draw any conclusions about the reliability of CMS' estimation of beneficiary savings. Another commenter stated that the observation that beneficiary cost-sharing sometimes exceeded a hospital's 340B purchase price describes the intended design of the 340B statute, in which the differential between acquisition cost and payer reimbursement is the mechanism by which Congress chose to fund safety-net care.
Response: We thank the commenters for expressing their concerns. As we acknowledged throughout the proposed rule and this final rule, including the regulatory impact section, this policy will largely be implemented in a budget neutral manner. From an individual beneficiary experience, their reduced payment for 340B drugs will be substantial and noticeable. We also emphasize that our proposal to apply this reduction to non-excepted, off-campus PBDs will not be budget neutralized and therefore will generate savings for beneficiaries.
Comment: Some commenters expressed concern that the proposed payment adjustment would arbitrarily create cost-sharing disparities between Medicare beneficiaries. These commenters pointed out that while a beneficiary who receives a Part B drug at a 340B hospital will see reduced coinsurance liability for that drug, a beneficiary receiving the identical drug at a non-340B hospital will face higher coinsurance despite having the same coverage via Medicare. Some of these commenters said that this disparity could result in a distortion of the beneficiary experience. Since beneficiary out-of-pocket liability would vary significantly by facility status, ( printed page 70541) patients would be steered toward specific health systems based on financial incentives rather than quality, provider access, or clinical outcomes. Similarly, these commenters contend, this payment structure would place a disproportionate burden on beneficiaries whose care needs are driven by procedures, diagnostic scans, or emergency visits rather than specialty Part B drugs.
Response: The intent of our proposed policy is to better align payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs as demonstrated by the ODACS. A consequence of that increased accuracy is that beneficiaries will pay more accurate copayments. We do not think that it would be appropriate to continue to pay what we now know to be less accurate rates for drugs, and make beneficiaries pay higher copays for those drugs, simply to maintain parity in beneficiaries' copayment experience between 340B and non-340B hospitals. With respect to the proposed reduction having a disproportionate effect on beneficiaries whose care needs are driven by non-drug items and services, we reiterate our response to the previous comment. We note that the 340B program in general is outside the scope of this final rule with comment period.
Comment: One commenter stated that because the large majority of Part B coinsurance is paid not by beneficiaries out of pocket but by supplemental coverage, including Medigap, employer wrap plans, and Medicaid, realized out-of-pocket savings to beneficiaries are a fraction of the amount cited by CMS. The commenter additionally noted that budget neutrality requires an increase of approximately 8.44 percent in the conversion factor for non-drug services, which raises beneficiary coinsurance on every non-drug outpatient service at every OPPS hospital and that the proposed rule nowhere nets this offsetting increase against the claimed drug savings.
Response: We note that, even though many beneficiaries have supplemental coverage, beneficiaries often pay a premium for such supplemental coverage and those plans make coinsurance payments for the beneficiary. Thus, to the extent Medicare would be lessening the coinsurance amount such supplemental plans would have to make, we would expect the price of such plans to decrease or otherwise reflect these lower costs in the future, thereby lowering the amount that beneficiaries pay for supplemental plan coverage. Further, for the millions of Medicare beneficiaries who do not have supplemental coverage at all or who have a supplemental plan that does not cover all of a beneficiary's cost-sharing obligation, the proposed policy would directly lower out-of-pocket spending for 340B-acquired drugs for those beneficiaries. We also note that the budget neutral nature of this policy is required by statute.
We thank commenters for their input. As we indicated above, we are revising 42 CFR 419.41(d) and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement our finalized policy to pay ASP minus 28 percent for all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program . We anticipate that this policy will collectively reduce beneficiary copayments for drugs by an estimated $1.1 billion for CY 2027.
8. 340B Payment Policy Exemptions
We proposed to exempt children's hospitals and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from our proposed policy to adjust OPPS payments for drugs acquired under the 340B Program. In accordance with section 1833(t)(7)(D)(ii) of the Act, we make transitional outpatient payments (TOPs) to both children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals. This means that these hospitals are permanently held harmless to their “pre-BBA amount,” and they receive hold harmless payments to ensure that they do not receive a payment that is lower in amount under the OPPS than the payment amount they would have received before implementation of the OPPS. Accordingly, if we were to reduce drug payments to these hospitals on a per claim basis, it is very likely that the reduction in payment would be paid back to these hospitals at cost report settlement, given the TOPs structure. Consequently, we believe it is appropriate to exempt children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from the alternative 340B drug payment methodology.
In addition to the children's and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, Medicare has long recognized the particularly unique needs of rural communities and the financial challenges rural hospital providers face. Across the various Medicare payment systems, CMS has established a number of special payment provisions for rural providers to maintain access to care and to deliver high quality care to beneficiaries in rural areas. With respect to the OPPS, section 1833(t)(13) of the Act provided the Secretary with the authority to make an adjustment to OPPS payments for rural hospitals, effective January 1, 2006, if justified by a study of the difference in costs by APC between hospitals in rural areas and hospitals in urban areas. Our analysis showed a difference in costs for rural SCHs. Therefore, for the CY 2006 OPPS, we finalized a payment adjustment for rural SCHs of 7.1 percent for all services and procedures paid under the OPPS, excluding separately payable drugs and biologicals, brachytherapy sources, and devices paid under the pass-through payment policy, in accordance with section 1833(t)(13)(B) of the Act. We have continued this 7.1 percent payment adjustment since 2006.
For CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed that rural sole community hospitals (as described under the regulations at 42 CFR 412.92 and designated as rural for Medicare purposes), children's hospitals, and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals would be exempted from the 340B payment adjustment and that these hospitals would continue to generally be paid ASP plus 6 percent for drugs. We stated that we may revisit our policy to exempt rural SCHs, as well as other hospital designations for exemption from the 340B drug payment adjustment, in future rulemaking.
We noted that hospitals listed under 42 CFR 419.20(b),[140] such as Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) and Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs), would not be subject to our proposed payment adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs.
We sought comment on our proposal to exempt children's hospitals, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and rural SCHs from the 340B drug payment adjustment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: All commenters that commented on our proposed exemption for rural SCHs supported the exemption. These commenters emphasized that rural SCHs already operate on thin margins and are frequently the only source of hospital-based and emergency care across large, sparsely populated service areas. They appreciated CMS' recognition of the unique role they play in ensuring access to care and supporting the health of rural populations and the unique financial challenges they face.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: Nearly all commenters that commented on our proposed exemption for PPS-exempt cancer hospitals supported the exemption. These ( printed page 70542) commenters appreciated CMS's acknowledgement that PPS-exempt cancer centers necessitate unique reimbursement structures and indicated that a cancer-specialty hospital's portfolio of 340B drugs is focused upon high-complexity, high-cost anti-cancer therapeutics, that cancer-specialty hospitals are already subject to a highly restrictive version of the 340B Program rules that include the GPO prohibition and orphan drug exclusion, and that the exception would ensure that they would be able to continue to provide high complexity care to socioeconomically vulnerable populations.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: A commenter opposed the proposed exemption for PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from the 340B payment adjustment. The commenter disagreed with our rationale for excluding them, that PPS-exempt cancer hospitals receive transitional outpatient payments under section 1833(t)(7)(D) of the Act and that a reduction in claim-level drug payment could therefore be offset, in whole or in part, through the hospital's subsequent hold-harmless payment at cost-report settlement. The commenter stated that that interaction, by itself, should not justify maintaining ASP plus six percent payment for 340B-acquired drugs at these hospitals. Instead, the commenter recommended that CMS determine whether the transitional outpatient payment methodology can be administered, consistent with the statute, so that it does not negate an otherwise applicable acquisition-cost-based payment adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs. The commenter also expressed concern that exempting PPS-exempt cancer hospitals would perpetuate different Medicare payment for the same 340B-acquired drug based solely on the institutional status of the hospital furnishing it. It would allow qualifying cancer hospitals to continue receiving ASP plus six percent even when the hospital's acquisition cost is substantially below ASP, while other 340B hospitals would receive payment based on the survey-derived acquisition-cost relationship. Such a distinction would undermine CMS's objectives of aligning payment with acquisition cost, reducing inappropriate payment differentials, and reducing beneficiary cost sharing. If CMS nonetheless proceeds with exempting PPS-exempt hospitals, the commenter requested that CMS explain the statutory constraint in detail, quantify the resulting payment and beneficiary cost-sharing effects, and consider any available mechanisms to prevent the hold-harmless methodology from restoring 340B drug payments that exceed acquisition costs.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input; however, we do not think that the qualified exemption for PPS-exempt cancer hospitals suggested by the commenter would be administratively feasible. As previously described, by statute, these hospitals are permanently held harmless to their “pre-BBA amount,” and they receive hold-harmless payments to ensure that they do not receive a payment that is lower in amount under the OPPS than the payment amount they would have received before implementation of the OPPS. Accordingly, if we were to reduce drug payments to these hospitals on a per claim basis, it is very likely that the reduction in payment would be paid back to these hospitals at cost report settlement, given the TOPs structure.
Comment: All commenters that commented on our proposed exemption for children's hospitals supported the exemption. These commenters stressed that children's hospitals serve a uniquely vulnerable patient population and rely on 340B savings to help offset systemic underpayments and sustain access to specialized pediatric services.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: Several commenters requested that we make our exemptions for rural SCHs, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and children's hospitals permanent.
Response: As noted in the proposed rule, we are proposing the exemptions for rural SCHs, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and children's hospitals for CY 2027 and subsequent years; however, we may revisit these exemptions in future rulemaking.
Comment: A commenter cautioned that, to the extent CMS retains exemptions, they should be justified narrowly by identifiable statutory, payment system, or access considerations.
Response: We agree with the commenter that we should employ a careful and considered approach in determining whether to continue or discontinue an exemption.
Comment: One commenter requested that the final rule and implementation guidance confirm that the term “rural sole community hospitals” includes an SCH reclassified as rural under 42 CFR 412.103.
Response: Hospitals must (1) either be a sole community hospital, as set forth in the regulations at 42 CFR 412.92, or be an essential access community hospitals, which is considered to be an SCH under section 1886(d)(5)(D)(iii)(III) of the Act, that is (2) located in a rural area, as defined in § 412.64(b), or is treated as being located in a rural area under § 412.103. Comment: Many commenters requested CMS to provide exemptions for additional hospital types and services. Multiple commenters stated that the proposed exemptions do not capture the universe of disadvantaged rural safety-net providers and requested that other rural hospitals, including SCHs, MDHs, and LVHs be exempted. Some of these commenters requested that all rural hospitals be exempted. These commenters stated that these hospitals serve the same populations as rural SCHs and depend on 340B savings for the same reasons. Others maintained that rural SCHs were exempted from the 340B payment adjustment primarily because these hospitals are in a more vulnerable financial position and already receive a special payment adjustment under OPPS and, given that reasoning, CMS should extend the exemption to the additional rural hospital designations as well. Others suggested that all DSHs or DSH safety-net hospitals operating oncology programs serving high Medicaid, uninsured, and medically vulnerable populations be exempted. Others suggested rural referral centers and academic medical centers. Other commenters requested more general exemptions for “hospitals serving high proportions of Medicaid, uninsured, and low-income patients and hospitals located in or primarily serving health professional shortage areas and medically underserved areas,” and “hospitals with substantial federal engagement and funding that serve very large rural regions.” Other commenters invited CMS to use its equitable adjustment authority to exempt hospitals with significant safety-net responsibilities that would be disproportionately affected by the proposed payment adjustment. These commenters offered various criteria for CMS to use to define these hospitals along with names to identify them: “essential health systems,” “qualifying disadvantaged hospitals,” “frontline hospitals,” and “hospitals with extraordinary safety-net responsibilities.” One commenter stated that an exemption limited to IPPS-exempt children's hospitals would not fully protect the pediatric delivery system and requested that all children's hospitals, including freestanding children's hospitals, children's hospitals within larger systems, and pediatric service lines be exempted. Finally, a few commenters suggested more targeted exemptions such as qualifying sites that administer complex cell and gene ( printed page 70543) therapies or cancer and infusion services.
Response: We understand commenters' concerns; however, we emphasize that the exemptions we are proposing are justified by the very specific circumstances of the hospital types we propose to exempt. As explained in the proposed rule, we proposed to exempt rural SCHs based on our historical analysis of the costs between hospitals in rural areas and urban hospitals, which revealed a difference in costs for rural SCHs. We also proposed to exempt PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and children's hospitals due to their unique payment structure. We decline at this time to exempt hospitals not falling into either of these two categories; however, we may revisit our policy to exempt other hospital designations from the 340B drug payment adjustment in future rulemaking.
Comment: One commenter requested clarification as to whether the proposed payment adjustment would apply to hemophilia treatment centers.
Response: Hospitals paid under the OPPS, including excepted and non-excepted provider-based departments of the hospital, are subject to this policy. To the extent that entities are paid under OPPS and participate in the 340B Program, they are subject to the payment policy unless otherwise exempted.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to exempt rural SCHs, children's hospitals and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals from our proposed policy to adjust OPPS payments for drugs acquired under the 340B Program as proposed for CY 2027 and subsequent years.
9. 340B Payment Policy for Drugs Furnished by Nonexcepted Off-Campus Departments of a Hospital
In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79699), we discussed implementation of section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-74), enacted on November 2, 2015, which amended section 1833(t) of the Act. Specifically, this provision amended section 1833(t) of the Act by amending paragraph (1)(B) and adding a new paragraph (21). As a general matter, under sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(v) and (t)(21) of the Act, applicable items and services furnished by certain off-campus outpatient departments of a provider on or after January 1, 2017, are not considered covered OPD services as defined under section 1833(t)(1)(B) of the Act for purposes of payment under the OPPS and will instead be paid “under the applicable payment system” under Medicare Part B if the requirements for such payment are otherwise met. We indicated that, in order to be considered part of a hospital, an off-campus department of a hospital must meet the provider-based criteria established under 42 CFR 413.65. Accordingly, we refer to an “off-campus outpatient department of a provider,” which is the term used in section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, as an “off-campus outpatient provider-based department” or an “off-campus PBD.” For a detailed discussion of the legislative history and statutory authority related to payments under section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, we refer readers to the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79699 through 79719) and interim final rule with comment period (81 FR 79720 through 79729).
To implement the amendments made by section 603 of Public Law 114-74, we issued an interim final rule with comment period (81 FR 79720), which accompanied the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period to establish the PFS as the “applicable payment system” that applies in most cases, and we established payment rates under the PFS for those nonexcepted items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. Specifically, we established a PFS relativity adjuster that is applied to the OPPS rate for the billed nonexcepted items and services furnished in a nonexcepted off-campus PBD to calculate payment rates under the PFS. The PFS relativity adjuster reflects the estimated overall difference between the payment that would otherwise be made to a hospital under the OPPS for the nonexcepted items and services furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs and the resource-based payment under the PFS for the technical aspect of those services with reference to the difference between the facility and nonfacility (office) rates and policies under the PFS. The current PFS relativity adjuster is set at 40 percent of the amount that would have been paid under the OPPS (90 FR 53770). These PFS rates include the same packaging rules that are unique to the hospital outpatient setting under the OPPS, including the packaging of drugs that are unconditionally packaged under the OPPS. This includes packaging certain drugs and biologicals that would ordinarily be separately payable under the PFS when furnished in the physician office setting. For a full discussion of our initial implementation of section 603, we refer readers to the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79699 through 79719) and the interim final rule with comment period (79720 through 79729). For a detailed discussion of the current PFS relativity adjuster related to payments under section 603, we refer readers to the CY 2018 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (82 FR 52356 through 52637) and the CY 2019 PFS final rule with comment period (82 FR 59505 through 59513).
We note that, ordinarily, Medicare pays for drugs and biologicals furnished in the physician's office setting at ASP plus 6 percent. This is because section 1842(o)(1)(A) of the Act provides that if a physician's, supplier's, or any other person's bill or request for payment for services includes a charge for a drug or biological for which payment may be made under Medicare Part B and the drug or biological is not paid on a cost or prospective payment basis as otherwise provided in this part, the amount for the drug or biological is equal to the following: The amount provided under section 1847, section 1847A, section 1847B, or section 1881(b)(13) of the Act, as the case may be for the drug or biological.
Generally, in the hospital outpatient department setting, low-cost drugs and biologicals are packaged into the payment for other services billed under the OPPS. Separately payable drugs (1) have pass-through payment status, (2) have a cost per day exceeding a threshold, or (3) are not policy-packaged or packaged in a C-APC. As described in sections V.A. and V.B. of this final rule with comment period, section 1847A of the Act establishes the ASP methodology, which is used for payment for drugs and biologicals described in section 1842(o)(1)(C) of the Act furnished on or after January 1, 2005. The ASP methodology, as applied under the OPPS, uses several sources of data as a basis for payment, including the ASP, the WAC, and the AWP (90 FR 53682). As noted in section V.B. of this final rule with comment period, since CY 2013, our policy has been to pay for separately payable drugs and biologicals at ASP plus 6 percent in accordance with section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(II) of the Act (the statutory default) (90 FR 53702). Consequently, in the case of services furnished in a hospital outpatient department, Medicare has historically paid ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable Part B drugs and biologicals. For a detailed discussion of our current OPPS drug payment policies, we refer readers to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53697 through 53766). ( printed page 70544)
As a general matter, in the nonexcepted off-campus PBD setting, we pay hospitals under the PFS for all drugs and biologicals that are packaged under the OPPS based on a percentage of the OPPS payment rate, which is determined using the PFS relativity adjuster. Because OPPS packaging rules apply to the PFS payments to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs, the PFS payment for some nonexcepted items and services that are packaged includes payment for some drugs and biologicals that would be separately billable under the PFS if a similar service had been furnished in the office-based setting. As we noted in the CY 2017 final rule with comment period, in analyzing the term “applicable payment system,” we considered whether and how the requirements for payment could be met under alternative payment systems in order to pay for nonexcepted items and services, and considered several payment systems under which payment is made for similar items and services (81 FR 79712). Because the PFS relativity adjuster that is applied to calculate payment to hospitals for nonexcepted items and services furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs is based on a percentage (40 percent) of the amount determined under the OPPS for a particular item or service, and the OPPS is a prospective payment system, we believed that items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs paid under the PFS were payable on a prospective payment basis. Therefore, we believed we had flexibility to pay for separately payable drugs and biologicals furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs at an amount other than the amount dictated by sections 1842(o)(1)(C) and 1847A of the Act.
As discussed previously, our proposal to adjust the payment rate for separately payable drugs and biologicals (other than vaccines, drugs on pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs) acquired under the 340B Program from ASP plus 6 percent to ASP minus 33.4 percent would apply to separately payable drugs and biologicals paid under the OPPS. Under sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(v) and (t)(21) of the Act, however, nonexcepted items and services furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs are not covered outpatient department services and, therefore, are not payable under the OPPS. This means that, absent our inclusion of them in our proposed policy, nonexcepted off-campus PBDs would not be subject to the payment changes we proposed. Because hospitals can, in some cases, acquire drugs and biologicals under the 340B Program for use in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs, we believe that not adjusting payment for these departments would present a significant incongruity between the payment amounts for these drugs depending upon where (for example, excepted or nonexcepted PBD) they are furnished. This incongruity would distort the relative accuracy of the resource-based payment amounts under the site-specific PFS rates and could result in significant perverse incentives for hospitals to acquire drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals under the 340B Program and avoid Medicare payment adjustments that account for the discount by providing these drugs to patients predominantly in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. It would also undermine our goals of reducing beneficiary cost-sharing for these drugs and biologicals and moving towards site neutrality through the section 603 amendments to section 1833(t) of the Act. To avoid such perverse incentives and the resulting distortions, we proposed for CY 2027 and subsequent years, to pay an amount equal to ASP minus 33.4 percent, or equivalent, for drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program that are furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs.
Consistent with the approach to budget neutrality we adopted when we previously implemented a reduction for 340B-acquired drugs furnished by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs (83 FR 59021) and our approach to budget neutrality for items and services provided by nonexcepted off-campus PBDs generally (83 FR 58832), these adjusted payments would not be budget neutralized.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: A few commenters supported our proposal to apply the proposed 340B payment adjustment to drugs furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. A commenter stated that consistent payment treatment for 340B-acquired drugs would help ensure that the site at which a drug is administered is not selected merely because of a payment differential. Another commenter stated that they “particularly support[ed] applying the proposed 340B payment adjustment to drugs furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs.” The commenter explained that “[t]hese departments remain hospital-owned and may have access to 340B acquisition discounts even though Medicare generally pays for their services under a methodology intended to approximate payment in the physician office setting. Leaving 340B-acquired drugs furnished in these departments at ASP plus six percent would preserve a substantial payment advantage based solely on hospital ownership, and undermine the purpose of moving toward site neutral payment.” The commenter agreed with CMS that failing to apply the adjustment would create distorted incentives for hospitals to furnish 340B drugs through these departments and encouraged CMS to continue examining Medicare payment policies that create different financial incentives for the same service based primarily on site of care or ownership. “Payment differentials can influence organizational decisions about where services are furnished and contribute to consolidation without improving the care patients receive.” The commenter concluded by encouraging CMS to consider the proposed 340B payment adjustment “as part of its broader efforts to reduce unnecessary site-of-service payment disparities while ensuring that savings attributable to these reforms benefit patients and the Medicare program.”
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comment: Several commenters referenced previous comments they or others made to the CY 2019 final rule alleging that CMS lacks the authority under 1833(t)(21)(C) of the Act to adjust drug payments to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs or to do so in a non-budget neutral manner.
Response: We direct readers to our responses to those comments in the CY 2019 final rule at 83 FR 59020 through 59022.
Comment: Several commenters alleged that CMS's proposal is arbitrary and capricious because it undermines Congress's intent under the 340B statute.
Response: We have explained earlier in this rule why we do not believe that our proposed policy undermines Congress's intent under the 340B statute. The purpose of this policy is to align Medicare payment with average acquisition costs as required by statute.
Comment: A commenter stated that we lack a sound rationale for applying the proposed reduction to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. The commenter contends that we provide no empirical evidence for our conclusion that not applying the reduction to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs could result in significant perverse incentives for hospitals to acquire drugs under the 340B Program and avoid Medicare payment adjustments. The commenter ( printed page 70545) requests that CMS publish the data and methodological information necessary to independently verify the accuracy of the agency's estimates, including which 340B providers CMS used to estimate its payment impact, whether the agency applied any exclusion criteria, and how CMS accounted for hospitals that are not included in the OPPS impact file but would be subject to the agency's proposed 340B payment adjustment policy.
Response: We disagree that we lack a sound rationale for applying the proposed reduction to nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. We do not think that it is unreasonable to assume that if an entity can furnish a drug in one setting and receive significantly more (nearly 40 percent) payment for the drug then it would receive furnishing the same drug in a different setting, that there exists an incentive for the entity to provide the drug in the setting in which they would receive the higher payment.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to apply our payment policy to 340B-acquired drugs furnished in nonexcepted off-campus PBDs as proposed.
We expect that for CY 2027 this will result in savings of approximately $640 million to the Medicare Part B Trust Fund and would collectively reduce beneficiary copayments by an estimated $160 million. These beneficiary savings are included in the $1.1 billion figure for reduced beneficiary copayments for drugs in section 7. Beneficiary Copayments.
To effectuate the payment adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs, we proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, providers who are not exempted from the 340B payment adjustment would report modifier “JG” (Drug or biological acquired with 340B Drug Pricing Program Discount) to identify if a drug was acquired under the 340B Program. The phrase “acquired under the 340B Program” would include all drugs acquired under the 340B Program or Prime Vendor Program, regardless of the level of discount applied to the drug. Drugs that were not acquired under the 340B Program would not be reported with the modifier “JG.” For separately payable drugs (status indicator “K”), application of modifier “JG” would trigger a payment adjustment such that the 340B-acquired drug is paid at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
We additionally proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, for drugs or providers that are exempted from the 340B drug payment policy for CY 2027, which include pass-through drugs (status indicator “G”), non-opioid treatment for pain relief drugs authorized under section 4135 of the CAA, 2023 (status indicator “K1”), rural SCHs, children's hospitals, and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, should not report modifier ”JG.” Instead, these exempted providers should report the informational modifier “TB” (Drug or Biological Acquired With 340B Drug Pricing Program Discount, Reported for Informational Purposes) to identify OPPS separately payable drugs purchased with a 340B discount. The informational modifier “TB” will facilitate the collection and tracking of 340B claims data for OPPS providers that are exempted from the payment adjustment in CY 2027. However, use of modifier “TB” will not trigger a payment adjustment, and these providers will generally receive ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable drugs furnished in CY 2027, even if such drugs were acquired under the 340B Program.
We also proposed that, beginning January 1, 2027, all providers report a distinct modifier to identify drugs and biologicals that were not acquired under the 340B Program. Specifically, we proposed to establish a new modifier, designated in the proposed rule with the placeholder modifier code “XX” (Drug or biological not acquired under the 340B Drug Pricing Program), which would be required to be reported for all separately payable drugs that were purchased outside of the 340B Program.
The requirement to use modifier “XX” would apply to all providers paid under the OPPS, including excepted and nonexcepted off-campus PBDs. Reporting the modifiers “XX,” “JG,” or “TB” for applicable drugs would ensure that all drug claims are consistently categorized as either 340B-acquired or non-340B-acquired. We believe that requiring the use of modifier “XX” for non-340B drugs will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data, facilitate program integrity and oversight, and enhance our ability to monitor acquisition patterns across providers. The use of modifier “XX” would not trigger a payment adjustment and such drugs would continue to be paid at the applicable OPPS rate (generally ASP plus 6 percent for separately payable drugs) consistent with existing policy. In summary, we proposed all separately paid drug claims reported under the OPPS would be reported with a modifier of either “JG,” “TB,” or “XX” (Table 75). We solicited comment on our proposal to require all separately paid drug claims to be reported with a modifier of either “JG,” “TB,” or “XX.”
As stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we believe the addition of this new modifier is consistent with the decisions that hospitals are already making (is the drug a 340B-acquired drug or a non-340B-acquired drug) when billing for these drugs. As previously mentioned, we believe requiring the use of modifier “XX” for non-340B drugs will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data—this requirement could even decrease burden on hospitals as it may improve the accuracy of billing, thus decreasing the need for hospitals to reprocess claims that were billed incorrectly. We requested comment as to whether the addition of modifier “XX” would create unnecessary, undue burden for hospitals.
Additionally, we acknowledged this billing modifier proposal would have implications for how we identify billing units of drugs acquired through the 340B Program under the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program. In the CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (89 FR 98583), we codified at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) that we will exclude from Part B rebate calculations separately payable billing units in claim lines for institutional claims that are billed with the “TB” modifier for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2025. As we stated in the proposed rule, establishing a requirement to use the “JG” modifier, in addition to the requirement to use the “TB” modifier would necessitate changes to how we identify 340B units to exclude from Part B rebate calculations.
Consequently, we proposed a conforming change at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to reflect proposed changes to the requirements to use billing modifiers for 340B-acquired drugs as described in section V.B.10. of this final rule with comment period. Specifically, to account for these billing modifier proposals, at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv), we proposed to add “or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units.” This means, for the purposes of Part B inflation rebate calculations, we would exclude billing units acquired under the 340B Program as identified through separately payable units in claim lines billed with the “TB” modifier, or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units for 340B-acquired drugs, for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2025. Therefore, as a matter of operations, effective January 1, 2027, CMS would identify separately payable billing units in claim lines billed with the “TB” modifier and proposed “JG” modifier. We recognized that policy amendments for the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program are typically proposed in the PFS; however, we believed it was appropriate to propose an amendment to § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) in the OPPS/ASC proposed rule due to timing differences in the publication of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule relative to the OPPS/ASC proposed rule and to ensure we are able to appropriately exclude 340B units from Part B rebate calculations starting January 1, 2027.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Some commenters unreservedly supported our proposals relating to modifiers. One commenter stated that, “taken together, these three modifiers would, for the first time, categorize every separately payable drug claim under the OPPS as either 340B-acquired or non-340B-acquired. That completeness will further make the data usable and meaningful.” Another commenter praised the proposal as a step toward greater transparency in the 340B Program. A third commenter called the modifier “long awaited” and stated that it would help ensure Medicare has reliable claims-level data to distinguish drugs that should be subject to the 340B payment adjustment from those that should not, helping prevent inaccurate payments before they are made. Another commenter stated that ensuring every separately paid drug claim is consistently categorized as either 340B or non-340B will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data, facilitate program integrity oversight, and enhance CMS's ability to monitor acquisition patterns.
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comment: Several commenters provided suggestions for the use of the ( printed page 70547) modifiers beyond what we proposed. One commenter suggested that we use the claims modifiers to annually recalculate the budget-neutrality adjustment factor to ensure that the 340B payment policy is being implemented in a consistently budget-neutral manner. Another commenter urged CMS to expand the application of the XX claims modifier and require all Medicare claims, including under Part D and Medicare Advantage, to have the appropriate modifier within 10 days of dispense. A third commenter recommended that CMS consider the following implementation refinements to ensure consistent administration and compliance with the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA): (1) extend this requirement beyond drugs paid for under the OPPS to all Part B claims that report a drug; and (2) extend the XX modifier requirement to all non-340B drugs, not just those that are separately payable.
Response: We thank commenters for their suggestions and will potentially consider them for future rulemaking where appropriate.
Comment: A commenter supported the use of modifiers but requested that we limit their application to separately payable drugs furnished by 340B hospitals.
Response: We thank the commenter for their suggestion; however, for the reasons discussed in the proposed rule, it is necessary to apply the proposed modifier requirement to 340B and non-340B hospitals to effectively implement our 340B Payment Policy.
Comment: Many commenters opposed the proposal as being administratively burdensome. These commenters expressed concern with the costs associated with implementing the modifiers such as adapting their electronic health record and billing systems and training their staff. A commenter noted the immense technical complexity of adopting the new modifier, requiring extensive reconfigurations across electronic health records (EHRs), pharmacy management systems, charge description masters, and revenue cycle platforms systemwide. Another commenter stated that “because 340B drugs are generally managed through a replenishment model, the purchasing information necessary to identify how a drug is ultimately replenished may not be available at the same point in time that the claim is submitted. This may require hospitals to develop additional processes to reconcile pharmacy purchasing information with claims data.” The commenter encouraged CMS to ensure that any modifier requirements account for the operational realities of the 340B replenishment process and do not add administrative burden. Many commenters claimed that it would not be feasible to implement the proposed changes by January 1, 2027, and requested a delayed or phased-in implementation start date coupled with robust implementation guidance. These commenters stated that hospitals would need to modify their systems, interfaces, edits, training, quality controls, reconfigure charge description masters, pharmacy inventory systems, split billing software, claim scrubbers, and revenue cycle logic, and retrain pharmacy and billing staff between publication of a final rule around November 1 and an effective date of January 1. Commenters suggested various alternative timeframes for making the modifier changes effective as well as requesting that CMS issue sub-regulatory billing guidance by a date certain, provide claim edit testing, and refrain from denials or recoupments for good-faith modifier errors during a defined transition period.
Many commenters stated that the scope and complexity of implementing the new modifier would greatly increase the risk of errors. A commenter stated that it would be difficult to identify every non-340B claim accurately and that that would create a high volume of potential billing mistakes, which could lead to rejected claims or compliance audits. Another commenter cautioned that minor misconfigurations or data mapping errors could trigger widespread claim rejections and payment denials. A third commenter found the XX modifier to be especially concerning because non-340B status may depend on purchasing, replenishment, mixed-use inventory, patient eligibility, accumulator logic, wholesaler data, and retrospective claim information and a missing or incorrect modifier could result in denials, underpayment, reprocessing, audits, and compliance exposure.
Many commenters also allege that new modifier XX is unnecessary and duplicative. These commenters state that the new modifier is not needed because CMS would be able to identify 340B drugs with the TB and JG modifiers. A commenter stated that “[a]ny drugs that do not have either of those modifiers appended would be a non-340B drug, so the `XX' modifier is unnecessary.” Another commenter alleges that “[a]ny claim line without either modifier is, by definition, already identifiable as a non-340B drug. The XX-placeholder modifier is therefore redundant: requiring hospitals to affirmatively identify what is already the logical default would add a data field without providing new information.”
A commenter urged CMS to consider other, less-burdensome options, such as creating a neutral clearinghouse for 340B claims.
Response: We recognize that implementation of the new XX modifier may be the source of some amount of administrative burden for some hospitals. However, the XX modifier is a necessary component of our proposal, and we do not believe that its implementation would be unduly burdensome or warrant a delay or phased-in approach. This modifier does not require the provider to obtain any additional information to use as it only requires information that the provider already has: whether the drug was acquired under the 340B Program.
The addition of this new modifier is consistent with the decisions that hospitals are already making (is the drug a 340B-acquired drug or a non-340B-acquired drug) when billing for these drugs. As previously mentioned, we believe requiring the use of modifier “XX” for non-340B drugs will improve the completeness and consistency of claims data—this requirement could even decrease burden on hospitals as it may improve the accuracy of billing, thus decreasing the need for hospitals to reprocess claims that were billed incorrectly.
We question those commenters who stated they would be unable to identify the non-340B claims as the provenance of the drug is something that the entities should know.
With respect to comments about timing to operationalize the new modifier, we note that hospitals have been on notice since the proposed rule went on display at the Office of the Federal Register on July 7, 2026 that CMS was considering establishing a new modifier for non-340B drugs, if finalized. In addition, the new modifier will not be required until January 1, 2027, which after display of this final rule with comment period will give hospitals two additional months to operationalize the modifier. Under section 1835(a) of the Act, providers have 12 months after the date of service to timely file a claim for payment. Therefore, for those hospitals that may need more time to ensure that they are in compliance with the modifier requirements, they have 12 months from the date of service to do so.
Comment: A few commenters commented on our proposed conforming amendment to 42 CFR 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to account for successor billing modifiers used to ( printed page 70548) identify 340B units. All commenters supported our proposal. One commenter suggested additional textual revisions. Specifically, the commenter recommended that CMS conform the regulatory text to the preamble by using disjunctive rather than conjunctive phrasing: “The preamble proposes to add `or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units, `but the proposed regulatory text reads' billed with the `TB' modifier and successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units.' Read literally, the codified text's conjunctive phrasing would require both modifiers on the same claim line. Because TB and JG are mutually exclusive in CMS's own design, that reading would exclude far fewer 340B units than CMS intends and would increase manufacturers' rebatable billing units correspondingly. CMS should revise the codified text to reflect the disjunctive phrasing in the preamble.”
Response: We appreciate the feedback from the commenter and, after reviewing the proposed regulation at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv), we agree that this appears to be an unintended technical error. We are therefore finalizing a modification to the text at § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to replace “and” with “or” so that it reads: “Separately payable billing units in claim lines billed with the `TB' modifier or successor billing modifiers to identify 340B units, for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2025.”
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to require all separately paid drug claims to be reported with a modifier of either “JG,” “TB,” or “XX” as proposed. We note placeholder “XX” is being replaced with permanent modifier “ND” as reflected in the final table below. We are also finalizing with modification our proposal for a conforming amendment to 42 CFR 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to account for successor billing modifiers used to identify 340B units.
D. CY 2027 OPPS Payment Methodology for Non-340B-Acquired Drugs Based on ODACS
CMS analyzed acquisition cost data collected through the ODACS for drugs acquired outside the 340B Program and evaluated several methodologies for estimating the relationship between hospitals' acquisition costs and ASP-based payment amounts as previously discussed in this section.
Using our preferred proposed methodology, which calculates acquisition cost margins using the geometric mean of survey-reported acquisition costs, we estimate that hospitals' acquisition costs for non-340B drugs were approximately 2.7 percent above ASP during the survey period. However, we recognize that acquisition costs reported through the survey may not fully reflect all manufacturer rebates, chargebacks, administrative fees, or other post-purchase price concessions received by hospitals, as we have not included GPO discounts into the ASP plus 2.7 percent figure. Therefore, even ASP plus 2.7 percent, the reported acquisition costs, may overstate hospitals' net acquisition costs. As a result, the estimated margin of ASP plus 2.7 percent may, in part, reflect differences in how manufacturer ( printed page 70549) rebates and other retrospective discounts were reported rather than solely the underlying acquisition costs of the drugs.
The survey results for non-340B drugs exhibit greater variation than the survey results for 340B-acquired drugs. As a result, the confidence intervals for the estimated non-340B acquisition cost margins span a slightly wider range of potential values. We believe this finding is expected given the diversity of purchasing arrangements, contracting structures, and acquisition channels available to hospitals when acquiring drugs outside the 340B Program. The broader distribution of survey-reported acquisition costs suggests greater uncertainty regarding the precise average acquisition cost margin for non-340B drugs relative to the margin observed for 340B-acquired drugs.
Although the survey data suggest that hospitals' acquisition costs for non-340B drugs may be lower on average from the current payment rate of ASP plus 6 percent, the survey results are subject to slightly greater variability and may be affected by differences in the reporting of manufacturer rebates and other price concessions. Consequently, we believe the survey data should be interpreted further as we assess the need for a payment rate change for non-340B drugs.
Given the need to further consider the non-340B survey results for the reasons mentioned, including the range of reasonable acquisition cost estimates supported by the data, we did not propose to establish a survey-based payment rate for non-340B drugs. Rather, for CY 2027, after taking into account the survey results, we proposed to continue paying separately payable non-340B drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals as we do in CY 2026, which is generally at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent. We believe this approach appropriately considers the survey findings, including the uncertainty associated with manufacturer rebate reporting and the broader distribution of acquisition cost estimates, while maintaining stability in payment rates and allowing CMS to continue evaluating acquisition cost information obtained through its survey authority under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act.
Under the same survey-based methodology proposed for determining payment for 340B-acquired drugs, such an approach for non-340B drugs would be based on the geometric mean acquisition cost estimate derived from the survey data, resulting in a payment rate of approximately ASP plus 2.7 percent. In the case of the 340B-acquired drugs, the discrepancy between acquisition cost and Medicare payment is substantial and obviously apparent; however, the discrepancy between acquisition cost and Medicare payment for non-340B acquired drugs is much less significant. Therefore, we proposed to continue paying for non-340B acquired drugs at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent. We also intended to continue evaluating the acquisition cost survey data for non-340B-acquired drugs and noted we may consider the results of this analysis in future rulemaking.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters supported our proposal to maintain the current payment rate for CY 2027 for separately payable drugs and biologicals without pass-through payment status that are not acquired under the 340B Program. These commenters stated that this method of payment makes hospital reimbursement predictable, accurate, and maintains parity with the physician office setting. One of these commenters stated that applying a payment change to non-340B drugs on the strength of data that is more widely dispersed than the data for 340B drugs would introduce risk for products that are dispensed infrequently as compared to non-orphan drugs. Several of these commenters cautioned CMS against future reductions to non-340B drugs. A commenter opined that applying any reimbursement reductions for drug purchases would be particularly difficult to justify because non-340B hospitals generally acquire drugs without the substantial discounts available through the 340B Program. Multiple commenters observed that since survey reported acquisition costs were only 2.7 percent above the mean ASP and 2.8 percent above the median ASP, that this means that for any given non-340B drug, it is likely that ASP will be roughly the same as the non-340B purchase price.
Response: We thank commenters for their support. With respect to future payment adjustments to non-340B drugs, as we indicated in the proposed rule, we are continuing to evaluate the survey data.
Comment: Several commenters expressed concern with the asymmetry of applying survey findings to reduce OPPS payment for 340B drugs but not to adjust payment for non-340B drugs. One commenter alleged that this demonstrates that CMS is “applying the survey aggressively when it produces savings but disregards it where application would reduce payment to non-340B hospitals.” The commenter contends that this inconsistency undermines our rationale that payments should reflect actual acquisition cost. The commenter also pointed out that the failure to reduce OPPS payments for non-340B drugs will create a situation where non-340B hospitals will see their total OPPS reimbursements increase due to budget neutrality. The commenter finds this outcome to be unfair and discriminatory based on 340B status. The commenter contends that the proposed payment rate will result in an underpayment for some 340B drugs since the 340B discount can range from 23.1 percent to 100 percent depending on manufacturers' actions. CMS' proposal to apply a single ASP percentage reduction of 33.4 percent to all drugs supposedly will underpay hospitals for 340B drugs subject to any discount above 33.4 percent. The commenter says that based on this underpayment of some 340B drugs, they will choose to not dispense a 340B drug to patients where the 340B payment would result in an underpayment. Instead, the commenter will purchase those drugs at the list price (wholesale acquisition cost), submit the claim without a 340B modifier, and receive the ASP plus 6 percent payment. It is the commenter's belief that other hospitals and health systems will do the same thing, which will significantly impact CMS proposed budget savings of $5.7 billion from this proposed payment adjustment.
Response: We acknowledge that we are proposing to adjust payment for 340B-acquired drugs but not for non-340B-acquired drugs in CY 2027. However, this asymmetry is simply the result of our analysis of the survey data in conjunction with ceiling prices required under the 340B Program for which there is no corollary outside of that program. As we explained in the proposed rule, based on the respective confidence intervals for 340B and non-340B drugs, we believe it is appropriate to move forward with an adjustment for 340B-acquired drugs in CY 2027 but to continue to study the data with respect to non-340B-acquired drugs. We disagree with the commenter that we are discriminating against 340B hospitals in doing so. We are better aligning our payment for 340B-acquired drugs with the cost of their acquisition, as demonstrated by the survey and supported by ceiling-price data, in compliance with section 1833(t)(14) of the Act and we are budget neutralizing that payment adjustment in compliance with our statutory budget neutrality ( printed page 70550) obligations. The nearly 40 percent discrepancy for 340B-acquired drugs is so drastic and obvious it needs to be addressed immediately; however, the preliminary non-340B average acquisition cost is only a few percentage points away from the current payment rate and warrants additional consideration before proposing changes, especially considering there is no non-340B corollary to 340B ceiling prices.
Comment: One commenter suggested that, based on the confidence interval spread for 340B drugs, CMS should conclude that the current payment rate for non-340B drugs is in fact the current payment rate for non-340B drugs (ASP plus 6 percent). Alternatively, the commenter indicated that they also supported our determination in the proposed rule that hospital acquisition data is not currently available for non-340B drugs such that payment under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(II) ( i.e., ASP plus 6 percent) continues to be appropriate.
Response: We thank the commenter for their suggestion and for their support of our proposal to pay ASP plus 6 percent for non-340B-acquired drugs for CY 2027. As we indicated in the proposed rule, we continue to evaluate acquisition cost information obtained through CMS's survey authority under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to continue paying for non-340B-acquired drugs at a rate of ASP plus 6 percent for CY 2027.
In summary, after consideration of public comments received, for the reasons discussed above, we are not finalizing our proposal for CY 2027 and subsequent years to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent. Instead, we are finalizing our alternative proposal for CY 2027 and subsequent years to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 28 percent and are revising 42 CFR 419.41(d) and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement this payment change. We are finalizing our proposal to pay for drugs acquired outside of the 340B Program at ASP plus 6 percent. We are also finalizing our proposal to exempt rural SCHs, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals and children's hospitals from the 340B Payment Policy for CY 2027 and subsequent years. We are also finalizing our proposal that hospitals paid under the OPPS, other than a type of hospital excluded from the OPPS (such as CAHs or REHs) or exempted from the 340B drug payment policy for CY 2027, are required to report modifier “JG” on the same claim line as the drug HCPCS code to identify a 340B-acquired drug; the modifier “TB” for all pass-through drugs, non-opioid treatment for pain relief drugs, and 340B-acquired drugs reported by rural SCHs, children's hospitals and PPS-exempt cancer hospitals for informational purposes; and the modifier “XX” (finalized as “ND”) for all drugs that were not acquired through the 340B Program. We note these payment policies apply to both excepted and non-excepted provider-based departments of a hospital. Finally, we are finalizing our proposal with modification to make a conforming change to § 427.303(b)(1)(iv) to ensure our process to identify 340B units for purposes of Part B inflation rebate calculations aligns with our proposed 340B modifier billing requirements. All of these finalized proposals are effective January 1, 2027.
As we proposed the previously defined payment adjustments through our authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act, we also proposed making this adjustment in a budget neutral manner. To maintain budget neutrality within the OPPS, we estimated that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs would be reduced by approximately $4.85 billion in CY 2027; however, these payments would be redistributed in an equal offsetting amount to all hospitals paid under the OPPS through increased payment rates for non-drug items and services furnished by all hospitals paid under the OPPS. Specifically, the redistributed dollars would increase the conversion factor for OPPS non-drug items and services by 8.44 percent for CY 2027.
We also estimated the alternative methodology previously described to pay 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28 percent, which is the average acquisition cost calculated from the 340B ceiling prices and volume weighted by OPPS utilization data. Through this method, we estimated that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs would be reduced by approximately $4.68 billion in CY 2027. Specifically, the redistributed dollars would increase the conversion factor for OPPS non-drug items and services by 8.14 percent for CY 2027.
For additional details on our proposed budget neutral implementation of this policy, please see section II.B. of this final rule with comment period.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters acknowledged our statutory obligation to budget neutralize our proposed payment adjustment. One commenter stated that “this adjustment is both appropriate and required.”
Response: We thank commenters for recognizing our statutory obligation to budget neutralize our proposed payment adjustment.
Comment: Several commenters supported budget neutralizing our proposed payment adjustment due to the benefit the budget-neutral redistribution would provide to many hospitals, including those serving rural and underserved communities. One of these commenters expressed disappointment that physician practices would not receive the corresponding increase in OPPS payment for non-drug items and services. The commenter opined that payment under the Medicare PFS continues to lag OPPS payment for many comparable services and stated that this distributional effect underscores the need for CMS, through PFS rulemaking, to ensure that payment to independent physician practices reflects the realistic cost of furnishing high-quality care and supports continued beneficiary access.
Response: We thank commenters for their support. With respect to the commenter's suggestion that we address differences in payment between the PFS and the OPPS, as acknowledged by the commenter this issue is outside the scope of this rulemaking.
Comment: Several commenters, including MedPAC, supported reducing payment for 340B-acquired drugs generally but lamented our statutory obligation to budget neutralize those reductions. These commenters disliked its effect of increasing beneficiary copayments for non-drug items and services and contributing to greater differences in Medicare's payment rates for those services delivered in both the hospital and office settings. These commenters urged us to work with Congress to enable us to implement the payment adjustment in a non-budget neutral manner.
Response: We thank MedPAC and the other commenters for their feedback and will take their suggestion under consideration for future rulemaking, if applicable.
Comment: Many commenters requested that CMS recalculate the budget-neutrality adjustment on an annual basis, using OPPS claims data from the prior year to ensure the policy is implemented in a fully budget neutral manner. These commenters pointed to ( printed page 70551) the implementation of our previous 340B payment policy and stated that because we did not recalculate the budget neutrality adjustment to account for volume changes in drug claims and non-drug claims over the duration of that policy, the original adjustment did not reflect actual claims.
Response: We are fully implementing budget neutrality for CY 2027. We will consider recalculating the budget-neutrality adjustment on an annual basis for future rulemaking.
