Comment: Many commenters claimed that budget neutrality does not require a uniform redistribution across hospitals and that CMS should prioritize “essential hospitals,” “true safety-net hospitals,” teaching hospitals, non-exempted children's hospitals, “hospitals that demonstrably serve the greatest numbers of Medicare beneficiaries, Medicaid beneficiaries, dual-eligible individuals, and low-income patients,” and “hospitals whose operations and missions are consistent with the intent of the 340B Program, particularly nonprofit hospitals with a demonstrated commitment to providing charity care and serving underserved populations” in the budget neutral redistribution.
Response: While we recognize the commenters' concerns regarding the effect of budget neutrality on the hospital types they list, we note that the purpose of the 340B Payment Policy is not to replace the 340B Program. We have attempted to address some of these concerns through the finalized exemptions for rural sole community hospitals, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, and children's hospitals.
Comment: Many commenters observed that the 8.44 percent increase to payment for non-drug items and services would not make all hospitals whole. The commenters state that hospitals with substantial 340B drug volume would experience a drug payment reduction, while hospitals with comparatively little or no 340B exposure would receive the benefit of the increased payments for non-drug services. A commenter stated “[t]here is no assurance that the hospital will recover what it loses.” Another commenter observed that “[a] hospital that experiences a substantial reduction in drug payments will not necessarily receive sufficient additional reimbursement through non-drug services to offset its actual losses. CMS should therefore evaluate budget neutrality at the hospital level and by hospital type rather than relying solely upon aggregate OPPS neutrality.”
Response: We acknowledge that some hospitals will potentially experience greater reductions to drug payments than increases to non-drug items and services as a consequence of our policy. However, that does not change our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to conduct a survey of drug acquisition costs and adjust payment rates taking those costs into account.
Comment: A commenter expressed concern about APC calibration. The commenter stated that “[w]hile CMS anticipates that reductions in 340B drug reimbursement will be offset through corresponding increases in payment for non-drug OPPS services, hospitals must have confidence that the APC recalibration accurately and fully reflects the funds removed from 340B drug reimbursement. However, CMS has not demonstrated that the resulting redistribution appropriately reflects the hospitals, service lines, and patient populations most affected by the proposed drug payment reductions. Because reductions in drug reimbursement and increases in APC payments are not distributed uniformly across providers and service lines, the effects of the proposal are likely to vary considerably across hospitals and clinical programs. Therefore, CMS should provide greater transparency regarding both the calculation of the budget neutrality adjustment and the distributional impact of the proposal to ensure that hospitals can appropriately evaluate its effects.”
Response: We agree that it is important to provide transparency in calculating budget neutrality for this finalized payment adjustment. For this reason, we have provided discussion throughout the proposed and final rules regarding the calculations and impact involved. We further note that we provide a separate column describing the impacts of the budget neutral distribution for this adjustment for various categories of OPPS providers in section XXVII of this final rule.
Comment: Many commenters requested that we conduct additional analyses and release additional information relating to budget neutrality before finalizing our proposal. Multiple commenters requested CMS conduct and publish a detailed analysis of the proposal's impact on 340B hospitals, safety-net providers, access to care, and essential outpatient services before finalizing the policy. A commenter suggested that CMS publish hospital-specific net-impact estimates before finalizing the policy and establish protections for hospitals facing material losses. The commenter additionally requested that CMS evaluate whether the redistribution changes incentives to furnish complex outpatient therapies or affects access in communities already experiencing hospital financial stress. Another commenter requested that CMS publish a combined beneficiary cost-sharing analysis that nets the claimed drug coinsurance savings against the coinsurance increases produced by the budget-neutral conversion factor adjustment.
Another commenter alleged that CMS provided no explanation of its methodology for calculating the impact of the payment reductions and included no accompanying data files providing the data that went into its calculation of the aggregate impact. The commenter stated that “[i]t is imperative that prior to implementing a policy of such magnitude, CMS be transparent in its methodology for modeling the cut and the corresponding budget neutrality adjustment, so that interested parties can replicate these models and verify CMS' calculations. CMS should publish its methodology for modeling the impact, which would include how CMS identified 340B hospitals and 340B drugs, including which data sources it used. CMS should also publish a hospital-level impact file with the results of the payment cut.”
Response: We thank commenters for their many suggestions for information for us to release and analyses for us to conduct prior to finalizing our proposal. As we have noted previously; however, we believe that the payment misalignment that our policy will address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy without delay now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is not even close to a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition. With respect to the commenter's suggestion to establish protections for hospitals facing material losses, as we discussed in our earlier response to a commenter, we have attempted to address some of these concerns through the finalized exemptions for rural sole community hospitals, PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, and children's hospitals. We also note that with respect to potential future impacts, our budget neutrality calculations are based on what exists in the claims data and the direct changes associated with policy. We do not predict behavioral changes or hospital decisions as a result of those policies. With respect to beneficiary cost savings, these savings are likely to stay flat or increase, saving beneficiaries more as a result. As is true of any update, there will be some redistribution of ( printed page 70552) copayments because the 20 percent beneficiary cost sharing for drugs gets “transferred” over as 20 percent into the broader OPPS through the conversion factor budget neutrality adjustment for the 340B policy. That budget neutrality adjustment will make many of the overall OPPS payment rates and their associated copayments higher. OPPS cost-sharing for a service is capped at the applicable Part A hospital inpatient deductible amount for that year for each service. That means that when OPPS payments and therefore their associated copayments, increase relative to that fixed amount, more services are likely to get capped at the inpatient deductible amount. Finally, we note that the impact file includes all proposed/final budget neutrality adjustments and updates, as well as the 340B remedy where applicable. The impact analysis looks at the existing claims, applies the proposed/finalized policies but not does not consider behavioral changes or provider decision making.
We thank commenters for their input. We estimate that OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs will be reduced by approximately $4.65 billion in CY 2027 as a result of our adoption of this policy. When factoring in our finalized policy for 340B drug payment in non-excepted PBDs, our total estimated reduction in 340B drug spending is $5.45 billion for CY 2027, which includes both Medicare and beneficiary payments.
G. Final Payment Rates for Skin Substitute APCs
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a policy to separately pay for skin substitute products as incident-to supplies in the physician office, hospital outpatient, and ambulatory surgical center settings effective January 1, 2026 (90 FR 53729 through 53748). We excluded skin substitutes approved as biological products under section 351 of the PHS Act, which would continue to be paid consistent with section 1847A of the Act, from our policy to pay for skin substitute products as incident-to-supplies. As part of this final policy, we assigned sheet-form skin substitute products to one of three clinical APCs we created on “FDA regulatory categories”: [141] APC 6000 (PMA Skin Substitute Products), APC 6001 (510(k) Skin Substitute Products), and APC 6002 (361 HCT/P Skin Substitute Products). For CY 2026, we set an initial payment rate of $127.14/cm2 for APCs 6000 (PMA Skin Substitute Products), 6001 (510(k) Skin Substitute Products), and 6002 (361 HCT/P Skin Substitute Products). We stated we would update the payment rates for skin substitute categories annually through rulemaking using the most recently available calendar quarter of ASP data, when available, to set the rates. In the event ASP data was not available for a particular product, we stated we would use the outpatient hospital MUC data. If MUC was not available, we stated we would use the product's WAC or 89.6 percent of AWP if WAC was also unavailable. We finalized a policy to include all skin substitute products used across both settings as well as the combined product utilization patterns and, as soon as data was available that reflects the results of this policy, to determine a weighted average per-unit cost by group to set the payment rates for each of the three categories.
As stated in the proposed rule, at this time, we do not believe we have sufficient data upon which to propose a revised payment rate for all three skin substitute product APCs. We also believe that updating the payment rates for CY 2027, before the impacts of the payment policy are reflected in the CY 2026 claims that will be used for CY 2028 OPPS/ASC and PFS rulemakings, could result in payment disruptions or introduce unnecessary volatility. Because updated use patterns reflecting the CY 2026 policy changes are not yet available, we proposed for CY 2027 to continue the policy finalized for CY 2026 in its entirety, which includes maintaining the payment rate of $127.14/cm2 for APCs 6000 (PMA Skin Substitute Products), 6001 (510(k) Skin Substitute Products), and 6002 (361 HCT/P Skin Substitute Products).
We note that, effective April 1, 2026, CMS created new HCPCS Level II codes to describe the application of non-sheet form skin substitute products HCPCS codes G0681 through G0684:
G0681—Application of a premarket approval (pma), 510(k), 361 human cells, tissues or cellular and tissue-based products (hct/p) non-sheet form skin substitute for a wound surface area up to 100 sq cm; first 25 sq cm or less of wound surface area.
G0682—Application of a premarket approval (pma), 510(k), 361 human cells, tissues or cellular and tissue-based products (hct/p) non-sheet form skin substitute for a wound surface area up to 100 sq cm; each additional 25 sq cm wound surface area, or part thereof (list separately in addition to code for primary procedure).
G0683—Application of a premarket approval (pma), 510(k), 361 human cells, tissues or cellular and tissue-based products (hct/p) non-sheet form skin substitute graft for a wound surface greater than or equal to 100 sq cm; first 100 sq cm wound surface area, or 1 percent of body area of infants and children.
G0684—Application of a premarket approval (pma), 510(k), 361 human cells, tissues or cellular and tissue-based products (hct/p) non-sheet form skin substitute graft for a wound surface greater than or equal to 100 sq cm; each additional 100 sq cm wound surface area or part thereof, or each additional 1 percent of body area of infants and children, or part thereof (list separately in addition to code for primary procedure).
As explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC Final Rule, we did not finalize changes to the payment arrangement under the OPPS for products that are not in sheet form and explained that we would continue to explore the issue for future rulemaking (90 FR 53739). Accordingly, we assigned the new non-sheet form application codes a status indicator of “N” to indicate that payment for the application is packaged effective April 1, 2026.
For CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the payment arrangement for non-sheet form skin substitute products under the OPPS; we proposed to assign status indicator “N” to both the non-sheet form application codes (G0681 through G0684) and the non-sheet form skin substitute products, themselves. Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to continue to package both the non-sheet form products and the application codes used to apply them.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Commenters generally supported finalizing a single blended payment rate for CY 2027. Commenters supported a period of stable payment to ensure beneficiary access to skin substitute products. ( printed page 70553)
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: Some commenters did not support continuing to pay for sheet-form skin substitute products at the $127.14/cm2 payment rate for CY 2027 as proposed. Some commenters believed that the proposed payment rate is punitive and overcorrects for abuses seen in the skin substitute space. Commenters suggested that targeted program integrity tools directed at improper billing patterns rather than an across-the-board payment reduction that applies to both compliant and noncompliant providers would more precisely address CMS's concerns without impacting access to medically necessary care. Several commenters requested that CMS finalize a payment rate that is more reflective of the costs and utilization volume for skin substitute products. Some commenters recommended that we finalize a revised payment rate between $478/cm2 and $715.45/cm2 . Several commenters did not recommend a new specific payment rate and instead proposed alternative methodologies for calculating a new payment rate for skin substitute products. For example, several commenters requested that we reconsider using OPPS utilization data to determine the payment rate for skin substitute products in the HOPD and physician office setting, with some explaining that the quantity of a skin substitute purchased or utilized is not a measure of its clinical value. A few commenters suggested that we revise the payment methodology finalized in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule to instead utilize providers' acquisition costs up to a CMS-established payment ceiling, at the lower of an invoice or a cap. These commenters believed a cap would minimize payment-driven selection of products, support clinically appropriate utilization, and ensure providers are compensated for the resources required to deliver high-quality patient care. Other commenters recommended that, if utilization data were to be used, CMS adopt a volume-weighted geometric mean instead of a volume-weighted arithmetic average to determine the payment rate.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input regarding the proposed CY 2027 payment rate of $127.14/cm2 for sheet-form skin substitute products and for their suggestions on alternative payment methodologies to calculate a new payment rate. We note that several of the comments were extremely similar to those provided to CMS in response to the proposed payment methodology for skin substitute products in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. As we explained in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule, we calculated a single rate for each FDA regulatory category by taking the volume-weighted average ASP for skin substitute products in each FDA regulatory category from Q4 2024, using hospital outpatient utilization to weight each category, and applied the highest of the three resulting rates uniformly across all three categories for CY 2026. We used the highest average for the three FDA regulatory categories to ensure we would not underestimate the resources involved with furnishing these services. We refer readers to the discussion in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule for a summary of the comments and detailed responses regarding the payment methodology that was finalized for CY 2026 (90 FR 53728 through 53748).
We continue to believe that it is premature to adjust the payment rate for skin substitute products because updated use patterns reflecting the CY 2026 policy changes are not yet available. Therefore, we are finalizing our proposal to maintain the $127.14/cm2 payment rate for sheet-form skin substitute products paid under the OPPS.
Comment: Several commenters requested CMS evaluate utilization patterns following the implementation of the revised $127.14/cm2 rate and to monitor beneficiary access and distinguish reductions in inappropriate utilization from reductions in clinically appropriate utilization. Commenters requested that we review the available 2026 claims data to assess changes in several measures, including utilization rates of skin substitute products by site of service; clinical outcomes for patients with chronic, non-healing wounds, and utilization rates of medical visits.
Response: We thank the commenters for their suggestions. CMS is generally interested in better understanding the effects of all of our payment policies, including potential impacts to beneficiary access and clinically appropriate utilization. We do not yet have a sufficient volume of claims data reflecting the revised payment rate to draw reliable conclusions regarding several of the measures requested by the commenter as the policy was only implemented in CY 2026. We intend to continue monitoring relevant claims data as it becomes available.
Comment: Several commenters requested that CMS update the payment rate for skin substitute products using a defined inflation index, such as the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) or the Medicare Economic Index, rather than recalculating them based on new ASP data. Commenters thought updating the payment rate annually for inflation would keep reimbursement aligned with rising costs and help ensure continued beneficiary access to advanced wound care technologies.
Response: We appreciate the commenters for their input. We believe that, over time, the ASP data we are collecting will more accurately reflect the market impacts of our policy to treat skin substitute products as incident-to supplies. By relying on ASP, payment updates will be responsive to changes in the actual cost of skin substitute products as a result of market pressures, whereas an index like the CPI-U is a general inflation measure that does not account for pricing dynamics. Therefore, we believe that updating the payment rates, based on ASP data will more likely result in payment rates that reflect the changing dynamics of the market rather than anchoring the cost to the initial payment rate for CY 2026, and finalized payment rate for CY 2027, based on data collected prior to the implementation of this policy. We do understand the merits of the commenters' suggestion and will keep it under consideration for future policy development as this policy evolves.
Comment: We received two comments regarding the payment methodology for skin substitute products licensed as biological products under section 351 of the PHS Act, meaning those that have gone through the FDA BLA process. A commenter supported continuing this approach because it recognizes their distinct regulatory status. Another commenter did not support continuing to pay for 351s under the ASP plus 6 percent methodology arguing that evidentiary standards for 351s are likely being lowered due to external pressure to reduce the barrier-to-entry for approval.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input and perspective on this issue. We note that the evidentiary standards for biological products under section 351 of the PHS Act are out of scope for CMS rulemaking. We are not finalizing changes to the ASP methodology for biological products licensed under section 351 of the PHS Act at this time.
Comment: We received comments regarding our proposal to continue to categorize skin substitute products by FDA regulatory pathway, as finalized in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule. While one commenter supported implementing a three-tiered approach with differing payment rates per FDA regulatory category, most commenters urged CMS not to pursue payment differentiation or categorize skin ( printed page 70554) substitute products by FDA regulatory category. A commenter noted that because FDA regulatory requirements and pathways evolve over time, using regulatory history as a permanent basis for payment differentiation would also create arbitrary disparities among products that serve the same clinical purpose today, based solely on when and how each product entered the market. The commenter recommended that CMS should base any future payment distinctions on demonstrated clinical performance and resource costs, not regulatory classification. Similarly, another commenter requested that CMS clarify that FDA regulatory pathway by itself will not establish clinical superiority or therapeutic hierarchy among skin substitute products. A commenter explained that products previously subject to more burdensome PMA requirements would today likely enter the market under a 510(k) pathway, so relying on FDA regulatory history as a proxy for payment differentiation risks entrenching outdated distinctions that no longer reflect current practice. One commenter further supported maintaining a single payment rate for all three categories because they believed the waste, fraud, and abuse observed in the skin substitute market is the result of certain 361 HCT/P manufacturers taking advantage of easy market entry to manipulate reimbursement, and that by differentiating payment by FDA approval, CMS risks enabling further price manipulation from some 361 HCT/Ps without the moderating impact of PMA and 510(k) product prices.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We continue to believe that categorizing skin substitute products by FDA regulatory pathway remains appropriate at this time. We note, however, that under the finalized policy, for CY 2027, all sheet-form skin substitute products would be paid at the same $127.14/cm2 rate. We continue to believe that it is premature to adjust the payment rate for skin substitute products because updated use patterns reflecting the CY 2026 policy changes are not yet available. We will continue to analyze claims data as it becomes available and will propose any changes in payment through the rulemaking process.
Comment: We received several comments requesting that we align payment for non-sheet form skin substitutes with payment for sheet-form skin substitute products. Specifically, commenters requested that CMS change the status indicator of the non-sheet application codes (HCPCS codes G0681-G0684) from “N” to “T” to allow for payment, and assign the non-sheet application codes to the same APCs as the sheet-form application codes (CPT codes 15271-15278). Specifically, commenters requested that CMS assign HCPCS code G0681 to APC 5053 (Level 3 Skin Procedures) and HCPCS code G0683 to APC 5054 (Level 4 Skin Procedures). HCPCS codes G0682 and G0684, which describe add-on codes, should be treated the same as the sheet-form application add-on codes (CPT codes 15272, 15274, 15276, and 15278) and be assigned to status indicator “N,” per the commenters. In addition, commenters requested that CMS pay separately for non-sheet skin substitute products to align with payment for sheet-form skin substitute products. Commenters believed that non-sheet products service similar clinical purposes as sheet products, and, therefore, aligning for non-sheet forms and sheet-forms recognizes the clinical non-sheet forms offer, preserves physician flexibility to select the best product for each patient, supports innovation, ensures skin substitute products are evaluated on therapeutic value rather than disadvantaged by coding or reimbursement policy, and maintains site neutrality with products applied in the physician office setting.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. Payment for application of non-sheet skin substitute products could benefit from parity with payment for the application of sheet form skin substitute products, and not doing so could fail to appropriately recognize the resource costs expended when applying non-sheet products. Accordingly, we are not finalizing our proposal to maintain the status indicator of “N” for HCPCS codes G0681 and G0683. For CY 2027, we are finalizing to change the status indicator for HCPCS codes G0681 and G0683 from “N” to “T” and assign G0681 to APC 5053 (Level 3 Skin Procedures) and G0683 to APC 5054 (Level 4 Skin Procedures), consistent with the APC assignments for the analogous sheet form application codes (CPT codes 15271 through 15278). We are finalizing assignment of status indicator “N” to add-on codes G0682 and G0684, consistent with the treatment of the sheet form application add-on codes (CPT codes 15272, 15274, 15276, and 15278), as proposed. The final CY 2027 payment rates can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment via the internet on the CMS website. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 of this final rule with comment period for the status indicator definitions for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 can also be found via the internet on the CMS website. As previously discussed, we will continue to monitor the effects of this policy in general, including this newly finalized aspect.
We are not finalizing separate payment for non-sheet skin substitute products at this time. Non-sheet products are not manufactured, applied, or measured in the same standardized manner as sheet form products, which are billed in per cm2 units. Because of these differences, we believe it is more appropriate to continue packaging payment for non-sheet form products under the OPPS. We recognize the interest commenters have expressed in separate payment for non-sheet form skin substitute products, and we will continue to consider the issue of separate payment for non-sheet products moving forward.
Comment: We received a comment requesting that CMS provide a clear, operational definition of a non-sheet skin substitute product.
Response: We thank the commenter for this suggestion and will take it into consideration. One difficulty with the commenter's request is that non-sheet products cover a wide range of physical forms and may not share a common structure the way sheet-form skin substitute products do. We note that we have described the form of some non-sheet skin substitute products in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC Final Rule as gels, powders, liquids, injectables, 3D-printed constructs, etc. (90 FR 53739) that have units that are difficult to standardize for payment purposes. We will consider providing additional clarifications in future rulemaking.
Comment: We received a comment from a manufacturer requesting separate payment for Omeza Complete Matrix, a non-sheet skin substitute product described by HCPCS code A2014 (Omeza collagen matrix, per 100 mg). The commenter stated that separate payment is appropriate for this product because, in the commenter's view, a product's starting form as a non-sheet product should not determine its payment category so long as the product forms a sheet-like scaffolding once applied.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's request. We believe it is necessary to apply a consistent payment methodology across non-sheet form skin substitute products for CY 2027. Consistent with the approach finalized in this final rule, application of Omeza Complete Matrix, as described by HCPCS codes G0681 and G0683, will be paid separately, while the product itself will be packaged for CY 2027. We do not believe it is appropriate to except ( printed page 70555) this product from the non-sheet product payment methodology based on its post-application form, given that the product is supplied in mg and applied in non-sheet form. As stated earlier, we will continue to consider the issue of separate payment for non-sheet products more broadly.
Comment: We received requests for billing guidance pertaining to our skin substitute payment policies. Several commenters requested that CMS provide guidance clarifying that providers may bill for the total amount of skin substitute product clinically necessary to treat a wound, rather than only the two-dimensional surface area of the wound bed. Commenters explained that, especially for deep wounds, the amount of product needed to treat the wound often exceeds the cm2 surface area. Commenters requested CMS provide billing instructions that would allow providers to calculate the relevant surface area for the application codes based on the interior surface area of the wound plus an appropriate margin for graft fixation. A commenter recommended a specific formula for providers to use to calculate the total therapeutic area. Commenters requested that CMS provide guidance that states that providers can bill for the total amount of skin substitute product needed to treat the entire wound area, for sheet form and non-sheet form products, to enable providers to bill accurately for the services they furnish and to give MACs a consistent framework for adjudication.
Response: We appreciate the input from the commenters. We do not believe it is necessary at this time to issue additional guidance on how providers should bill for the total amount of skin substitute product used to treat a wound. The application codes that would be used to bill for the application of the products, namely CPT codes 15271 through 15278 for sheet form products and HCPCS codes G0681 through G0684 for non-sheet products, already specify defined wound surface area amounts for purposes of reporting the applicable code. Providers are expected to select the appropriate application code and report the units of product that correspond to the total wound surface area treated. We note that this same coding structure, and the same expectation that providers report the total wound surface area treated using these application codes, were in place prior to the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC skin substitute policy was in effect, even when the products were packaged into the application payment at that time. We do not believe the manner in which the application codes describe and are used to report wound surface area has changed in a way that necessitates new guidance at this time. However, we will continue to consider whether such guidance is necessary going forward.
Comment: We received a comment from Kerecis, a skin substitute product manufacturer, explaining that two of their products have different code coding classifications. Specifically, the manufacturer stated that one product is described by a Q-code and another is described by an A-code. Per the manufacturer, the coding classification distinction creates administrative burden due to the confusion it causes for both physicians and MACs. The commenter requested that CMS address this issue to ensure there are no inappropriate burdens or barriers to accessing clinically appropriate skin substitute products.
Response: We appreciate the commenter for sharing their concern regarding the current bifurcated system. We will take comments about the coding differences between the products into consideration for future rulemaking.
In summary, for CY 2027, we are finalizing the $127.14/cm2 payment rate for all sheet form skin substitute products as proposed. We are also finalizing our proposals regarding payment for non-sheet skin substitute application codes and non-sheet products with modifications. Specifically, we are finalizing to assign HCPCS code G0681 to APC 5053 (Level 3 Skin Procedures) with status indicator “T” and G0683 to APC 5054 (Level 4 Skin Procedures APC) with status indicator “T.” We are finalizing to continue to assign HCPCS codes G0682 and G0684 to status indicator “N,” as proposed. Finally, we are not finalizing changes to the current payment arrangement under the OPPS for products that are not in sheet form at this time and, therefore, non-sheet skin substitute products will remain assigned to status indicator “N.” We refer readers to Addendum B for the final CY 2027 APC and status indicator assignments for skin substitute products. The final CY 2027 payment rates can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment via the internet on the CMS website. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 of this final rule with comment period for the status indicator definitions for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 can also be found via the internet on the CMS website.
H. Add-On Payment for Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) Derived From Domestically Produced Molybdenum-99 (Mo-99)
As discussed in prior rulemaking, in collaboration with the Department of Energy, National Nuclear Security Administration (DOE/NNSA), CMS provided an additional payment of $10 for the marginal cost for Tc-99m produced by non-Highly Enriched Uranium (HEU) sources in an effort to support access to Technetium-99m (Tc-99m), a critical radioisotope used in the majority of diagnostic imaging services, and produced through the radioactive decay of molybdenum-99 (Mo-99) from CY 2013 to CY 2025. We stated that we believe such an adjustment would ensure equitable payments in light of market influences, cost differentials, and cost variations and their potential to create significant payment inequities among hospitals (77 FR 68323). Accordingly, we established HCPCS code Q9969 (Tc-99m from non-highly enriched uranium source, full cost recovery add-on per study dose) to describe the Tc-99m radioisotope produced by non-HEU methods and used in a diagnostic procedure.
In January 2022, the Secretary of Energy issued a certification that stated that there is a sufficient global supply of non-HEU-sourced Mo-99 to meet the needs of patients in the United States (86 FR 73270). Additionally, in March 2023, the last major global producer of Mo-99 converted from HEU to low-enriched uranium (LEU) targets, and all Mo-99 used in the United States is now produced without HEU. As such, in the CY 2024 OPPS final rule with comment period (88 FR 81803), we adopted a policy to end the additional $10 add-on payment described by HCPCS code Q9969 for non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m at the end of CY 2025. We explained that given that all Mo-99 used in the U.S. is now produced without HEU, we believe that starting in CY 2026 the Medicare claims data utilized to set payment rates would only include claims for diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals that utilized non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m, meaning the data would reflect the full cost of the Tc-99m diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals that providers would use in CY 2026. That being the case, we believe there would no longer be a need for the additional $10 add-on payment for non-HEU-sourced Tc-99m for CY 2026 or future years.
In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period (89 FR 59377 through 59378), we shared that the Department of Energy and other interested parties raised another issue ( printed page 70556) affecting the domestic supply chain for Mo-99 and Tc-99 that, left unaddressed, could also cause payment inequity among outpatient hospital providers. We noted that foreign Mo-99 production has historically been subsidized by foreign governments, resulting in prices below the true cost of production. These artificially low, foreign government-subsidized prices have created a disincentive for domestic investments in Mo-99 production infrastructure and a barrier to entry for new producers, including U.S. companies, which in turn has resulted in unreliable production and periodic shortages. Subsequently, using our equitable adjustment authority under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act, we proposed and finalized a policy to address the payment inequity resulting from the higher cost of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 by establishing a new add-on payment of $10 per dose for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 starting on January 1, 2026. Furthermore, we stated that the Department of Energy, National Nuclear Security Administration (DOE/NNSA) would establish the criteria to certify whether the Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical dose is derived from domestically produced Mo-99 and eligible for the add-on payment, which would be included in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed rule with comment period. We also stated that we would continue to develop the technical implementation of this additional payment after a definition for domestically produced Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical was established, including any requirements for providers to document that the Tc-99m radiopharmaceutical used in a procedure was domestically produced and could qualify to receive the add-on payment. Additionally, we stated that our intent was to have the regulatory framework for this policy in place prior to the domestic production of Mo-99 and Tc-99m, to increase provider awareness of the availability of additional payments for domestically sourced Tc-99m radiopharmaceuticals. Likewise, producers of domestic Mo-99 would have certainty that the Medicare OPPS payment policy takes into account the additional costs of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99.
a. Criteria for Classifying a Tc-99m Radiopharmaceutical Dose as Domestically Produced
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53751-53755), for purposes of the add-on payment for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99, we finalized our definition of a domestically produced dose of Tc-99m as a dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99. We also finalized the following definitions:
Domestically produced dose of Tc-99m: A dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99;
Domestically produced Mo-99: Mo-99 that was both irradiated and processed in the U.S.;
Irradiated: The process of bombarding a uranium or molybdenum target with radiation in order to produce Mo-99, and to specify that irradiation is typically performed with a nuclear reactor or particle accelerator;
Processed: In this context, processed refers to the purification of Mo-99 from irradiated material.
Additionally, we finalized a policy that a dose of Tc-99m generated from Mo-99 that was irradiated or processed outside the U.S. would not qualify for this add-on payment, even if the Mo-99 was loaded into a Tc-99m generator in the U.S. or if the Tc-99m was eluted at a radiopharmacy in the U.S. We also finalized the codification of the aforementioned definitions and references for domestically produced Mo-99 to § 419.49 to specify when a dose of Tc-99m generated from domestically produced Mo-99 could be eligible for the add-on payment.
b. Coding and Documentation for the Add-On Payment for Tc-99m Derived From Domestically Produced Mo-99
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53751-53755), we also finalized the establishment of HCPCS C-code C9176 (Tc-99m from domestically produced non-HEU Mo-99, [minimum 50 percent], full cost recovery add-on, per study dose), effective January 1, 2026. Hospitals may report HCPCS code C9176 once per dose, along with any diagnostic scan or scans furnished using Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99, if they can certify that at least 50 percent of the Mo-99 in the Tc-99m generator used to produce the Tc-99m was domestically produced Mo-99. We also finalized the implementation plan, including the $10 per-dose add-on payment and the certification and tracking approach described in the CY 2026 rulemaking.
For CY 2027, we did not propose any changes to the add-on payment policy for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. We received public comments regarding this policy, which we summarize and respond to below.
Comment: Although we did not propose any changes to the add-on payment for radiopharmaceuticals that use Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99 for CY 2027, we received comments regarding the policy. One commenter supported continuation of the $10 per-dose add-on payment and HCPCS code C9176, stating that the policy helps account for the higher costs associated with domestic production and supports investment in a more secure and resilient domestic Mo-99 supply chain. The commenter also encouraged CMS to continue monitoring whether the $10 add-on payment remains sufficient over time in light of production, compliance, transportation, and supply-chain costs.
Another commenter opposed continuation of the add-on payment and urged CMS to discontinue the policy for CY 2027. The commenter stated that the add-on payment does not effectively incentivize domestic Mo-99 production because payments are made to hospitals rather than directly to domestic producers and expressed concern that hospitals may have difficulty identifying when a dose qualifies for the add-on payment. The commenter also stated that the policy could disrupt existing Tc-99m supply and distribution arrangements, including generator contracting, and potentially affect patient access, particularly in rural communities.
Response: We thank the commenters for their feedback. As discussed in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we established the $10 per-dose add-on payment using our equitable adjustment authority under section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act to address the payment inequity resulting from the higher cost of Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized the implementation framework for this policy, including the criteria for a domestically produced dose of Tc-99m, the 50-percent threshold for domestically produced Mo-99, and HCPCS code C9176.
We continue to believe that the add-on payment appropriately accounts for the additional costs to hospital outpatient departments associated with utilizing Tc-99m derived from domestically produced Mo-99. As we explained in prior rulemaking, establishing the payment framework in advance of domestic production provides hospitals with information regarding the availability of additional payment for qualifying doses and provides domestic producers with greater certainty that Medicare OPPS ( printed page 70557) payment policy takes into account the additional costs associated with domestic production. After a consideration of the comments received, noting we did not propose changes to this policy for CY 2027, we are continuing the existing policy without modification.
We appreciate commenters' perspectives regarding the amount of the add-on payment, implementation of the policy, and potential effects on the Mo-99 and Tc-99m supply chain. We will continue to monitor relevant information regarding the implementation of the policy, including information regarding the costs associated with domestically produced Mo-99 and the availability of Tc-99m, and may consider whether future refinements are warranted.
VI. Estimate of OPPS Transitional Pass-Through Spending for Drugs, Biologicals, Radiopharmaceuticals, and Devices
A. Amount of Additional Payment and Limit on Aggregate Annual Adjustment
Section 1833(t)(6)(E) of the Act limits the total projected amount of transitional pass-through payment for drugs, biologicals, and categories of devices for a given year to an “applicable percentage,” currently not to exceed 2.0 percent of total program payments estimated to be made for all covered services under the OPPS furnished for that year. If we estimate before the beginning of the calendar year that the total amount of pass-through payments in that year would exceed the applicable percentage, section 1833(t)(6)(E)(iii) of the Act requires a uniform prospective reduction in the amount of each of the transitional pass-through payments made in that year to ensure that the limit is not exceeded. We estimate the pass-through spending to determine whether payments exceed the applicable percentage and the appropriate pro rata reduction to the conversion factor for the projected level of pass-through spending in the following year to ensure that total estimated pass-through spending for the prospective payment year is budget neutral, as required by section 1833(t)(6)(E) of the Act.
For devices, developing a proposed estimate of pass-through spending in CY 2027 entails estimating spending for two groups of items. The first group of items consists of device categories that are currently eligible for pass-through payment and that will continue to be eligible for pass-through payment in CY 2027. The CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (72 FR 66778) describes the methodology we have used in previous years to develop the pass-through spending estimate for known device categories continuing into the applicable update year. The second group of items consists of devices that we know are newly eligible, or project may be newly eligible, for device pass-through payment in the remaining quarters of CY 2026 or beginning in CY 2027. The sum of the proposed CY 2027 pass-through spending estimates for these two groups of device categories equals the proposed total CY 2027 pass-through spending estimate for device categories with pass-through payment status. We determined the device pass-through estimated payments for each device category based on the amount of payment as required by section 1833(t)(6)(D)(ii) of the Act, and as outlined in previous rules, including the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53766 through 53769). We noted that, beginning in CY 2010, the pass-through evaluation process and pass-through payment methodology for implantable biologicals newly approved for pass-through payment beginning on or after January 1, 2010, that are surgically inserted or implanted (through a surgical incision or a natural orifice) use the device pass-through process and payment methodology (74 FR 60476). As has been our past practice (76 FR 74335), we include an estimate of any implantable biologicals eligible for pass-through payment in our estimate of pass-through spending for devices. Similarly, we finalized a policy in CY 2015 that applications for pass-through payment for skin substitutes and similar products be evaluated using the medical device pass-through process and payment methodology (79 FR 66885 through 66888). In CY 2026, we finalized a policy to consider skin substitutes with an approved Biologics License Application (BLA) under transitional drug pass-through payment status, while skin substitutes with FDA Premarket Approval or FDA 510(k) clearance continue to be evaluated under transitional device pass-through payment status (90 FR 53636). Therefore, for CY 2027, we also proposed to include an estimate of any skin substitutes and similar products with FDA Premarket Approval or FDA 510(k) clearance in our estimate of pass-through spending for devices and skin substitutes with an approved BLA under transitional drug pass-through spending for drugs and biologicals.
For drugs and biologicals eligible for pass-through payment, section 1833(t)(6)(D)(i) of the Act establishes the pass-through payment amount as the amount by which the amount authorized under section 1842(o) of the Act (or, if the drug or biological is covered under a competitive acquisition contract under section 1847B of the Act, an amount determined by the Secretary equal to the average price for the drug or biological for all competitive acquisition areas and year established under such section as calculated and adjusted by the Secretary) exceeds the portion of the otherwise applicable fee schedule amount that the Secretary determines is associated with the drug or biological. Consistent with current policy, we proposed to apply a rate of ASP plus 6 percent to most drugs and biologicals for CY 2027, and therefore our estimate of drug and biological pass-through payment for CY 2027 for this group of items was $12.2 million.
Payment for certain drugs,[142] specifically contrast agents without pass-through payment status, is packaged into payment for the associated procedures, and these products are not separately paid. In addition, we policy-package non-pass-through drugs and biologicals that function as supplies when used in a diagnostic test or procedure unless a high-cost diagnostic radiopharmaceutical with a per-day cost greater than the finalized per-day cost threshold referenced in section II.A.3.c. of this final rule with comment period is used for the diagnostic test or procedure. We policy-package all drugs and biologicals that function as supplies when used in a surgical procedure or for anesthesia, and other categories of drugs and biologicals, as discussed in section V.B.1.c. of this final rule with comment period. Consistent with current policy, for CY 2027, we proposed that policy-packaged drugs and biologicals with pass-through payment status will be paid at ASP plus 6 percent, like other pass-through drugs and biologicals less the policy-packaged drug APC offset amount described later in this section of the preamble. Our estimate of pass-through payment for policy-packaged drugs and biologicals with pass-through payment status approved prior to CY 2027 is not $0. This is because the pass-through payment amount and the fee schedule amount associated with the drug or biological will not be the same, unlike for separately payable drugs and ( printed page 70558) biologicals. In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (88 FR 81774 through 81776), we discussed our policy to determine if the costs of certain policy-packaged drugs or biologicals are already packaged into the existing APC structure. If we determine that a policy-packaged drug or biological approved for pass-through payment resembles predecessor drugs or biologicals already included in the costs of the APCs that are associated with the drug receiving pass-through payment, we offset the amount of pass-through payment for the policy-packaged drug or biological. For these drugs or biologicals, the APC offset amount is the portion of the APC payment for the specific procedure performed with the pass-through drug or biological, which we refer to as the policy-packaged drug APC offset amount. Consistent with current policy described in section V.A.5. of this final rule with comment period, if we determine that an offset is appropriate for a specific policy-packaged drug or biological receiving pass-through payment, we proposed to reduce our estimate of pass-through payments for these drugs or biologicals by the APC offset amount.
Similar to pass-through spending estimates for devices, the first group of drugs and biologicals requiring a pass-through payment estimate consists of those products that were recently made eligible for pass-through payment and that will continue to be eligible for pass-through payment in CY 2027. The second group contains drugs and biologicals that we know are newly eligible, or project will be newly eligible, in CY 2027. The sum of the CY 2027 pass-through spending estimates for these two groups of drugs and biologicals equals the total CY 2027 pass-through spending estimate for drugs and biologicals with pass-through payment status.
We did not receive public comments on this provision, and therefore, we are finalizing as proposed.

VIII. Payment for Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient Services
Since CY 2000, Medicare has paid for partial hospitalization program (PHP) services under the OPPS. Beginning in CY 2024, as authorized by section 4124 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA), 2023 (Pub. L. 117-328), Medicare began paying for intensive outpatient program (IOP) services furnished by hospital outpatient departments, community mental health centers (CMHCs), Federally qualified health centers, and rural health clinics, in addition to opioid treatment programs. Additional background on the partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient benefits is included in the following paragraphs.
We note that some commenters made comments on PHP and IOP topics that were not discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule. These topics are out of scope for purposes of this notice and comment rulemaking, but we will consider these comments as we consider these issues for future rulemaking.
1. Partial Hospitalization
A partial hospitalization program (PHP) is an intensive outpatient program of psychiatric services provided as an alternative to inpatient psychiatric care for individuals who have an acute mental illness, which includes, but is not limited to, conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders (SUD). Section 1861(ff)(1) of the Act defines partial hospitalization services as the items and services described in paragraph (2) prescribed by a physician for an individual determined (not less frequently than monthly) by a physician to have a need for such services for a minimum of 20 hours per week and provided under a program described in paragraph (3) under the supervision of a physician pursuant to an individualized, written plan of treatment established and periodically reviewed by a physician (in consultation with appropriate staff participating in such program), which sets forth the physician's diagnosis, the type, amount, frequency, and duration of the items and services provided under the plan, and the goals for treatment under the plan.
Section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act describes the items and services included in partial hospitalization program services. Section 1861(ff)(3)(A) of the Act specifies that a PHP is a program furnished by a hospital to its outpatients or by a CMHC, as a distinct and organized intensive ambulatory treatment service, offering less than 24-hour-daily care, in a location other than an individual's home or inpatient or residential setting. Section 1861(ff)(3)(B) of the Act defines a CMHC for purposes of this benefit. We refer readers to sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(i), 1833(t)(2)(B), 1833(t)(2)(C), and 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act and 42 CFR 419.21, for additional information regarding PHP.
PHP policies and payment have been addressed under OPPS since CY 2000. In CY 2008, we began efforts to strengthen the PHP benefit through extensive data analysis, along with policy and payment changes, by implementing two refinements to the methodology for computing the PHP median. For a detailed discussion on these policies, we refer readers to the CY 2008 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (72 FR 66670 through 66676). In CY 2009, we implemented several regulatory, policy, and payment changes. For a detailed discussion on these policies, we refer readers to the CY 2009 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (73 FR 68688 through 68697). In CY 2010, we retained the two-tier payment approach for partial hospitalization services and used only hospital-based PHP data in computing the PHP Ambulatory Payment Classification (APC) per diem costs, upon which PHP APC per diem payment rates are based (74 FR 60556 through 60559). In CY 2011 (75 FR 71994), we established four separate PHP APC per diem payment rates: two for CMHCs (APC 0172 and APC 0173) and two for hospital-based PHPs (APC 0175 and APC 0176). We also instituted a 2-year transition period for CMHCs to the CMHC APC per diem payment rates. For a detailed discussion, we refer readers to section X.B. of the CY 2011 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (75 FR 71991 through 71994). In CY 2012, we determined the relative payment weights for partial hospitalization services provided by CMHCs based on data derived solely from CMHCs and the relative payment weights for partial hospitalization services provided by hospital-based PHPs based exclusively on hospital data (76 FR 74348 through 74352). In the CY 2013 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized our proposal to base the relative payment weights that underpin the OPPS APCs, including the four PHP APCs (APCs 0172, 0173, 0175, and 0176), on geometric mean costs rather than on the median costs. For a detailed discussion on this policy, we refer readers to the CY 2013 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (77 FR 68406 through 68412).
In the CY 2014 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (78 FR 43621 through 43622) and CY 2015 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (79 FR 66902 through 66908), we continued to apply our established policies to calculate the four PHP APC per diem payment rates based on geometric mean per diem costs using the most recent claims data for each provider type. For a detailed discussion on this policy, we refer readers to the CY 2014 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (78 FR 75047 through 75050). In the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (80 FR 70453 through 70467), we described our extensive analysis of the claims and cost data and ratesetting methodology, corrected a cost inversion that occurred in the final rule with comment period data with respect to hospital-based PHP providers, and renumbered the PHP APCs. In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79687 ( printed page 70562) through 79691), we continued to apply our established policies to calculate the PHP APC per diem payment rates based on geometric mean per diem costs and finalized a policy to combine the Level 1 and Level 2 PHP APCs for CMHCs and for hospital-based PHPs. We also implemented an 8-percent outlier cap for CMHCs to mitigate potential outlier billing vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive description of PHP payment policy, including a detailed methodology for determining PHP per diem amounts, we refer readers to the CY 2016 and CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rules with comment period (80 FR 70453 through 70455 and 81 FR 79678 through 79680, respectively).
In the CYs 2018 and 2019 OPPS/ASC final rules with comment period (82 FR 59373 through 59381 and 83 FR 58983 through 58998, respectively), we continued to apply our established policies to calculate the PHP APC per diem payment rates based on geometric mean per diem costs, designated a portion of the estimated 1.0 percent hospital outpatient outlier threshold specifically for CMHCs, and proposed updates to the PHP allowable HCPCS codes. We finalized these proposals in the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (84 FR 61352).
In the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (84 FR 61339 through 61350), we finalized a proposal to use the calculated CY 2020 CMHC geometric mean per diem cost and the calculated CY 2020 hospital-based PHP geometric mean per diem cost, but with a cost floor equal to the CY 2019 final geometric mean per diem costs as the basis for developing the CY 2020 PHP APC per diem rates. Also, we continued to designate a portion of the estimated 1.0 percent hospital outpatient outlier threshold specifically for CMHCs, consistent with the percentage of projected payments to CMHCs under the OPPS, excluding outlier payments.
In the April 30, 2020 interim final rule with comment (85 FR 27562 through 27566), effective as of March 1, 2020 and for the duration of the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency (PHE), hospital and CMHC staff were permitted to furnish certain outpatient therapy, counseling, and educational services (including certain PHP services), incident to a physician's services, to beneficiaries in temporary expansion locations, including the beneficiary's home, as long as the location met all conditions of participation to the extent not waived. A hospital or CMHC could furnish such services using telecommunications technology to a beneficiary in a temporary expansion location if that beneficiary was registered as an outpatient. In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 72247), we confirmed that these provisions applied only for the duration of the COVID-19 PHE. On May 11, 2023, the COVID-19 PHE ended, and accordingly, these flexibilities ended as well.
In the CY 2021 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (85 FR 86073 through 86080), we continued our current methodology to utilize cost floors, as needed. In the CY 2022 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (86 FR 63665 and 63666), as a result of the COVID-19 PHE, we finalized our proposal to calculate the PHP per diem costs using the year of claims consistent with the calculations that would be used for other OPPS services, by using the CY 2019 claims and the cost reports that were used for CY 2021 final rulemaking to calculate the CY 2022 PHP per diem costs. In addition, for CY 2022 and subsequent years, we finalized our proposal to use cost and charge data from the Hospital Cost Report Information System (HCRIS) as the source for the CMHC cost-to-charge ratios (CCRs), instead of using the Outpatient Provider Specific File (OPSF) (86 FR 63666).
In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 71995), we finalized our proposal to use the latest available CY 2021 claims but use the cost information from prior to the COVID-19 PHE for calculating the CY 2023 CMHC and hospital-based PHP APC per diem costs. The application of the OPPS standard methodology, including the effect of budget neutralizing all other OPPS policy changes unique to CY 2023, resulted in the final calculated CMHC PHP APC payment rate being unexpectedly lower than the CY 2022 final CMHC PHP APC rate. Therefore, we finalized utilizing the equitable adjustment authority of section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act to appropriately pay for CMHC PHP services at the same payment rate as for CY 2022, that is, $142.70. In addition, we clarified the payment under the OPPS for new HCPCS codes that designate non-PHP services provided for the purposes of diagnosis, evaluation, or treatment of a mental health disorder and are furnished to beneficiaries in their homes by clinical staff of the hospital that would not be recognized as PHP services; however, none of the PHP regulations would preclude a patient that is under a PHP plan of care from receiving other reasonable and medically necessary non-PHP services from a hospital (87 FR 72001 and 72002).
In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (88 FR 81811), we revised the regulation at § 424.24(e)(1)(i) to require the physician certification for PHP services to include a certification that the patient requires such services for a minimum of 20 hours per week, as required by section 1861(ff)(1) of the Act, as amended by section 4124(a) of Division FF of the CAA, 2023. In addition, we modified the regulations for PHP at § 410.43 to include references to SUD. In the same CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we also established separate payment rates for PHP days with 3 services and days with 4 or more services. Accordingly, we established four separate PHP APC per diem payment rates: one for CMHCs for 3-service days and another for CMHCs for 4-service days (APC 5853 and APC 5854, respectively), and one for hospital-based PHPs for 3-service days and another for hospital-based PHPs for 4-service days (APC 5863 and APC 5864, respectively). We also finalized a policy to utilize the separate CMHC rates for 3-service and 4-service PHP days as the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS) rates, depending upon whether a nonexcepted off-campus hospital outpatient department furnishes three or four PHP services in a day. Lastly, we finalized several changes beginning in CY 2024 to align coding, billing, and payment between PHPs and intensive outpatient programs.
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53770 through 53780), we modified the payment rate methodology for calculation of CMHC costs for PHP. We applied the 40 percent MPFS Relativity Adjuster to the hospital-based PHP costs to determine the CMHC costs for PHP.
2. Intensive Outpatient Program Services
Section 4124(b) of the CAA, 2023, amended section 1861(ff) of the Act, establishing Medicare coverage for intensive outpatient services effective for items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2024. An intensive outpatient program (IOP) is a distinct and organized program of psychiatric services for individuals who have an acute mental illness, which includes, but is not limited to, conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, and SUD. Intensive outpatient services are not required to be provided in lieu of inpatient hospitalization. Section 1861(ff)(4) of the Act defines intensive outpatient services as the items and services described in section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act prescribed by a physician for an individual determined (not less ( printed page 70563) frequently than every other month) by a physician to have a need for such services for a minimum of 9 hours per week and provided under a program described in paragraph (3) under the supervision of a physician pursuant to an individualized, written plan of treatment established and periodically reviewed by a physician (in consultation with appropriate staff participating in such program), which plan sets forth the physician's diagnosis, the type, amount, frequency, and duration of the items and services provided under the plan, and the goals for treatment under the plan. Section 1861(ff)(2) of the Act describes the items and services included in intensive outpatient services. Section 1861(ff)(4)(C) of the Act specifies that an IOP is a program furnished by a hospital to its outpatients, by a CMHC, by a Federally qualified health center (FQHC), or by a rural health clinic (RHC) as distinct and organized intensive ambulatory treatment service, offering less than 24-hour-daily care, in a location other than an individual's home or inpatient or residential setting. Section 1861(ff)(3)(B) of the Act defines a CMHC for purposes of this benefit. We refer readers to sections 1833(t)(1)(B)(i), 1833(t)(2)(B), 1833(t)(2)(C), and 1833(t)(9)(A) of the Act and 42 CFR 419.21, for additional information regarding IOP.
In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (88 FR 81812 through 81857), we established payment and program requirements for the IOP benefit furnished by a hospital to its outpatients, or by a CMHC, an FQHC, or an RHC. In addition, we established Medicare Part B coverage for IOP services provided by Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) for the treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD).
Consistent with the statutory definition of intensive outpatient services under section 1861(ff)(4) of the Act, we finalized regulations at 42 CFR 410.44 to set forth the conditions and exclusions applicable for intensive outpatient services, and at § 424.24 to set forth the content of the certification and plan of treatment requirements for intensive outpatient services. We also revised certain existing regulations at §§ 410.2, 410.3, 410.10, 410.27, 410.150, and 419.21 to add a regulatory definition of intensive outpatient services and to include intensive outpatient services in the regulations for medical and other health services paid for under Medicare Part B, and in the case of § 419.21, under the OPPS. Additionally, we created regulations at § 410.111 to establish the requirements for coverage of IOP services furnished in CMHCs, and at § 410.173 to establish conditions of payment for IOP services furnished in CMHCs. Lastly, we revised § 410.155 to exclude IOP services from the outpatient mental health treatment limitation, consistent with the statutory requirement of section 1833(c)(2) of the Act, as amended by section 4124(b)(3) of the CAA, 2023.
In addition, as discussed in greater detail in the following sections, we established coding, billing, and payment policies for IOP that align with the policies established for PHP provided in the same settings. Specifically, we established four separate IOP APC per diem payment rates at the same rates we proposed for the PHP APCs: one for CMHCs for 3-service days and another for CMHCs for 4-service days (APC 5851 and APC 5852, respectively), and one for hospital-based IOPs for 3-service days and another for hospital-based IOPs for 4-service days (APC 5861 and APC 5862, respectively). Similar to the policy finalized for PHP, we finalized a policy to utilize the CMHC rates for 3-service and 4-service IOP days as the MPFS rates, depending upon whether a nonexcepted hospital outpatient department furnishes three or four IOP services in a day.
For IOP services provided by an RHC or FQHC, we established a three-service per day payment rate based on the same rate as APC 5861, which is the three-service hospital-based IOP rate (§ 405.2462(j)). In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we established a four or more services per day payment rate for an IOP provided by an RHC or FQHC based on the same rate as APC 5862, which is the four or more services hospital-based IOP rate (89 FR 98017 and 98018). Information regarding payment policies for IOP services furnished by FQHCs and RHCs, including information regarding CY 2027 policies for those settings, can be found in the CY 2027 PFS final rule, which is published elsewhere in the Federal Register .
Furthermore, in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we established a payment adjustment for IOPs provided by an OTP based on three times the payment rate for APC 5861 beginning in CY 2024 (§ 410.67(d)(4)(i)(F)). We finalized regulations at § 410.67(d)(4)(ii) to add that the payment amount for OTP intensive outpatient services will be geographically adjusted using the Geographic Adjustment Factor (GAF) described in § 414.26. Lastly, we amended § 410.67(d)(4)(iii) to add that payment for OTP intensive outpatient services is updated annually using the Medicare Economic Index described in § 405.504(d). Payment rates for IOP provided in the OTP setting are updated as part of the OTP fee schedule and are not addressed in this final rule with comment period.
In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53770 through 53780), we modified the payment rate methodology for calculation of CMHC costs for IOP. We applied the 40 percent MPFS Relativity Adjuster to the hospital-based IOP costs to determine the CMHC costs for IOP.
B. Coding and Billing for PHP and IOP Services Under the OPPS
In the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a billing requirement that all providers use condition code 41 to indicate that a claim is for partial hospitalization services and use condition code 92 to identify intensive outpatient claims, effective January 1, 2024. Since the statutory definitions of both IOP and PHP generally include the same types of items and services covered, we stated in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period that we believe it is appropriate to align the programs using a consistent list of services, so that level of intensity would be the only differentiating factor between partial hospitalization services and intensive outpatient services. The use of condition codes 41 for PHP claims and 92 for IOP claims allows us to differentiate between these services for billing purposes.
We recognize that the level of intensity of mental health services that a patient requires may vary over time; therefore, we believe utilizing a consolidated list of HCPCS codes to identify services under both the IOP and PHP benefits supports a smooth transition for patients when a change in the intensity of their services is necessary to best meet their needs. For example, a patient receiving IOP services may experience an acute mental health need that necessitates more intense services through a PHP. Alternatively, an IOP patient that no longer requires the level of intensity provided by the IOP can access less intense mental health services, such as individual mental health services. The full list of HCPCs codes recognized under the PHP and IOP benefits can be found in the Medicare Claims Processing internet Only Manual, Chapter 4, sections 260.1 and 261.1, respectively, and their subsections, available at https://www.cms.gov/​regulations-and-guidance/​guidance/​manuals/​downloads/​clm104c04.pdf.
To qualify for payment for the IOP APC (5851, 5852, 5861, or 5862) or the PHP APC (5853, 5854, 5863, or 5864), ( printed page 70564) one service provided that day must be from the Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient Primary list. We refer readers to the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period for further discussion regarding our expectation that at least one of the services on the PHP and IOP Primary list will be indicated per day for patients who need the level of care offered by a PHP or IOP program. The PHP and IOP Primary List can be found in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period at 88 FR 81821.
Beginning in CY 2024, we recognized caregiver training services and Principal Illness Navigation (PIN) services as PHP and IOP services. We explained that the reported costs associated with providing such services are included when we calculate the PHP and IOP payment rates; however, these services do not count toward the determination of whether a PHP or IOP day is paid at the 3-service or 4-service rate. We refer readers to the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period for a detailed discussion of this policy (88 FR 81823 through 81825).
As finalized in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (88 FR 81821 and 81822), if new codes are established that represent the PHP and IOP services described under §§ 410.43(a)(4) and 410.44(a)(4), respectively, such codes are added to the list of codes recognized for payment for PHP or IOP through sub-regulatory guidance. We note that coding updates frequently occur outside of the standard rulemaking timeline. We adopted this sub-regulatory process to pay expeditiously when new codes are created that describe any of the services enumerated at §§ 410.43(a)(4) and 410.44(a)(4), which PHPs and IOPs, respectively, would provide. We explained that this policy applies to new codes that are cross walked to a previously included code, or whose code descriptor is substantially similar to a descriptor for a code on the list or describes a service on the list. We stated that any additional services not described at § 410.43(a)(4) or § 410.44(a)(4) would be added to the lists in regulation through notice and comment rulemaking.
In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (89 FR 94266 through 94268) and CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53770 through 53780), we did not add any new services not described at § 410.43(a)(4) or § 410.44(a)(4) to the list of PHP and IOP services.
We did not propose to add any new services to the list of PHP and IOP services for CY 2027. The following is a summary of the comments we received regarding these policies and our responses.
Comment: A few commenters expressed support for the PHP and IOP list of services, the two-tiered structure based on the number of services per day, and the consolidated list of HCPCS codes for PHP and IOP services.
Response: We appreciate commenters' support.
Comment: A commenter expressed support for our coding policies for occupational therapy services furnished in PHPs and IOPs, noting that these policies reinforce the importance of occupational therapy services in PHPs and IOPs. This commenter stated that providers misinterpret program requirements regarding reporting, documentation, and integration of OT services in PHP and IOP and requested that CMS clarify billing compliance and reimbursement guidelines to improve beneficiary access to OT services. This commenter also advocated for including measures specific to occupational therapy in quality reporting programs. They further stated that caregiver training and PIN services should count toward the determination of whether a PHP or IOP day is paid at the 3-service or 4-service rate.
Response: We thank the commenter for their support of our coding policies for occupational therapy services furnished in PHPs and IOPs. We will take the commenter's suggestions into consideration to potentially inform future rulemaking about quality measures. As explained in the CY 2024 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we believe it is appropriate to exclude caregiver-focused services from the determination of the number of services provided per day, but we do include such services in the calculation of cost per day for determining the PHP and IOP payment rates (88 FR 81822).
Comment: A commenter encouraged CMS to ensure that future payment analyses and policy development recognize the resources required to provide comprehensive medication management as part of high-quality behavioral health care and that such services be reimbursed appropriately.
Response: We appreciate the comment regarding the importance of medication management. We agree that medication is an integral part of partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient programs and note that under §§ 410.43(a)(4) and 410.44(a)(4), partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient services include drugs and biologicals furnished for therapeutic purposes (other than drugs that can be self-administered); the services of social workers, trained psychiatric nurses, and other staff trained to work with psychiatric patients (including patients with substance use disorder); and patient training and education, to the extent the training and educational activities are closely and clearly related to the individual's care and treatment. Therefore, payment under the PHP or IOP benefit could include daily monitoring of medication compliance, side effects, and patient education. We further note that existing codes in the list of HCPCS applicable for PHP and IOP, such as CPT code 90792 (Psych diag eval w/med srvcs), include medication management (88 FR 81827 through 81828). We will take the commenter's recommendations into consideration as we consider potential future payment analyses and policy development.
Comment: A commenter stated that providers have communicated to them that the Medicare National Coverage Determination list of group 1 diagnosis codes for PHP or IOP approved for G0129 omits several commonly seen diagnoses including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), complex or prolonged grief diagnoses, borderline personality disorder (BPD), and generalized anxiety disorders (GAD). They requested that CMS include these diagnoses in the list of group 1 diagnosis codes for PHP or IOP approved for G0129.
Response: We thank the commenter for raising the concerns of providers on this topic. There is no National Coverage Determination for G0129. We are aware that there are Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient Services related Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs) and LCD Reference Articles that are developed by our Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs).
